item.title: Silicon Valley Makes Too Much Money, and That's Why California's Government Has No Incentive to Improve
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-allin-硅谷太赚钱-反而让加州政府没有变好的动力/
item.description: California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax revenue is so abundant that the government doesn't need to survive on performance. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.
item.content:encoded:
California has been a one-party state for 16 years — not because voters want big government, but because Silicon Valley's tax revenue is so abundant that the government doesn't need to survive on performance. Gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton says the price is the highest poverty rate, unemployment rate and cost of living in the country.

What's worth listening to are two verifiable causal chains: how Sacramento's bill assembly line has piled up 420,000 regulations, and how Silicon Valley's tax money lets the government skip improving.

5:04 The rules aren't written, they're piled up every year
Hilton gives a countable form to the consequences of one-party rule: Sacramento passed 1,118 bills last year, and when he printed them out, the stack was twice his height — "nobody is reading this." Do you think Gavin Newsom reads them before signing? The result is that California has accumulated more than 420,000 regulations, and he promises to cut that to under 200,000 in his first term. Who are the bills written for? He says for the narrow interest groups that control the process: unions, plaintiff lawyers, and people who donate to politicians. That's why California is the highest litigation-risk place in the country, and starting a company in California has a 90% chance of ending up in court. Structurally, over 16 years Democrats have taken every one of the eight statewide elected offices, a two-thirds majority in the state legislature, every major county and city, and a 6-to-1 majority on the state Supreme Court.

13:08 The key is that 26% of undecided voters
What he offers isn't a "Republicans flip it" story but an arithmetic problem: internal polling at the start of the campaign was 33% firmly for him, 41% firmly for Becerra, 26% undecided. Those 26% are the key — mostly Democratic voters but not die-hards, overwhelmingly non-college-educated working people who are financially maxed out, and their top concern is the cost of living. So the platform is all priceable line items: cancel high-speed rail, cut the government payroll by 10%, stop funding nonprofits that make homelessness worse, and assemble a "first $150,000 exempt from state income tax"; gas goes from $6 toward $3, because the low carbon fuel standard and cap and invest add roughly $150 to the price of gas, and cap and invest money is flowing to high-speed rail; cap the vehicle registration fee at $73 by abolishing the DMV. The polling gap has narrowed from 30 points on primary night to 8 points recently.

19:14 Silicon Valley's money removes the pressure to perform
This is the most counterintuitive part of the whole piece. One host cites Peter Thiel's observation from years ago: Silicon Valley is like a resource curse for California — it generates so much wealth and tax revenue that the state doesn't need a good government, and that's also why one-party rule persists. Hilton adds the evidence: before the primary, Becerra was asked on CNN what policies he would change given homelessness, the highest poverty rate, the highest unemployment rate, and a terrible cost of living. His answer was that it's the world's fourth-largest economy, people still love coming to Disneyland and the beaches, so things must be heading in the right direction. Hilton's rebuttal is that the fourth-largest economy figure includes the size of the government itself — which has doubled in a decade — while net private-sector job creation in California since the pandemic is essentially zero.

23:19 What works is the content, not the AI
Spencer Pratt is running for mayor of Los Angeles as an independent and got a huge amount of free media with a batch of AI-generated videos. He breaks down the mechanism himself: what actually works is what the videos say — he goes on every platform and just tells the truth as he knows it, and then creative people across the country throw ideas into this "machine." "I don't think it's the AI that's working; it's just one piece of the puzzle." He thinks there's evidence for this: most of his voters are Democrats. He also claims that if the 200,000 registered Republicans in Los Angeles had actually turned out, he would have won.

27:21 Taxpayers fund needles handed out in the park
Hilton and Spencer together describe MacArthur Park: last Tuesday at 10:30 a.m., downtown Los Angeles, beautiful sunshine, and in every direction people are smoking crack, injecting drugs, some bent over from fentanyl. The reason is that four nonprofits show up every day to hand out crack pipes, needles and drug supplies, and the money comes from taxpayers. Spencer adds the follow-up: one of the needle distributors was found to be selling drugs at the same time. Hilton stresses this isn't unmanaged — Los Angeles has a new DA cracking down on drugs and crime, and there are federal prosecutors going after gangs and cartels — but the scene in the park is the same every Tuesday.

29:22 Doing right is punished, doing wrong is rewarded
A Latino couple in South LA ran a shoe store for 14 years, the shop was spotless, and they paid taxes, licenses, electricity, and permits that got more expensive every year. They asked Hilton to step outside and look at the sidewalk two blocks away: it was entirely vendors selling shoes, clothes and T-shirts who pay no taxes, no electricity, no rent, no license. That's why the couple is closing. When did it start? In the last six or seven years — in 2018 Sacramento passed a bill legalizing street vending statewide, and cities and counties have no authority over it. His conclusion: here doing right is punished and doing wrong is rewarded, the whole situation is upside down. Spencer adds the numbers: 50,000 food vendors, a permit costs only $21, yet the city council allocated $500,000 to buy them carts, while the unrepaired Palisades reservoir cover would cost only $200,000.

42:32 Ballot collection is legal, so it can't be audited
Spencer's claim is: it's not fake ballots, it's ballot harvesting, which California law allows. The mechanism has three steps: a witness signature can be a smiley face or an X; the same witness can witness 43,000 ballots, and there's no verification allowed; once ballots reach the counting center they're separated from the envelopes, the signatures stay on the envelopes, and the chain of custody is broken — so even if you know who these people are, you can't audit it, and a recount just recounts the same ballots. The other side's rebuttal: voter fraud is a felony and is prosecuted regularly; after Trump lost last time he filed 60 such lawsuits and lost them all. Asked directly whether he believes he lost due to fraud, Spencer's answer is "without evidence I'd say no," and he lists the 200,000 registered Republicans who didn't vote as one reason.

47:35 The empty reservoir and the reconstruction lawsuit
Spencer's house, his parents' house and his neighbors' houses all burned. Reconstruction is stuck on two things. First, that empty reservoir is still empty, even the one across from his house that he thought would never burn is empty, and Palisades is now supplied by a hose dragged all the way from Tanga through regrown dry brush. Second, they're pursuing a mass tort lawsuit with 10,000 victims, against Gavin Newsom's state parks, the city, and the city's water and power department. His chain of allegations: on New Year's Eve there was an 8-acre fire in Pacific Palisades, state parks should have monitored it per the manual but didn't, letting embers smolder into the known high-wind weather of January 6–7; a firefighter whistleblower told him there were visibly smoldering coals on the hillside, and state park employees produced photos in testimony showing smoke on the hillside.

item.title: Individual productivity triples, but company delivery only shrinks from 20 days to 17
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-lightstar-个人提效三倍-公司交付只从20天缩到17天/
item.description: AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.
item.content:encoded:
AI armed everyone, but the organization didn't get faster — because the weakest link isn't people, it's process. The real dividing line is whether you can transform processes and the organization, not whether you hand out tokens to employees.

A frontline CEO talks about building his own CEO AI, canceling weekly meetings, and using token consumption to identify elite performers — the mechanisms and numbers are concrete, and the decision hub section in the second half is the most valuable.

16:07 Individual productivity triples, delivery only speeds up by three days
NetEase did a survey last year: a software requirement, from the product manager receiving it and producing a design draft to the feature going live, averaged 20 working days. After AI coding crossed the inflection point, many engineers doubled or even tripled to quintupled their personal efficiency, some tenfold. But for features of similar scope, the entire process only shrank from 20 days to 17. The reason is that a team completing a complex task is like a barrel: of 20 staves, 10 are engineers, 3 are product, 3 are testing. The engineer and product manager staves rise rapidly, but some staves aren't people — they're processes — and they don't improve at all. So AI adoption must clear three hurdles: cognition, applying it to individuals' short-range tasks, and transforming processes and the organization. The third is the hardest.

20:11 Cancel weekly meetings: AI syncs information, humans only solve problems
Ruan Liang asked friends who run companies whether they still hold weekly meetings; 99% said yes. Weekly meetings usually serve three purposes: sync information, discover problems and opportunities, and make decisions. Previously they held 2.5-hour weekly meetings, but the time spent on this meeting could be ten times 2.5 hours — every department prepared materials layer by layer, and information sync itself wasn't done well, because no one listened attentively the whole time and might miss a sentence relevant to them. After the reform: the general manager and management agreed on what information was needed, everyone filled in a template and stored it in the knowledge base, and AI scanned and integrated it into a focused, interactive HTML report where people could leave comments and follow-up questions; an AI agent produced a preliminary list of problems and opportunities, which human brains confirmed and supplemented; solving problems and making decisions became dedicated meetings.

28:20 SaaS isn't dead, but ordinary SaaS will die
Ruan Liang doesn't think SaaS is dead: SaaS is essentially Service, and Service always exists, just in different forms — AI as a Service and Agent as a Service are themselves software. But ordinary SaaS may indeed die; truly good SaaS that has entered a company's critical processes will instead get better and better, because it becomes internal infrastructure. Previously humans used software, limited by time and energy; in the future, a large number of Agents will call databases, APIs, security APIs, review APIs, HR APIs, CRM APIs — call volumes far exceeding the number and actions of humans, which will increase dramatically, and the more it's called, the more entrenched it becomes. The premise is that this Service itself is critical enough within the enterprise.

32:21 Distill top salespeople into skills and distribute to everyone
Bosses have two headaches: the sales team has only one or two strong performers and the rest are mediocre; or a salesperson is too strong — what if they leave? Previously there was no solution, but now you can distill or extract the actions, scripts, and behaviors of good salespeople into skills. Two uses: distribute them to other salespeople for direct use; and let AI turn elite salespeople into teachers to train ordinary salespeople. What training should distill isn't the salesperson, it's the customer — take the customer interaction data (calls, WeChat, emails, etc.) that salespeople have had contact with, and let AI simulate various customers to train salespeople. Online sales are purely digital and on record; for offline sales, it's recommended or even required to equip them with a recording card, and after a visit, while memory is fresh, record a two-to-three-minute voice memo, because salespeople dislike CRM (they think CRM is for managing them), but they don't mind a recording card, because it's also useful for their own customer review.

44:31 Fewer middle managers, strong individuals lead Agent legions back to the front line
Ruan Liang judges that middle managers will become fewer and fewer, but not necessarily eliminated — rather, they'll go to the front line, and the front line can also lead a bunch of agents. Middle managers with management responsibilities will become fewer and fewer, while elite individuals with strong skills will become more and more. He gives the example of an engineering team: previously, socialized division of labor made software development more and more specialized — front-end, back-end, algorithm, test engineers; in the past half year, it has clearly reverted to full-stack, everyone becoming full-end engineers. In the future, organizations will increasingly resemble a distributed structure, with countless highly capable engineers, one mother peak commanding some engineers, and countless agents fighting a battle. He envisions a future interview negotiation scenario: a candidate says, "I'm not one person, I bring an AI team, a summary of all my past experience and skills," and the premium the company pays might be some kind of OPC.

50:35 AI value formula: quality times time saved
Ruan Liang gives a formula referencing a paper: AI value = quality of AI completing the task (as a ratio of human quality) × time saved × the company's economic value per unit time. For example, a human makes a cup of coffee at 8 points, AI also makes it at 8 points, so the quality coefficient is 1; a human takes 20 minutes, AI takes only 10 seconds, saving 14 minutes 50 seconds; multiply by the company's economic value per unit time, and you can calculate ROI. Prioritize four types of tasks for AI: time-consuming, high-frequency, unavoidable, and tasks where different people produce roughly the same result. Once calculated, you can immediately decide whether to use AI. He also suggests first using the most expensive AI (Claude, GPT) to prove the task can be done, solidify the process, then switch to cheaper ones — if the most expensive can do it, within two months the cheaper ones can too.

59:40 Token consumption leads by a landslide, output also leads by a landslide
NetEase started a points system in 2024, trying to quantify engineers' work tasks into points with work value. By the AI era, they found a group of people whose token consumption was astonishing, and whose work output and work value were also astonishing, forming a statistical pattern: people whose token consumption leads by a landslide are most likely building systems for themselves, saving their own work time and increasing thinking time, so their work quality and results also lead by a landslide. Many bosses worry about AI abuse causing waste; Ruan Liang's hot take is that truly excellent or elite people won't waste — the company has audits but doesn't tell colleagues, and through statistics they found elite colleagues didn't waste. He also says small companies are more likely to fully embrace AI, because there are fewer organizational relationships, the boss uses it first, there are fewer layers, and the chain is shorter.

1:11:50 The core of a decision hub is decision history, not the model
Building an AI decision hub essentially requires a high-quality knowledge base, and what really matters is the historical decision-making process and decision basis. This year NetEase preserved historical decisions, incorporated them into the knowledge base, combined the two types of knowledge to train an agent or skill, then fed back hundreds of original cases for the agent to judge, achieving over 90% accuracy. Ruan Liang also mentions that Bridgewater Associates equipped researchers and analysts with agents they built themselves, precipitating the decision-making process and decision history into a decision knowledge base; what Bridgewater did better was making the agent a learnable, evolvable part — after a person adjusts it, the confirmed adjustment actions enter the next round of reinforcement, keeping pace with the times, equivalent to human-machine collaborative self-evolution.

item.title: Mooncakes Sell Only Two Months a Year, Yet Build a 28.2 Billion Yuan Business
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-23-beiwanglu-月饼一年只卖两个月-却做成了282亿的生意/
item.description: Bound to Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are trapped in a short sales window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gift-giving scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.
item.content:encoded:
Bound to Mid-Autumn Festival, mooncakes are trapped in a short sales window, but the 28.2 billion yuan scale comes from gift-giving scenarios and flexible custom production lines, not from flavor innovation.

Worth listening for food industry practitioners and those wanting to understand holiday consumer business, but information density is low, with much time spent on explaining factions and flavors, while the business mechanics are concentrated in the middle and later sections.

6:06 Zongzi can be sold year-round, mooncakes cannot
Zongzi is tied to Dragon Boat Festival, but after vacuum-sealing for long shelf life, it can be sold all year round. Wufangzhai even opened restaurants to put zongzi into daily scenarios. The problem with mooncakes is not that the craft cannot achieve long shelf life, but that it is defined as a "traditional festival pastry mainly eaten during Mid-Autumn Festival," and the national standard GB19855 directly writes the season into the definition. So for the same festival food, zongzi can decouple from the festival through shelf life and channels, but mooncakes cannot.

12:12 National standard draws hard lines for fillings
Lotus seed paste mooncakes must have at least 60% lotus seed content, fruit mooncakes must have at least 25% fruit products, and five-kernel mooncakes must use walnut kernels, almond kernels, olive kernels, melon seed kernels, and sesame seeds. The purpose of this line is to raise ingredient costs and prevent cheap candied winter melon, green and red shreds, and inferior nuts from being used as fillers. For consumers, the order of ingredients on the label can indicate how much is used.

26:30 Why custard lava mooncakes are made so small
Custard lava mooncakes are small not because of stinginess, but because of structure. They have a flaky crust outside, a custard layer in the middle, and a lava layer at the center. The custard layer acts as a moisture barrier. Production requires two rounds of baking to keep the lava semi-solid, and the melting point of the lava must be designed—solid during transport, and after a few seconds in the microwave, it becomes a flowing liquid. If overheated, the lava is absorbed by the crust, and it reverts to an ordinary custard mooncake.

37:34 Five prerequisites for everything to become mooncake
Not everything can be stuffed into a mooncake. First is water content: hot and sour soup mooncake cannot be made because there is too much water to wrap. Second is safety: meat, eggs, and dairy are also loved by microorganisms, so processing temperature and sterilization processes must be repeatedly tested. Third is particle size: too large and the crust cannot hold it, too fine and it cannot be tasted. Fourth is flavor restoration after high-temperature baking: some aromas disappear after baking. Fifth is whether the cost can be handled. So long-term stable flavors are confirmed by generations.

44:40 Choosing an OEM is not about the biggest
When big brands make brand mooncakes and look for OEMs, there is a common misconception: they must choose the best OEM in China. But the production scale of top OEMs actually does not match yours. Indicators that can be screened include registered capital, tax payment records, number of employees with social security contributions, and accumulated safe production days. In addition, the nine major factions correspond to different factories; it is impossible to have Guangzhou Restaurant produce Shanxi egg-skin mooncakes, as they do not have the capability or production line.

48:44 Flexible production lines can take orders of a few hundred boxes
Mooncake production is semi-automated and semi-manual. The wrapping and shaping machines can do the work, but brushing egg wash, pressing patterns, and stamping require manual labor, which actually facilitates OEM and customization. Flexible factories can go as small as a few hundred boxes, and can do thousands or tens of thousands of boxes. If a company has only 50 employees, they can directly use the factory's existing mooncakes and only need to design the paper box. This small-order quick-response capability is the core of mooncakes being able to do corporate custom business.

51:47 The 28.2 billion scale is supported by gift-giving
In 2025, China's mooncake production was 518,000 tons, with sales scale of 28.2 billion RMB, both down from the previous year. At 80 grams each, that is about 6.4 billion pieces; at 100 grams, about 5.18 billion pieces. With a population of 1.4 billion, that averages three to four pieces per person. In comparison, Dragon Boat Festival zongzi annual sales scale is about 10 to 11 billion, and instant noodles about 68 to 120 billion. Mooncakes selling only two months a year to achieve 28.2 billion is core to gift-giving attributes—brands prepare large amounts of PR gifts at the two nodes of Chinese New Year and Mid-Autumn Festival, and zongzi's gift-giving attribute is far weaker than mooncakes.

58:55 499 yuan is a number forced by regulatory line
In 2022, the National Development and Reform Commission and three other departments jointly issued an announcement to implement key supervision on boxed mooncakes priced over 500 yuan per unit. So the highest price of mooncakes on the market is 499. The calculation logic is: a box of mooncakes costs about 70 yuan per box, plus channel deductions and shared expenses, it cannot exceed 500 yuan. In the past when the economy was good, there were sky-high mooncakes with very expensive tea or liquor, even wooden gift boxes, and both cost and price were very high.

item.title: AI for Science Is Stuck on the Last 0.001 Points, Not on Compute
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-latentspace-ai-做科学卡在最后-0-001-分-不是卡在算力/
item.description: ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say ‘you got this paper wrong’.
item.content:encoded:
ERA can churn out thousands of candidate notebooks, but it can't close the gap on the last 30 places — because the inner loop is a machine, and the outer loop still needs a human to say ‘you got this paper wrong’.

High information density, but it takes a little patience: the first half covers ERA's mechanics, the second half covers contrails, wildfires and quantum computing, all first-hand detail.

9:24 ERA's input is a chat, its output is a scored notebook
ERA's product form isn't having people write config files — you just start chatting. Because mapping a scientific problem onto a scorable task is itself non-obvious, Michael Brenner wrote a dedicated agent that conversationally helps you define which score to optimize. When the conversation ends, a Python notebook is generated underneath, containing a function that produces a score, and then the system starts mutating that notebook in a ‘clever way’, continually proposing new code to push the score higher.

10:24 It doesn't always pick the best candidate
ERA runs Monte Carlo Tree Search internally, keeping hundreds or thousands of notebook candidates alive at once, with the candidate pool arranged as a tree. Selection uses the upper confidence bound from reinforcement learning: estimate the 95th percentile outcome of a mutation and pick the one with the highest optimistic upper bound. So it isn't always greedily choosing the currently best-performing notebook; sometimes it picks the fifth-best, in order to explore more efficiently. It has also tried combining the ideas of two candidates to generate a third.

18:38 Evolutionary coding was stuck for decades because random mutation is useless
Platt says evolutionary coding goes back to the 1970s — mutating Lisp code and so on — but it never took off, because random mutation in code space is basically worthless: just like DNA, the vast majority of mutations are harmful. ERA works because the inner loop is itself an AI that knows which direction to try, which amounts to having a meaningful gradient underneath. The price is that it also overfits, and it also goes off the rails in ‘genie wish’ fashion.

22:44 Predictive models and descriptive models are two different things
John Platt splits scientific modeling into two kinds: a predictive model only seeks the lowest error rate on some dataset; a descriptive model is what science actually wants, because it contains some description of reality inside it, and therefore can extrapolate. His example is Newton: an apple falling can be fitted, but gravity isn't about apples — take a model that only fits apples and ask it about planets, and it has no planetary data, so it knows nothing. He admits the line is blurry, because the scientist themself also brings a pile of known facts and intuitions to constrain the model.

31:59 This is a power tool, and it will cut your fingers off
Faced with multiple hypothesis testing and overfitting, Platt's answer isn't a new method but a harsher version of an old one: because ERA is a power tool, you have to be stricter than before, with a holdout hidden so deep you never look at it yourself. He states plainly that no system yet discovers entirely new physics or entirely new science, and that scientists are still responsible for judging whether a conclusion is descriptive.

39:18 AI is stuck on the last 0.001 points
Ira pushed the score very close, but it couldn't close the last 30 places or so, because nobody goes and scrapes out that final 0.001 points. This exposes the system's real structure: the inner layer is a machine running for hours to produce candidates, and the outer layer is a human making judgments like ‘you got this paper wrong’. Platt compares it to a graduate student who never sleeps and is extremely eager — you tell it a direction, it goes and tries, but when it gets stuck a human has to change the approach.

48:08 The counterfactual model stalled the team for two years
To judge which contrail to avoid, you need to know how much warming it actually causes, and that's a counterfactual problem: you can't enter the universe where the contrail doesn't exist. The team built a version of the counterfactual model that worked for outgoing longwave radiation, but they could never build one for the part that reflects sunlight, and it stalled them for two years. They even self-tested with a dataset where contrails were artificially injected, and their own attempt couldn't pass their own test. In the end ERA found a simple model that searches over all confounders, passed the test, and cracked the problem.

1:24:27 A wildfire is best put out before it's room-sized
Google has a crisis resilience effort, and one project in it is called Firesat: a wildfire is extremely easy to extinguish when it's only as big as ‘this room’, and once it reaches an acre it's far harder, while the growth from room size to an acre may be exponential. The plan is a low-Earth-orbit satellite constellation using mid-wave IR (which corresponds to blackbody radiation, exactly the temperature of fire) for detection; roughly 50 to 80 satellites could cover the globe, spot a fire about 5 meters across, and raise an alarm within 15 to 20 minutes. The partner is the nonprofit Earth Fire Alliance, the satellites are built by Muon Space, and one prototype has already launched.

item.title: Trump Invites Xi to a Show. What Did the US Get in Return?
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-chinatalk-特朗普请习近平看戏-美国换到了什么实质东西/

item.description: This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question isn't whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.
item.content:encoded:
This state visit has almost no substantive agenda — it is pure symbolism and optics. The question isn't whether something goes wrong, but what the US is trading symbolism for in substance. So far: nothing.

The first half covers the summit and US-China relations; the middle and later sections on China after Xi and fifty years since Mao's death are denser with information and worth the listen.

6:06 This visit has no substantive agenda at all
Gewirtz's judgment is that this state visit has "there is not a very deep substantive agenda at all." Trump invited Xi mainly because he wants to put on a show, wants the pomp and the cameras, and incidentally wants to push issues like the Iran war out of the news. For Beijing, this actually makes them less nervous — because if it were a more confrontational meeting, they would be more anxious. But Gewirtz flags two things: Trump himself is extremely unpredictable, and Beijing has internalized that; and Beijing, watching the chaos in Washington, sees the American president himself often in a position they would never want Xi to be in — going to the wrong place, being photographed in unflattering images, being pressed by reporters. So the real question is not whether someone deliberately sets a trap, but whether they slip into the scenario they are trying hardest to avoid.

9:25 Symbolism for substance: where is the trade
Gewirtz characterizes this visit as "we are in a space of symbolism and optics." He says that in US-China relations, trading symbolism for substance is itself a reasonable play: give Beijing the pomp and cameras it craves, and get back something concretely useful to Americans and American interests. That was the model for US relations with the Soviets during the Cold War and after — the US gave symbolism, legitimacy and that handshake photo, and got a concession in return on a Third World country or a nuclear issue. But the problem this time is that the Trump administration doesn't even seem to have tried to design a set of "deliverables." Gewirtz says "it doesn't even seem like they're trying." So what to watch is not where something goes wrong, but "where is the trade happening."

11:37 The direction of concessions has been flipped entirely
Gewirtz points to a counterintuitive dynamic: concessions the US might once have given China have been flipped into "gifts" from China to the US. Pomp and cameras were what Beijing wanted, but in Washington they are treated as Xi's visit being a concession to the US. The same flip happens on advanced semiconductors: the US used not to sell these things, and opening up products like the H200 would have been a huge concession; now, if Beijing agrees to buy, many in Washington would see it as Beijing conceding to Trump. Gewirtz says this flip keeps recurring, and the reason it matters is not to score the administration but because it reflects what happens when the power gap in superpower competition narrows — very small differences, interpersonal dynamics, can produce much larger displacements in the overall strategic picture.

12:39 US-China relations are also K-shaped, held up by the upper leg
Gewirtz uses the "K-shaped" idea for US-China relations: one upward leg is the leader-level channel —密集 mutual visits, friendship, cameras; one downward leg is the competitive reality and the actions parts of both governments keep taking. The system is currently held up by the upward leg, but it is very fragile. He stresses the metaphor is not just a parallel analogy: saying "truce" or "detente" sounds too static, like a state already reached, but US-China relations are actually quite dynamic, quite unstable, moving in two directions at once. He applies the same K-shaped logic to China's economy — manufacturing and AI are flying, real estate and consumer demand are struggling, the upward leg is pulling the whole system forward, and the question is whether it can keep holding as the K widens.

22:03 The bipartisan consensus on China policy has shattered
Gewirtz argues that Trump changed the tone of America's China discussion in the 2016 election and became the symbol and standard-bearer of that turn; but now, after helping create that turn, he has helped destroy or transform it. He cites David Feith's article in the Reagan Institute on "a new cold war in an age of doubt" — that great rethink on China was not as great as many assumed. Gewirtz's conclusion: if the political dynamics are more complicated than imagined and the bipartisan consensus some people talk about doesn't exist, then this is a moment of "incredible fluidity." He says he has no confidence in the direction of either Democratic or Republican China policy in the medium term, and Beijing has no confidence either.

31:24 Chinese officials can't talk about risks they have no solution for
Gewirtz offers a different read on how the US should interpret Chen Yixin's article. On the surface, Americans are panicking about existential risk and China is panicking about regime security, and that's right. But he says: heads of American AI model companies can talk at length about risks they have no solution for — all of them do it; China's minister of state security cannot. In China, when you point out a risk in public, you are simultaneously saying "we the Communist Party see it, we will handle it, we have a solution." So the real question is: should we treat what we can see from Beijing as everything, or acknowledge there is more in the system that we cannot see. He gives an example from 25 years ago — Americans then predicted the internet would cause regime change in China, Clinton said that was like nailing Jell-O to the wall, and Beijing did in fact nail the Jell-O to the wall, namely the firewall.

35:37 Beijing hasn't decided how to regulate open models
Gewirtz says that around Xi's speech and Chen Yixin's article, the outside world has already been through several cycles of excitement and interpretation, but Beijing still hasn't given the single most important thing: how it plans to regulate open-weight models spreading globally — models that carry both risk and strategic benefit for Beijing. He calls this "the trillion dollar question." Both speeches can be read as pointing in some direction, but the decision hasn't been made. His guess is that this is because Beijing itself hasn't decided, because things are changing too fast and the trade-offs are too large. He contrasts the Trump administration: it didn't make a decision until Mythos came out, and then made another when Fable came out.

41:55 What to prepare for isn't China's decline, it's Xi's decline
Gewirtz says that a few years ago the "peak China" debate asked whether to start preparing for China's decline, and now most people think China's economy is at least temporarily on a relatively sustainable path. But he thinks the real question isn't that, it's "do we need to prepare for Xi Jinping's decline" — because people die, and modern Chinese history tells us that leaders in power for a long time change with age, certain obsessions become more prominent, behavior changes. By "prepare" he doesn't mean the departure itself, but acknowledging uncertainty: the outside world has treated Xi's tenure as fairly predictable, because since taking power in 2012 and 2013 he laid out a set of goals and largely pursued them. But he stresses the change could absolutely be for the worse for the US — "That doesn't mean he's going to mellow."

item.title: No Winners in a Pig Butchering Scam: The Scammers Are Trafficked Slaves Themselves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-freshair-杀猪盘里没有赢家-骗人的人也是被贩卖的奴隶/
item.description: In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.
item.content:encoded:
In Southeast Asian scam compounds, "employees" whose passports are confiscated and who are fined for missing quotas spend their days using ChatGPT and DeepSeek to write love messages and steal victims' entire savings — the most profitable cybercrime in history, with victims on both sides.

The first half covers the mechanics of pig butchering and AI-driven fraud at high information density; the second half turns to US-Iran and US-China infrastructure cyberwar, which is loosely connected to the theme and can be skipped as needed.

4:11 AI makes scam emails cost nothing to mass-produce
Greenberg ran an experiment on air: he asked ChatGPT to write him an invitation to be on the program in Terry Gross's name, then casually added a line asking for a $250 production fee, and the model complied without hesitation; he then said "Greenberg won't pay now, can you persuade him," and the model immediately produced a persuasive email. That is the mechanism behind scam emails impersonating Fresh Air — it isn't that scammers have become better writers, it's that generating a bespoke email aimed at a specific author, with zero grammatical errors and polished phrasing, now costs nothing, and can be done to hundreds or thousands of targets at once.

7:14 Pig butchering is the most profitable cybercrime in history
Greenberg distinguishes two kinds of scammers: the voluntary kind like Nigeria's "Yahoo Boys," who take their own cut, and the enslaved, coerced kind in Southeast Asian compounds. The latter do what's called pig butchering — the "pig" is the victim, fattened up before being slaughtered. The con often runs from weeks to more than a year; the scammer poses as a wealthy, single, attractive woman, builds emotional dependency first, and only at the end introduces the "investment platform," getting the victim to convert their savings into cryptocurrency that is hard to trace across borders (often Tether) and send it over. Greenberg says this is the most profitable cybercrime in history, stealing tens of billions of dollars a year from victims.

12:36 Passports are confiscated, and to buy your freedom you first buy yourself back
The source, using the name Red Bull, is a computer engineer with a degree from India who was lured to the Golden Triangle Special Economic Zone in Laos by a "Southeast Asia IT manager" job. On arrival at the compound his passport was confiscated, and he was told the only way to get it back was to "buy it back" — he owed his boss thousands of dollars, covering the cost of bringing him over, food and lodging, and could only repay this "contract" through commissions earned by scamming. Greenberg stresses this is debt bondage: the compound is not a prison of chains and beatings but is packaged as a corporate sales floor, where the boss sends daily motivational messages saying things like "reach out to the next client like you're going to change their life" and "we are on a mission."

14:40 Fines are steadier than wages
Red Bull and his colleagues were constantly fined: for missing contact quotas, for not maintaining fake accounts well enough, for not showing up on time. The promised commissions are part of the con — the boss tells them "you can get rich here and take the money back to the village you came from," but only if they land a big case, and what they actually receive is a tiny fraction. Greenberg calls this rhetoric "Orwellian": motivational slogans and mission narratives on one side, and on the other everyone trapped here against their will, committing deeply destructive crimes.

15:45 Video calls run on a dedicated face-swap model
Red Bull says everyone in the compound was trained to use ChatGPT and the Chinese AI chatbot DeepSeek to come up with new topics, polish their language, never run out of graceful phrasing, even write little motivational poems, and find just the right goodnight line. More critical is video: the boss instructs them to discourage victims from video calls as much as possible and to stall with excuses; when stalling fails, the compound has a dedicated room and a model who does video all day, using face-swap software to change the model's face into the photo originally sent to the victim. Greenberg says this software isn't perfect, but by the video-call stage the victim wants so badly to believe it's real that they overlook the flaws.

18:54 The next step is fully autonomous AI pig butchering
Greenberg's judgment is that AI is currently just a tool for human scammers, but the next step — already starting to appear — is fully autonomous AI fraud. He cites a case from an Anthropic report the previous week: a Chinese group built 20 dating apps populated entirely by AI, where victims must keep paying to continue the conversation, and "most" of the other side are actually fully autonomous large models. He also mentions a study showing that at most stages of the scam process, AI is better than a real person at building relationships — more responsive, more invested, more attentive — and that is precisely what the con is doing for the vast majority of the time before it reaches the endgame of asking for money.

23:08 Thirty people, three months, only $2.2 million
Greenberg gives a concrete scale: Red Bull's group of about 30 people earned only about $2.2 million in total over the three months that Red Bull recorded and leaked to Wired. This shows pig butchering is a game of probability — a single group's output is limited, but Laos alone has dozens of such compounds, with more in Cambodia and Myanmar, and together they add up to the multi-billion-dollar annual scale. Greenberg also notes that Red Bull himself was a "very inefficient scammer," so he was penniless, eating only the compound cafeteria's rice and vegetables that tasted of strange chemicals, constantly sick, and disgusted by what he was doing.

24:12 Forging a police letter to escape, then beaten when it was seen through
Red Bull's escape attempt was to forge a letter from the police in his home state in India, saying he was under investigation and had to return to deal with it or his boss would also be in trouble. Greenberg advised him against it, but he went ahead, and the forgery was immediately seen through. The boss locked him in a room, beat him, kicked him, denied him food, interrogated him, and even gave him a glass of water with white powder dissolved in it and forced him to drink it — Greenberg guesses it was some kind of stimulant, making him talk more while his skin broke out in hives. They never found out he was in contact with a journalist; Greenberg says if they had, he would certainly have been killed.

item.title: Supersonic Passenger Flight Stalled for Fifty Years — the Blocker Was the Engine, Not Aerodynamics
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-allin-超音速客机没落五十年-卡在发动机不在空气动力学/
item.description: Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because its sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.
item.content:encoded:
Concorde was banned not because the technology failed but because its sonic boom hit the ground; Boom uses atmospheric refraction to bend the boom skyward, and the ban goes away. What actually held supersonic back for half a century was the engine — and that engine is now going to data centers to generate power first.

The founder's own account of the full path from being turned down by Bezos to building engines in-house and pivoting to data-center power generation, with specific numbers and regulatory detail, at high information density.

5:12 Bend the sonic boom and the ban disappears
Boom's answer to the sonic boom is not to make the aircraft quiet but to use the atmosphere's own refractive capacity to redirect the boom back up into the sky. Blake calls it boomless cruise; engineers call it Mach cutoff: the boom is still generated at the aircraft as usual, at normal strength, but it bends sharply in the air and never reaches the ground. This works below Mach 1.3 — that is, 50% faster than today. So no full speed over land, but a 9am departure from New York and a 9:30am arrival in San Francisco still holds. Over the ocean nobody is listening, so full speed is allowed. Pushed to its logical extreme, it comes down to this: if there is no sonic boom at all, there is nothing to argue about.

5:12 From executive order to act of Congress, unanimous
The US ban on overland supersonic flight, in place since 1973, ended last June 6. But Blake knew an executive order can in theory be overturned by the next person, so he turned to pushing legislation through Congress. The Supersonic Legalization Act passed the House unanimously and recently cleared a Senate committee unanimously as well. He put the significance plainly: supersonic is not a partisan issue, which is the only way to get that kind of vote count. For a hardware company that has to span multiple administrations on a timeline measured in decades, upgrading regulation from executive order to law turns policy risk from a variable into a constant.

6:12 Getting stood up by a big company saved the company
Blake says one of the dumbest things he ever did was outsource engine development to an established large company; the plan failed, the split with Rolls-Royce was public, and everyone said Boom was finished. So they decided to do what everyone said was impossible: build the engine from scratch in-house, and not just design it — manufacture even the hardest parts, like turbine blades, themselves. His judgment: engineering and manufacturing have to be done together, and if you want to reindustrialize America you have to invent the next generation of manufacturing technology here, not bring back what was offshored to China. That forced choice later became the source of the company's valuation — because an engine designed to run at full power for long periods at the high temperatures of Mach 1.7, with the front fan removed and a generator bolted on the back, is a power-generation device.

8:13 The supersonic engine's first customer is a data center
Boom's engine's first application is not in the sky but on the ground. Take off the fan, put a generator on the back, drop it into a few trailers, and you can do 42 megawatts of behind-the-meter generation — and because the engine core was designed to run at high temperature, it needs no water. Blake pointed out specifically that water is a common objection, so just make it disappear. The factory has already started producing the first parts, with a target of multiple gigawatts a year and more than 10 gigawatts added to the grid over the next five years. The financial point of this path: before the supersonic airliner has its airworthiness certificate, the company already has a product it can sell — and it is selling to the buyer that is least short of money right now.

10:14 Run on the ground first, then fly
Boom putting the engine to work in ground power generation first has an engineering side effect: it will be the most-tested new jet engine in history, because it will have run for enormous numbers of hours on the ground before ever being installed and flown. Blake admits many hard problems remain and success is not guaranteed. The promise to passengers: twice as fast over water, 50% faster over land with no sonic boom. The sequencing itself is worth noting — normally an aviation engine is validated by accumulating flight hours, and Boom has moved validation to the ground and to data-center scenarios, effectively having another market pay the test bill for the aviation business.

10:38 Transatlantic round trip, breakeven fare $3,500
The numbers Blake gives: a Mach 1.7 transatlantic round trip in 3 hours, breakeven fare around $3,500, with the actual price most likely higher, and every extra dollar is United's profit. His assessment of Concorde: zero out of three on safe, comfortable and cheap; Boom intends to take all three. On timeline, the target is 4 years, but he says explicitly that ‘fast matters more than predictable’, cannot give a firm date, and only promises to deliver at the earliest time physically possible — which from the outside looks like around 2030. There is a trade-off worth noting here: a hardware company publicly admitting it is unpredictable, trading certainty for speed.

13:15 Data-center demand is so large they plan to auction it
Asked whether the data-center business is a money printer, Blake's answer is ‘it's the most incredible money-printing business I've ever seen’, and he says his inbox holds tens of gigawatts of demand. The first engine will fire up next month, and then they intend to auction off all of the capacity. Asked whether he has talked to Elon, or whether this is for Colossus, Blake only says ‘you should ask Elon’. The value of this passage is the anomalous supply-demand signal it gives: for a power product not yet in mass production, demand already far exceeds capacity, and the pricing mechanism has gone from a quote to an auction.

16:19 Break the sound barrier Monday, model in the Oval Office Thursday
Blake walked through how fast this regulatory push moved: broke the sound barrier on a Monday, posted it, Elon reposted, flew to Washington that night to start lobbying for legalization, and by the time he landed had an invitation from the White House; into the West Wing on Tuesday, and by Thursday the aircraft model was in the Oval Office — and it is still there. From launch to signature, the executive order took 115 days, which he considers slow but admits would be slower under a different administration. His assessment of this administration: ‘I like that it moves fast’. This is the most concrete policy-operations sample in the whole episode: how a single technical milestone gets converted directly into political attention.

item.title: Why rebranding a charity is more dangerous than rebranding a company
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-masterscale-慈善机构改名-为什么比企业改名更危险/
item.description: Mercy Corps changed its name to Prosper Global not because its strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a name change can put staff more at risk.
item.content:encoded:
Mercy Corps changed its name to Prosper Global not because its strategy changed, but because the old name no longer fit what it was already doing — and in conflict zones, a name change can put staff more at risk.

Medium information density. The first half covers the disaster context and the rebranding logic; the second half, on the erosion of international humanitarian law and AI's entry into aid, is more valuable.

4:21 The name change isn't a strategy shift — the old name can't hold the new business
Jada says an organization's identity grows like a person's. The name Mercy Corps described the starting point of aid — rushing in to save people, handing out food, casting itself as the benevolent giver. But what she now discusses with potential donors is cash assistance, seed insurance, using blockchain for identity management, and the response is blunt: "That has nothing to do with your name." The name change isn't a change of mission; mission and values are the source of continuity, the name is not. Prosper Global wants to shorten the conversation and put values up front: we believe everyone has the capacity to prosper, not just survive.

6:31 Renaming in a conflict zone puts safety on the line
Prosper Global operates in more than 30 countries, many of them remote sub-offices, often in conflict zones. Communities recognize Mercy Corps' colors and know who to look for. Renaming means a phased rollout, country by country, with local people judging the timing and context. Jada is blunt: they don't rate armed guards, they don't carry weapons, and their ability to work rests entirely on the trust of the communities they serve. So this isn't an ordinary corporate logo swap; in the short term it may make frontline staff more at risk. Interestingly, 90% of staff live in the communities they serve, and many program staff were the first to understand the renaming — they don't want to be treated as "charity cases."

8:37 Syria is the best example of the rebranding logic
Jada drove from Aleppo to Damascus and saw rubble the whole way. Syria has just emerged from 14 years of civil war and is one of the few countries in the world where the population is returning rather than leaving, with millions going home at the same time. But many still live in camps, and returning communities have no working water systems and destroyed homes. She tells of a woman named Ola: her husband was injured in the war, she didn't work before the war, and her community wasn't used to women doing certain things, so she was forced to take over the farming and start cultivating. Prosper Global helped her with drip irrigation and repairing the local water system, and in the process she learned to ride a motorcycle and brought along another group of women. Jada says Syria may be one of the world's rare good-news stories, but it has been forgotten.

10:44 Oil in Hormuz decides whether African farmers plant at all
Prosper Global published a report called From Hormuz to Hunger, tracking how conflict in the Strait of Hormuz ripples into six fragile countries: Sudan, Somalia, Ethiopia, Pakistan, Myanmar, and Lebanon. The mechanism is this: these countries depend on Hormuz for basic fuel, and higher fuel prices hit fertilizer supply directly. When Jada was in Sudan, farmers had only a two-to-three-week window to get seeds in the ground, and fuel costs had already risen 60%. When farmers can't figure out what to plant or what inputs they can afford, some decide to abandon the land. This isn't just a problem for now; it cripples next season's food supply too. At the same time, aid organizations themselves are paying higher oil prices, so the same money serves fewer people.

12:47 Ukraine's grain silos are being bombed on purpose
Prosper Global just launched a grain storage project with the UN and the Ukrainian Red Cross. Jada says Ukraine actually had a good harvest this year, but Russia is increasingly targeting civilian and economic infrastructure, especially using drones against grain silos and storage facilities. The logic is direct: even with a good harvest, if silos and storage are bombed out, or roads and ports are bombed so grain can't move, that season's income is gone. This is a deliberate attack on that kind of infrastructure. What they do includes providing sleeved grain storage bags, helping farmers clear mines, and helping those who lost machinery rebuild or find alternatives. Ukraine was once the breadbasket for many countries; it needs that grain to feed itself and its own economy.

14:47 Prevention is seven times cheaper than disaster response, but nobody wants to fund it
Jada says there's a tendency in the current relationship with the US government to do only life-saving aid, which is actually the least efficient approach. Her number: doing prevention, trying to avert a crisis, is about seven times cheaper than intervening afterward. She also notes they had been ready to rename to Prosper Global before the Trump administration took office, but held off to see how things would shake out — funding had already vanished and the whole sector was in a tough spot. Instead they doubled down on helping Americans understand the nature of humanitarian need and what aid looks like today, correcting a lot of misinformation. She says the key to a leadership moment is intentionality: what are you letting go of, and what are you continuing to build on?

19:59 After USAID evaporated, the sector has to rebuild an architecture
Jada acknowledges they have to do more with less money, but stresses this isn't just about saving money — it's about rebuilding an architecture in a sense. USAID's offices and missions around the world used to carry a huge amount of coordination and information-sharing, and now all of that is gone. So the question isn't just "can AI help," but that the sector's entire coordination layer has been pulled out. She says AI can't physically deliver supplies for you and has limits in knowledge, but it's useful at the program level: accessing best practices, more precisely targeting what a community needs, anticipating certain needs. They haven't found that "magic solution" yet, but they're talking with AI companies, hoping to build something together that truly changes humanitarian aid.

23:02 International humanitarian law is eroding, starting with Ukraine
Jada says the checks and balances of international humanitarian law are being tested and violated, and that this is a broader trend. She believes the first case seen as a deliberate pattern was Russia's invasion of Ukraine — attacks on ports, bridges, and other civilian infrastructure traditionally considered untouchable appeared quickly. Then the pattern spread to the way war is waged in Sudan, and they believe violations of international law are also occurring in Gaza. She notes it took the deaths and destruction of millions after World War II to bring these rules into being: no collective punishment, people must be able to go to school and have hospital networks, civilians shouldn't pay the price. Now these rules are being violated everywhere. She says even the phrase "international humanitarian law" sounds like Greek to many people.

item.title: In the AI Era, the Most Valuable Thing Isn't Intelligence — It's the Audit Trail
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ilt-ai-时代最值钱的不是智能-是审计轨迹/
item.description: Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.
item.content:encoded:
Rogo founder Gabe Stengel says models are already smarter than anyone he knows, and what's left is all plumbing — whoever runs the pipes into banks' compliance and systems of record wins.

Worth listening for vertical AI founders, investment banking/PE practitioners, and enterprise software investors. The first half's product history is only moderately dense; the pricing, audit, and sales mechanics in the back half are worth more.

2:03 Model companies are refineries; vertical companies are chemical plants
Gabe reasons from Dario's line: if tomorrow an entire data center full of geniuses appeared at the door of Goldman, Millennium, Citadel, these institutions would still take a long time to figure out how to change the way they work and how to wire it into their systems. So he thinks the biggest challenge for every great investor over the next five years isn't getting access to intelligence, but wiring AI into the investment lifecycle. That's also why he isn't worried about Anthropic and OpenAI: finance is a collection of niches, each with different data, definitions, and regulatory requirements, and for Anthropic to stop and pick up this coin would be pulling over on the road from $100 billion in revenue to $1 trillion.

4:04 Applied AI companies have a first-mover disadvantage
Gabe says companies that did applied AI early were actually at a disadvantage: you think you know where the world is going, you build the product for that endgame, but the models aren't there yet, and users try it and just say ‘this is garbage.’ Rogo went through that phase itself. His judgment is that if your read on the endgame is right and you keep building toward it, the moment the models catch up is the magic moment. He ties Rogo's product eras directly to model eras: 01 Pro was the first version reliable enough to at least serve as a search tool; by Opus 4.5, and from late 2025 into early 2026, the models can basically do anything a junior investment or banking professional does, provided you give the right instructions and context.

6:06 The MD annotating on an iPad is the real last mile
Gabe gives an example as concrete as it gets: the typical workflow of an investment banking MD is to email deck comments to an analyst, and Rogo lets that MD email the comments to an AI analyst and get a revised draft back in 20 minutes instead of two days, while automatically notifying the junior analysts on the deal and showing a complete audit trail of every small change. He points out the key: this finance professional hasn't logged into a computer in ten years, but he has an iPad, and he knows how to annotate on an iPad. That kind of product detail for a specific end user can only come from someone with a spidey sense for the job.

16:57 The harness matters more than the model itself
Gabe compares Claude Code and Claude Cowork with ChatGPT: the models are actually similar, but Claude's harness and presentation are far better, letting the model exercise more long-horizon capability, and so usage and expansion took off. He extends the analogy to the brain: humans have high agency not just because of raw memory, IQ, and knowledge, but because there are a bunch of microservices in the head — how to store knowledge, how to retrieve it, how to trigger it, and emotion is one way of triggering a microservice. A great investor's judgment comes from seeing something in the market that triggers the memory of some event, leading to a creative decision. Those microservices are what vertical companies have to build.

23:43 Skip seat-based pricing and go straight to outcome-based
Rogo today is classic enterprise software: priced per seat, because buyers are used to comparing it to Bloomberg, FactSet, Capital IQ, PitchBook, and every deal needs an AE plus a solutions architect to shake hands and explain the integration. Gabe says Anthropic can sell to them easily, with spend rising exponentially and no human involvement, because it's a token-consumption model; but many industries can't ride the token-consumption wave, and Rogo is one of them, so it has to build its GTM machine at five times the speed. His pricing judgment is that every company goes through two pricing revolutions: first to usage-based, then to outcome-based. He'd rather skip tokens and usage entirely and ask the customer directly: how much do you charge per good investment idea? Per quarterly LP report? Per investment banking CIM?

31:19 Auditability matters more than accuracy
Gabe says accuracy is of course still super important, but auditability matters more than accuracy, and the two are often conflated. The logic: if the answer is wrong and you don't know how to check it or see where it came from, then whether it's accurate or not you can't use it, because you don't trust it. Conversely, if it's right most of the time, and even when it's wrong you can clearly see the assumptions and the data sources, it's still actionable and still saves time. As tools move from copilot to autopilot — not just retrieving information but having agency, actually making investment decisions or sending emails — you have to be able to look back at why it decided the way it did, because you need to debug it, just as when an individual investor makes a bad decision you check whether the data input was wrong or someone lied to him. In regulated capital markets, if you can't explain the basis for a decision, you simply don't get through.

34:48 The company brain is called Shrek, and every conversation is recorded
Every conversation inside Rogo is recorded, and new hires are told on day one ‘you are always being recorded,’ and that content is filtered into the company brain, named Shrek because the engineers thought that was funny. There's a dashboard that shows the ‘swamp’ of what everyone is working on; it's connected to the company's various systems and is very clear about company goals, values, what needs to be delivered to customers, and the north star metric, so it can shape every answer and deliverable. It's both passive and active: you can go in and ask ‘how should I pitch the value proposition and savings of model routing to a large institution,’ and it pulls the information out; it also proactively reminds you, ‘Patrick, I see you're meeting this private credit firm on Thursday, here's what you should know, the use cases that will resonate, and the ROI metrics companies you've worked with before want to hear.’ Gabe says this is the core problem of enablement: suck information in and give it out when people need it.

42:18 What it's like to be rejected by 40 investors in a row
Gabe says the hardest low point was the A round: at the time there were no star investors on the cap table, David Tisch introduced him to 40 investors, he met Sequoia, Kleiner, Benchmark and others, and all 40 passed. And it wasn't the send-a-deck-no-interest kind; it was ‘interesting, meet Gabe,’ ‘like Gabe, talk for an hour,’ ‘come to IC,’ ‘let's get a meal,’ ‘come back over the weekend’ — and then ‘we've decided not to invest.’ He says that phase had nothing to do with anything except you, like being dumped by 40 girlfriends, each time you fell in love and each time they said it wasn't for you. In the end Thrive didn't invest either; Keith Rabois came about a month after everyone had passed, and Gabe asked Keith back: if this isn't a contrarian bet, why do all your friends say it's a bad idea and none of them believe in me? He sums up the three reasons investors passed: they underestimated the finance TAM, the product really was bad at the time, and there weren't enough data points to believe he could chew glass and ship the next version.

item.title: The Rocky Statue Is Not Art, but It Became a Landmark Philadelphia Can't Tear Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-ninepi-洛奇雕像不是艺术品-却成了费城拆不掉的地标/
item.description: A bronze statue made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, and left to sit in a warehouse — and what finally saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.
item.content:encoded:
A bronze statue made for a movie was rejected by the art commission, moved to a sports arena, and left to sit in a warehouse — and what finally saved it wasn't artistic merit but the fact that Philadelphians claimed it. A statue's status is always granted by its audience, not by the experts.

A complete narrative arc in 30 minutes: class, artistic authority, race and monument politics, dense with detail and almost no filler.

4:09 Bronze instead of foam decided its fate
In Rocky III there's a scene: a fictional mayor stands on the museum steps and dedicates a statue to Philadelphia. The production could have had the art department make a prop out of painted plastic and foam and toss it in a dumpster after filming. Stallone didn't do that — he paid $53,000 to have the artist A. Thomas Schaumburg cast the statue in bronze. Laura Holzman says that choice was crucial: it wasn't made of a material you throw away after shooting, but of an art material. Stallone went to high school in Philadelphia, called Rocky a ‘euphemism’ for the city, and then offered to donate the 1,800-pound statue to Philadelphia to stand permanently at the top of the steps. Precisely because it was bronze and not foam, the fifty-year fight that followed became possible.

10:25 The root of the opposition was Philadelphia wanting to be Athens
The museum leadership opposed it most fiercely, and their reasons were far bigger than aesthetics. Philadelphia's glory days had long faded by the early 20th century, and by the 1976 Bicentennial it was the city that could never shake its bad luck: crumbling infrastructure, corrupt local politics. In the 1980s the arts world wanted to remake Philadelphia into a cultural metropolis and restore the title a famous architect had given it — ‘the Athens of the Western world.’ They had bet heavily on the city's most important museum, and they didn't think a nine-foot-tall, sharply abdominals boxing could help Philadelphia toward that dream. Art commission chairman F. Eugene Dixon Jr. wrote to a colleague that the statue standing temporarily on the steps was fine, but placing it permanently in the courtyard — ‘I hope you're joking.’ In the winter of 1980, the commission voted 6 to 2 against permanent placement; the remaining two votes were to ban it from the steps outright.

12:34 Thousands of signatures lose to eight people with votes
It was a grassroots campaign that brought the statue back to Philadelphia from Los Angeles. Local truck driver Art Gorman was one of its biggest champions — Mark Bowden describes him as a straight-talking Philadelphia guy from a blue-collar neighborhood, thinking: who are these self-appointed connoisseurs to tell us what we can see on the steps of the art museum. At the end of 1980 he drafted a petition, all in capital letters, knocked on doors for thousands of signatures, and drew a pile of media coverage. The show says it plainly: the story got told as blue-collar Philadelphia versus elite high-culture Philadelphia, a ‘slobs versus snobs’ narrative. But the petition couldn't change the commission's basic position — the snobs were still the ones voting.

13:34 The prop crew bolted the statue into the ground with steel bars
Rocky III opened in May 1982, and the art commission only allowed the statue back on the steps for the premiere; once it was over, it had to go. But the production company simply left it there, the city wouldn't pay to move it, and the museum had to deal with it. Months later the movers finally came and found an obstacle: the statue was bolted to the sidewalk with steel bars driven several feet into the ground — ‘as if the filmmakers intended it to stay there forever.’ In the end the statue was pried loose and hauled five miles away to the Spectrum arena in South Philadelphia, where it stood with other athletes' statues. Most people thought the fight was over, but Stallone spent the next twenty-five years repeatedly asking for it to return to the museum, and every time he got the same answer: no.

15:35 One phone call did more than twenty years of aesthetic debate
In 2006 things moved: the mayor was pushing a batch of public space renovation projects, Stallone was about to release his first Rocky film in 16 years, and the statue was sitting in a warehouse because the city was building a new sports complex. Stallone's friend Jimmy Binns, a lawyer who had appeared in the sequels and had real clout in Philadelphia, called the mayor and asked whether he'd help get the statue back to the museum. Binns recounted the conversation: he asked the mayor, do those museum trustees invite you to their homes for cocktails on Sundays? The mayor laughed and said no. Binns said, then to hell with them. The mayor said, alright, to hell with them. With the mayor behind it, even the Philadelphia Museum of Art started to give ground, and the compromise worked out was: the statue returns to the museum permanently, but not at the top of the steps — a little off to the side at the bottom. The only remaining obstacle was the art commission, which held the final vote.

19:46 By 2006 the debate was no longer about art
In May 2006 the commission announced it might move the statue, setting off a new round of public discussion. City official Harris Baum argued against it on the local NPR call-in show, on the grounds that the Parkway was to be developed into a cultural district like Paris's, ‘but that's not a work of art.’ The response he got was completely different from the 1980s: listeners didn't want to talk about art. Judy said the statue was an image of the blue-collar spirit; Jack, calling from Lansdale, said ideally he'd want it at the top of the steps, but a bunch of pretentious old guys in wigs wouldn't let that happen, and he called Baum a snob and insulting to boot. Baum was fighting the battle of twenty years earlier. On September 6, 2006, the art commission voted 6 to 2 in favor, and the minutes read: the majority believed the statue's iconic symbolic meaning had earned it a place in the city's identity. Less than a week later the statue was unveiled, fitted with nighttime lighting, and raised onto a brand-new granite pedestal.

26:14 The real champion's steps are called the Rocky steps
The 2015 Charleston church shooting (nine dead) set off a national reckoning with racist symbols, and the wind reached Philadelphia: the Columbus statue and the statue of former mayor Frank Rizzo, known for violent policing and racist demagoguery, became targets. When Monument Lab asked Philadelphians what kind of monuments they wanted to build, some began questioning whether Rocky was appropriate: Philadelphia has a real boxing history, and those fighters were mostly Black, including heavyweight champion Joe Frazier, who beat Muhammad Ali in a fight watched by more than 300 million people. The show points out that the two most famous things in the first Rocky training montage — running up the museum steps and punching raw meat — actually came from Frazier's real training routine. Frazier got a statue in 2015, but many Philadelphians feel the twelve-foot bronze is nowhere near worthy of a real champion: ‘His image isn't on the tour buses, and the steps he ran are called the Rocky steps.’

28:21 In the reckoning over monuments, Rocky became the city's emotional container
After George Floyd was killed in 2020, Philadelphia's largest Black Lives Matter demonstrations set out from the art museum steps every day, with thousands of protesters gathering right beside the Rocky statue. By then it was already a monument, and by rights it should have faced the same scrutiny — a statue erected for a fictional white movie character, taking the place of a real Black champion, its days should have been numbered. But no one tore it down; instead they folded it in: someone hung a sign reading ‘no justice, no peace’ on it, early in the pandemic it got a face mask, later a Ukrainian flag, and when the Eagles' Brandon Graham retired, his cleats were hung on it. Paul Farber saw the most contradictory scene: a Black family posing for a photo all raising Black Power fists, and three or four people later, a group of white men in their early twenties raising white power gestures — the two things happening almost simultaneously without conflict.

item.title: Vitamin K injection refusal rates have doubled, and infant brain bleeds are preventable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-tpwky-维生素-k-注射被拒率翻倍-婴儿脑出血本可避免/
