item.description: Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates rose from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.
item.content:encoded:
Every newborn is physiologically deficient in vitamin K at birth, and a single intramuscular shot drops the risk of late bleeding to near zero; but US refusal rates rose from 3% to 5.8%, and babies whose parents refuse face 81 times the risk of late bleeding.

High information density: it covers both the clinical mechanics of newborn bleeding and the discovery of vitamin K plus how a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust. The second half, on who refuses and why communication fails, is the most valuable part.

20:34 Every newborn is born deficient in vitamin K
Vitamin K does not cross the placenta effectively, so even if the mother supplemented during pregnancy, the newborn's vitamin K-dependent clotting factors do not rise appreciably. Add an immature gut microbiome and very little self-synthesized K2, and breast milk averaging only about 2.5 micrograms per liter, and a exclusively breastfed infant takes in less than 1 microgram a day for the first six months. The result is that every newborn is at high risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding. This is not an outlier phenomenon; it is the physiological norm.

22:35 Late bleeding often has no warning and goes straight to the brain
Vitamin K deficiency bleeding in newborns comes in three types: early, within 24 hours of birth; classic, within the first week; and late, from one week to six months. The late form is the most dangerous, with about 60% of cases being intracranial hemorrhage, and it often comes with no warning bleed, just a sudden brain bleed, seizures or unresponsiveness. Mortality ranges from 50% to 60% depending on era and country, with modern figures around 20%. That is why the value of a single preventive shot cannot be measured by "the bleeding probability is low."

25:46 One intramuscular shot pushes the risk to near zero
Since 2003 in the US, and in the vast majority of medical societies and public health agencies worldwide, a single intramuscular vitamin K shot at birth is recommended. It provides a stable supply for the first few months, cutting the risk of late bleeding from 4 to 7 cases per 100,000 live births (some countries report as high as 80) to about 0.4. Infants who receive no prophylaxis have 81 times the risk of late bleeding compared with those who do. Oral regimens also significantly reduce risk, but they require multiple doses, are affected by absorption and vomiting, are less effective than injection, and no oral formulation is approved by regulators in the US.

44:27 How a 1950s overdose scandal destroyed trust
In the postwar research climate, informed consent and patient protections had not yet entered the picture, and the logic was "vitamin is harmless and possibly beneficial, so give it to all premature infants." In the mid-1950s Britain gave some premature infants up to 60 milligrams of synthetic vitamin K, after which jaundice, hemolysis and kernicterus rose, and several infants died. The formulation was withdrawn and the dose dropped back to 1 milligram, but confidence had been shaken: of more than 16,000 infants born in Britain in a single week in 1970, only 20% received vitamin K. This history shows that the fallout from a single overdose incident can last for decades.

46:31 The 1990s leukemia scare still has not cleared
In the early 1990s two British studies linked intramuscular vitamin K to later leukemia risk, and the reaction was swift and strong: some countries switched to recommending oral dosing and reserved injections for the highest-risk infants, and British injection rates fell from 58% in 1988 to 38% in 1993. But the two studies had small samples and insufficient controls, and a large body of subsequent research and a WHO working group found no association, with IARC also concluding there was no evidence of carcinogenicity. The problem is that bad news travels fast and good news does not, just like MMR and autism: once doubt is planted, the world never fully recovers.

49:35 Refusal rates doubled, and the 81-fold risk is badly underestimated
US refusal rates nearly doubled from 2017 to 2024, rising from 3% to 5.8%, with some hospitals reporting higher. Infants whose parents refuse have 81 times the risk of vitamin K deficiency bleeding, a figure that is badly underestimated because the bleeding itself remains rare and communication is inadequate. Research shows most parents, whether they accept or refuse, know vitamin K is related to bleeding, but do not know that this bleeding can cause severe brain injury and a mortality risk above 20%. The information is present, but it is not being effectively conveyed.

50:36 Refusals fall into three categories, and birth attendants matter enormously
Reasons for refusal fall roughly into three categories: distrust of medicine, pursuit of "natural birth," and preference for alternative medical lifestyles. Some argue that if infants needed more vitamin K, evolution or God would have provided it; others read a recommendation to supplement vitamin K as "you are not fit to be a mother." Research also finds refusers are more likely to be white, college-educated, over 30, and planning a home or birth center delivery. The birth attendant's stance is critical: in a New Zealand survey, 100% of doctors thought all infants should receive vitamin K, while only 55% of midwives did, and 26% of those would not give it to their own children; in Canada, infants delivered by midwives were 8 times more likely to have vitamin K refused than those delivered by doctors.

55:46 Doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time
Some parents who lost a child or whose child suffered brain injury because vitamin K was not given are doing something very brave: saying publicly, "I made this decision, this is the consequence, do not do what I did." At the same time, doctors are seeing newborns bleed to death for the first time in their careers, and they are raising the alarm in their communities. Some researchers and doctors are pushing to establish a national US registry of vitamin K refusal and administration, because vitamin K deficiency bleeding is not a notifiable disease and cases are likely undercounted. In a post-pandemic era when expertise is treated as a dirty word, these preventable injuries and deaths will keep increasing.

item.title: US Strategic Oil Reserve Hits Bottom, and Venezuelan Oil Can't Save It
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-indicator-美国战略石油储备见底-委内瑞拉石油救不了它/

item.description: The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and over-withdrawal is dissolving the salt and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure, and it still can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.
item.content:encoded:
The salt-cavern reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and over-withdrawal is dissolving the salt and destabilizing the cavern structures; Venezuelan oil is a different grade and needs $100 billion in infrastructure, and it still can't get around the deadlock of congressional appropriations.

Medium information density, but it explains the physical degradation mechanism of the SPR — the part most coverage leaves out. Suited to anyone watching energy security and macro.

0:00 He promised to fill it, and it fell another 30%
In his inaugural address, Trump promised to fill the Strategic Petroleum Reserve "right up to the top," but since then the reserve has fallen another 30%. The Iran war closed the Strait of Hormuz, a huge amount of the world's oil couldn't get out, and the reserve was used as a price buffer to protect Americans from the global supply shortfall. The problem is that the buffer itself is nearly used up. Trump's new answer is Venezuelan oil, which he called "the biggest oil deal in our country's history," saying 65 billion barrels go to the US. But the question the show wants to press is: can Venezuelan oil really save the SPR? And what does this mean for ordinary people's wallets?

2:03 The reserve isn't tanks, it's salt caverns dissolved out of the ground
After the Arab oil embargo against the US in the early 1970s, the US government realized it needed a standby oil supply, and the SPR was born. About 30 countries around the world have standby reserves — Japan, Germany, Australia all have them — but the American version is unusual. Siddharth Mishra, a petroleum engineering professor at Texas A&M, says the US government decided the most efficient way to store millions of barrels of oil wasn't metal tanks but salt caverns. Engineers pump in huge amounts of water to dissolve underground salt layers and create cavities — these aren't traditional caves you can walk into, they're man-made caverns, single cylinders roughly the size of the Empire State Building or even bigger. Between Texas and Louisiana, 60 of these caverns make up the SPR.

4:10 Over-withdrawal is dissolving the caverns themselves
The SPR was first tapped in 1991 for Desert Storm, and then for Hurricane Katrina, the 2011 Arab Spring, and the 2022 Ukraine war. The 2022 global release saved Americans about 17 to 42 cents per gallon. But the reserve has fallen to its lowest level since 1982, and it's dropping fast — down 50% over the past six years, with 85% of that attributable to the Ukraine and Iran wars. The risk isn't just about volume: the lower the reserve, the more water needs to be injected, the more room there is for the oil to be contaminated, and refineries don't like contaminated oil, making it harder to sell; contamination also forms sludge that makes rapid extraction harder — and rapid extraction is the entire point of the SPR's existence. As water keeps being injected, the salt dissolves and the cavern structures become unstable; this engineering marvel that once amazed Mishra is being weakened.

5:13 Filling the reserve still runs into Congress having to pay
Joseph Mikit, an energy security expert at the Center for Strategic and International Studies, says the US is not in a position to simply buy oil and fill the reserve. Under the normal mechanism, Congress has to agree to buy oil and bury it underground, and with the deficit as severe as it is, that's a hard problem. Previous administrations thought up workarounds: during the Clinton and Bush years there was the royalty-in-kind program — when companies extracted oil from federally owned reserves, instead of paying the government in cash they handed over oil directly to go into the SPR. Now the government is looking at more unusual strategies: in April, Energy Secretary Chris Wright proposed drilling for oil under military bases, but nothing more was heard; the recent headline plan is Venezuelan oil, with a private company giving the US 20% control of its existing and future oil fields in Venezuela.

6:15 Venezuelan oil isn't the same grade as what's in the SPR
A key detail: Venezuelan oil is a completely different type from the oil in the US SPR, so it has to go through some kind of trading mechanism — sell one grade, buy another. Energy security expert Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, believing such a trade could work. He says the plan needs a lot of mechanisms to line up, but it adds a source of oil that won't cause large-scale market disruption, and it doesn't require the US to get Congress to agree to spend big on filling the SPR at a time of high oil prices and fiscal imbalance. In other words, any plan that doesn't require Congress to buy oil looks great. But the challenge is that getting oil out of the ground in Venezuela is notoriously difficult, and after years of underinvestment and corruption it needs enormous infrastructure investment.

7:19 $100 billion, and no one knows who pays
One Latin American energy expert puts the figure at $100 billion over the next decade to restore Venezuelan production to where it was 20 years ago. And it's unclear who foots the bill — oil companies, the US government, or someone else. Arnab Data, a managing director at Employ America focused on energy markets, flatly calls the Venezuela plan "a bit of a pipe dream." His objection: we can meet demand with production at home and among allies, so why support Venezuelan production? Rather than putting $100 billion into another country, coordinating between agencies, and untangling Venezuela's political chaos, it would be better to put that money into the SPR. His words: we don't need to go out looking for oil, there's plenty in the fridge, right here.

8:22 The current oil-lending mechanism is actually working fine
Arnab thinks the Trump administration's current strategy is working well: the Energy Department lends barrels to oil companies, which promise to return them later, at a premium of up to 24%. He sees this as a well-executed way of delivering to the market, and it also signals to the market that there's demand for US barrels. So here's the split: Joseph is optimistic about the Venezuela deal, seeing it as a source of oil that doesn't disrupt the market and doesn't need congressional appropriations; Arnab thinks it's a pipe dream, that the existing lending mechanism is good enough, and that the $100 billion would be better put back into the SPR. The show closes with a reminder: global oil supply keeps falling, another strait is under Houthi control and at risk of closing, and Americans don't know how much longer the SPR can shield them from higher costs.

item.title: Making a Child Perform Isn't Connection, It's Depletion
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-22-unruffled-让孩子表演不是连接-是在消耗他/
item.description: Connection isn't getting a child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.
item.content:encoded:
Connection isn't getting a child to repeat what he knows to please you — it's observing, receiving, and treating him as a person. Performance connection is fast food: gone the moment it's eaten.

This episode isn't dense — it's a single topic on a parenting podcast. But if you're dealing with relatives pushing your child to perform, or you want to understand what "connection" actually means, it's worth a listen.

1:04 Making a child perform is fast-food connection
A mother writes in that her 17-month-old son can identify shapes and colors, speak sentences, and name dinosaurs, but his grandmother always makes him "perform" — repeat what he's learned, clap — and when he won't cooperate she grabs his arm and does it for him, and recently even kicked him in the butt. Janet says this isn't an isolated case: we often think connecting with infants and toddlers means getting them to react to us, to imitate us. But that's "fast-food connection" — the child may smile because he's getting attention, but no one is truly seen.

4:08 We're performing too
Connection goes both ways: not only do we make the child perform, we ourselves are often performing rather than being ourselves. In her forthcoming book Baby Person, Janet writes that she used to dance, make funny faces, and try every trick to get a reaction out of babies in order to bond with them. These surface methods left her exhausted with a tiny, fleeting payoff — "I made her laugh" is just a moment. She says this isn't deep connection, it's all surface.

6:14 Performance connection teaches a child to be insincere
Janet lists five reasons connection shouldn't be a performance: one, it isn't real connection; two, it teaches the child insincerity — everything we do with a child teaches them something, and this teaches "connection requires performing rather than being yourself"; three, it wastes energy and effort, and parents can't afford it; four, it doesn't satisfy, and doesn't move the relationship toward trust; five, it subtly belittles the child — why should a child have to perform to hold our attention and interest?

8:19 Charismatic people are charismatic because they're paying attention to you
Janet quotes something she's always remembered: certain people are charismatic to us not because of how they perform or what they put out, but because they're genuinely interested in us, paying attention to us. Children especially need this, because it's harder for them to express themselves proactively and they don't know what to say to connect. They need us to tune in to their subtleties: what they're interested in, what their expressions are saying, who they are.

9:19 Even a parenting expert couldn't connect with her grandchild
Janet read a book by a well-known psychologist treated as a parenting expert, in which the author, now a grandparent, said she simply couldn't connect with a toddler grandchild and felt the child had no chemistry with her. Janet's immediate read: this grandparent was trying too hard — wanting to initiate games, wanting the child to cooperate, was "working it" rather than connecting. Her method works for every child from infancy on: observe, listen, receive, pay attention.

10:21 Comment on what you see, don't fake interest
The concrete practice: treat the child as a person with depth, talent, interests, and a real point of view worth knowing. Then comment on what you see — "You're looking over there, did you hear a dog?" "You seem really interested in those blocks, I see you're lining them up." Not faking interest, but genuinely becoming interested. Children can tell the difference between "good job" and "wow, that took a while, I saw you thinking about which one goes on top, and the round one rolled down."

12:31 Children can put a grandparent's behavior in context
How do you set down the fear that "this is bad for the child"? Janet says children are more aware than we think. They know "this is my grandparent, this isn't how my parents treat me, this is just how this person is." So it won't affect how they feel about themselves. Parents have enormous influence, but grandparents are different — even seeing them often, a child can put it in the context of "my relationship with that person."

14:34 Narrate instead of correcting
Janet advises this mother not to try to teach her mother or correct her, but to connect, reflect, and trust them to handle the relationship themselves. Concretely: if her son does what the grandmother asks, let it go; if he won't and the grandmother kicks him, don't say to the grandmother "you shouldn't do that," but say to her son "Grandma really likes it when you do what she asks, she's really into this" — without sarcasm, just stating what's happening. This is called sportscasting, and it helps both the child and the grandmother understand what's going on.

item.description: The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it, and APIs alone are not enough.
item.content:encoded:
The real miracle of the U-2 wasn't the aircraft — it was procurement reform, the intelligence analysis agencies, and the chain that carried judgment to the president. Today AI has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it, and APIs alone are not enough.

The first half uses the U-2 analogy to lay out clearly where the government's AI integration bottleneck is; the second half's judgments on procurement incentives, token economics and cybersecurity are worth more, but overall it's a loose conversational interview with medium information density.

2:02 The U-2's miracle isn't the plane, it's the procurement and analysis chain
Garrett says the U-2 story is usually told as a technology breakthrough, but what really mattered was three things: procurement reform that let government and industry work together that way, intelligence analysis being institutionalized (NPIC, which later became NGA), and getting judgment in front of the president and other decision-makers. That, he says, is the ‘miraculous’ part of the story. Today's AI problem is the exact inverse: the technology comes from the commercial world and moves too fast, and it has far outrun the government's ability to integrate it into systems, workflows and decision processes — so ‘APIs alone are not enough’.

9:06 AI is advancing fastest in warfighting, slowest in business systems
Garrett says the Pentagon and other departments have made visible progress in warfighting spaces like CJADC2: using AI to build situational awareness across the battlefield, identify targets, and get intelligence quickly to decision-makers at the front. But core business systems — logistics, personnel, finance — have seen the least progress. His personal view is that we should stop dividing systems into ‘mission systems’ and ‘business systems’, because to support the front you need clean, organized data usable at operational tempo, and these business systems were never built for operational tempo.

10:06 One policy rule blocks the data of twenty thousand logistics troops
He gives a concrete example: some business systems' rules say status only needs to be updated once a week. That's policy — someone wrote it down. But decision-makers now want that data daily, which means going to roughly ten or twenty thousand Army supply sergeants and saying ‘you have to enter it daily, not weekly’. That's ‘a big boat to turn around’, and there has to be clear value in it. Worse, the systems the government gave them were bad to begin with — you make it hard to enter data while demanding a big drop in data latency.

14:10 Government has no market competition as a forcing function
The host points out that a company that doesn't do AI gets eliminated, but the Air Force or the national security apparatus won't be ‘competed out’ — that kind of forcing function comes once or twice a century. Garrett agrees, but says we underestimate our own ability to manufacture mechanisms. He argues for using personnel policy and leadership as carrot and stick: reward people who take risks and take weird career paths, and let those who don't move fast enough face career stagnation or removal. He says it sounds ‘crude’, but that's the mechanism you have to follow.

19:18 Second-mover advantage: watch others burn money and step in potholes first
Garrett says this time it's the reverse of the U-2: the technology happens in the commercial sector first and then enters government, so government has a second-mover advantage and can see what's working. He cites the lesson of token economics: do you open it up like Uber and let everyone burn tokens without limit, blowing the budget in a quarter, or do you first understand token economics and then deploy to employees? Also, as the federal government, if it does this right it can act as a supersized buyer and negotiate bulk pricing.

23:20 To put GPUs at the edge, first clear the policy on who signs and who's liable
Garrett says if you put these tools in soldiers' hands, you'll be shocked by how innovative and clever they are at using them for their actual jobs, and that may mean pushing compute to the edge and putting GPUs in service members' hands. But the obstacle is policy: a logistics officer signs for $500,000 worth of chips — who's responsible if a chip breaks? He says you have to clear the policy and just say ‘we own this risk’, and if it means some GPUs get broken and money is lost, that's worth it, because the capability reaches the edge.

29:26 Intelligence analysis is more tractable than modeling decisions
Garrett thinks using AI to model strategic decisions is very hard, because it needs good data, and the decision process is deliberately opaque — you can't get all the private notes, emails and situation-room audio and video. But intelligence analysis is a more tractable project: the intelligence process is structured and rigorous, agencies have their own SOPs and training, there are decades of data, and there are signals of quality, so you can build benchmarks from it. Still, it's only one input to decisions — historically many decision-makers looked at the same intelligence and made completely different decisions.

38:36 Bill by the hour and someone will report more hours
Garrett says the government buys a lot on hourly rates by person and seniority, and this time and materials structure has a status quo bias. The logic is plain: if the incentive is for companies to report more hours, and there's no hard delivery requirement when the hours run out, they'll report more hours. He says there have been signs of change over the past 12 to 18 months, but looking at public spending data, there's no large-scale shift — most spending is still time and materials. He also mentions that top companies spend 10% of their budget on tokens, while the US government is nowhere near that level.

item.description: Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it harms you, and roughly one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.
item.content:encoded:
Procrastination is delaying despite knowing it harms you, and roughly one in five adults does it chronically. Anxiety, distraction, burnout and perfectionism each need a different fix, but they share one premise: change nothing about the plan and nothing about the result changes.

It breaks procrastination into types you can actually treat and hands you a concrete toolbox instead of another self-discipline sermon. Medium-to-high information density.

1:16 The definition of procrastination has reluctance buried inside it
Itamar's definition is: we delay something even though we did not intend to delay it, and we know it is bad for us. So deliberately deciding to do it later and feeling fine about that is not procrastination. The gray zone is: what if you think delaying is good for you but it actually harms you? His test is whether you could have anticipated that it would be better for you. About 20% of adults procrastinate chronically, and among students it is 50%. He stresses that procrastination does not only happen to people who do not care: highly conscientious people, genuinely productive people, people who truly want to make an impact, procrastinate too.

3:27 Procrastination is several types, not one thing
Treating procrastination as a single phenomenon makes two mistakes at once: you fail to see that it happens to people other than students, and you cannot deal with it in practice. A student who procrastinates from distraction, an executive who procrastinates from burnout, and an artist who procrastinates from perfectionism have different drivers and need different solutions. In his book Itamar distinguishes the anxious type, the type pulled away by external temptations, the burnout type, and a category he calls zigzaggers, closer to ADHD and impulsivity, who switch back and forth between internal rather than external distractions.

5:00 Anxiety has two faces: fear of the task or fear of the consequences
The mechanism by which anxiety causes procrastination is: doing this will hurt, the brain says I do not want to hurt, so you push it away. But anxiety also has an adaptive side: if what you are anxious about is not the task itself but the consequences of not finishing it, a little anxiety pushes you to act. The key variables are intensity and self-efficacy: a little anxiety may motivate you, a lot of anxiety paralyzes you no matter what it is aimed at, and if you also believe you are incapable of finishing, anxiety turns into paralysis more easily. Itamar adds one caveat: even when anxiety does push you, it is a dangerous source of motivation, because it also brings stress and a worse experience.

9:25 The biggest mistake is believing you will try harder next time
Itamar says the biggest mistake people make when tackling procrastination is falling into the self-control fallacy: believing that next time, if you just try harder and summon more willpower, you will get it done. The absurdity is that we watch it fail again and again and believe it again and again. The reasons include the bias blind spot, the inability to recognize your own biases, and the empathy gap, predicting in a cool state what you will do in a hot emotional state. The real harm of this belief is that it offers a superficially minimal silver bullet, which stops you from looking for what actually works. Spencer's addition: change nothing and the result will not change.

12:45 Design for your future self as if they were someone else
Spencer's approach is: do not assume that the you of two weeks from now will get it done on willpower, instead ask what would help a person very much like me get this done in two weeks, then set reminders, make social commitments, add rewards. Itamar says this is exactly an illustration of his core claim: procrastination is not a time management problem, even excellent time management can fail, what you should do is distance management. Addressing yourself in the second or third person, or using your name instead of "I", or asking what advice you would give a friend, all create psychological distance and help you enter wise reasoning, seeing through the situation and around your biases.

16:13 Anxious type: decatastrophize, or do it anxious
For the anxious procrastinator, Itamar's first choice is to decatastrophize: catastrophizing is overestimating both the probability that something bad happens and the harm it does to you. For example, "there is a typo in my proposal, so the agent will blacklist me, and will tell everyone to blacklist me too." The method is to ask: how likely is this to happen? If it did happen, how bad would it be? If it happened, how would I carry on? Spencer offers an almost opposite strategy: notice that this task makes me anxious, sit inside that feeling, feel it, and then do it anyway, which he calls metacognitive awareness. Itamar files it under the umbrella of mindfulness and self-compassion.

21:39 Procrastination is short-term emotional repair, and it reinforces itself
Spencer points out that anxiety creates anxiety: the moment you say "I am not doing this now", the anxiety usually drops immediately, so you are learning that procrastinating makes me feel better, which forms a reinforcement loop. Doing the opposite can unwind it: doing it while anxious functions like an exposure. Itamar says procrastination here is a defense mechanism: because you feel pressure or anxiety about what you should be doing, you push it away to avoid the painful emotion. It makes you feel better in the short term and worse in the long term, because you have not solved the problem, you have only arranged to face it again and again, or to face worse consequences.

26:39 The fix for the burnout type is to do less
Itamar admits this is the last thing burned-out people want to hear: if you are burned out because you do too much, or do things that drain you, you probably need to do less and take more deliberate care of yourself, which concretely means deciding more deliberately what to do and, more importantly, what not to do. He describes a loop: you are used to performing well, burnout makes your performance drop, so you work even harder, then burn out more, and it gets worse and worse. He calls this borrowing health and productivity from your future self. He also notes that burnout does not come only from hours: reasonable hours with tasks that are high-pressure, meaningless, or draining in other ways produce burnout too.

item.title: The cost of RLHF is mode dropping, not alignment

item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-latentspace-rlhf-的代价是-mode-dropping-不是对齐/
item.description: RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.
item.content:encoded:
RLHF forces models to be extremely conservative to avoid mistakes, poisoning the probability distribution over strings; TypeSafe's Jev takes another path, optimizing only intelligence per dollar.

High information density: Diogo goes deep on the trade-offs between RLHF, RLVR and RLCD, suited to anyone who needs to form a judgment on model training routes.

6:03 The cost of RLHF is mode dropping
Diogo thinks nobody pays attention to RLHF's downsides, especially mode dropping. The mechanism: to generate very long strings without making a mistake, the model has to be extremely conservative, because errors are visible at a glance while things that look correct but are subtly wrong are very hard to spot; this calibration is "total poison" for the probability distribution over strings. He uses this to explain why Yann LeCun's chart — "LLMs necessarily make mistakes as sequences get longer" — is mathematically obvious but empirically false: when you cover the distribution you aren't over-penalized by outliers, and it's mode drop that throws away the minority classes.

11:12 Refusing to answer is a type error, not a safety problem
Diogo distinguishes safety alignment from capability alignment: the latter is "doing what the user wants," the former is "following someone else's instructions," as with OpenAI and Anthropic. He thinks safety alignment is reasonable for products like ChatGPT and Claude, but in an API it's "nuts," "completely unacceptable" — if a dependency is running in the background, having your software randomly crash because a user sent a weird message is insanity. He opposes adding restrictions at the technical layer, on the grounds that every overfit fractures intelligence a little more, and today's models are already fractured enough.

18:15 Public benchmarks are a substitute for trust
Diogo says he is extremely anti-public benchmarks because they are extremely gameable: in the early days every lab had a team dedicated to collecting data like MMLU to pump up scores — essentially "benchmarking with extra steps." He admits intelligence has a je ne sais quoi (good model smell), so people need benchmarks to build trust, but in the long run you can only rely on vibes and trust, until you put the model into a concrete workflow and evaluate it there. He also says that if they wanted to make Jev dumber, they could have shipped that a year and a half ago.

27:34 RLCD is a new North Star, not a new algorithm
Diogo says the term RLHF has been conflated: the original work was Paul Christiano teaching a robot to do a backflip, then it was learning to summarize, and only later instruction following. What he actually calls RLHF is "instruction following as the North Star," with nothing to do with the PPO algorithm — just as DPO and its descendants don't use that paper's algorithm and still count as RLHF. RLCD is the same: a new task direction, programs in the loop, taking the human out of the loop.

40:38 Reliability is a catchall; the North Star is robustness
Diogo defines reliability as a catchall: if AI can't automate something, in the end it's always some kind of reliability problem — maybe type safety, maybe determinism, maybe just that the model is too jagged. He explicitly rejects determinism (same input, same output) as the North Star, holding that it's only slightly valuable for unit tests; what really matters is robustness — similar inputs getting similar outputs. The test is to stuff nonces like UUIDs into the prompt and see whether semantically identical questions get similar answers. He says that when people get burned by AI decisions, that's the layer where it happens.

1:17:12 Reliability is more underrated than speed and cost
Diogo thinks the industry is looking in the wrong place: "people focus too much on speed and cost and not enough on reliability." His judgment is that reliability is what makes people delighted, and what makes them dare to trust. He ties this to TFP growth — he expects TFP growth above 3% within five years, and says that's the mark of an economic revolution, and what the OpenAI charter originally meant to express. He estimates that all models today are still roughly at zero on valuable work in the world economy, maybe not even at 1%.

1:44:10 The optimal dose of RLVR is zero
Diogo says outright that for a model of TypeSafe's shape, the optimal amount of RLVR is zero. His argument is not "RLVR is useless" but that the "pacing the frontier" discussion smuggles in a premise: it assumes everyone must do more RLVR, and RLVR looks dangerous because it lets the model "do anything they want" mid-training — the less you restrict it, the stronger the model is on the outside. So the danger isn't a side effect, it's the design goal. He calls this a "disillusion of responsibility": taking "we must do more RLVR" as an axiom and then deriving the conclusion "we are heading toward a dangerous world."

2:09:13 The KV cache is a tyranny over coding agents
Diogo wants to explore coding agents "free from the tyranny of the KV cache." The KV cache locks you into one model, and for efficiency you have to keep appending, so you can't do state management, abstraction, decomposition — normal software practices. From this he explains several phenomena: why routing is hard, why sub-agents don't seem to work, why compaction is a hard problem — because passing state around requires intelligence that is much cheaper than reading state. Directions he imagines include: explicitly annotating state for subtasks, searching for relevant context in a tree of subtasks, parallel sub-agents reading each other's state, and coordinating with smart locks rather than basic-ass locks.

item.description: Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.
item.content:encoded:
Google alone burns through 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token, that's 12 gigawatts, against roughly 40 gigawatts of total US data center power. Naveen Rao thinks the only way to close that gap is to replace the underlying paradigm of the computer.

The first half is the energy math; the second half is his first public reveal of a physical dynamics computer prototype and measured efficiency numbers, which is rare hard information. The biology analogy in the middle can be fast-forwarded.

4:45 Energy isn't a cost line, it's the ticket to entry
Naveen's math: Google crosses 3.2 quadrillion tokens a month. At 10 joules per token — a low estimate — that's 12 gigawatts. The US puts roughly 40 gigawatts into data centers today; the world, under 100 gigawatts. So one company's AI service eats more than a tenth of global data center energy. His call is that we hit the energy ceiling in about three years. More important, the ranking of scarce resources in a data center has flipped: it used to be floor space, racks, networking gear, GPUs; today it's energy — get the power contract first, then figure out how to fill it. And energy is 50% of the cost of serving a token; hardware capex and site come after.

7:04 What a squirrel does on 8 milliwatts, a GPU needs watts for
A human brain is about 20 watts. Scale linearly by neuron count down to a monkey brain and you get one watt — exactly your phone in your pocket. Further down, rats and bats are in the milliwatt range. A squirrel leaping between branches lands it a thousand times out of a thousand on an 8-milliwatt brain. Which is to say your phone's battery could run a hundred-plus squirrel brains. Naveen's conclusion: biology has already built a physical substrate suited to intelligence, and synthetic systems took a different road. The human cortex moves only about 16 billion bits per second; a high-end GPU moves close to 30 trillion bits per second in and out of memory, and inside the chip it's another 10 to 100 times higher. The energy goes almost entirely into moving information, not computing on it.

10:06 Moore's Law stopped, and the abstraction layers still charge rent
Transistor counts are still climbing, but frequency stopped scaling long ago, single-thread performance stopped, and now even efficiency no longer improves as process nodes shrink — Naveen says flatly that Moore's Law is basically over. His diagnosis is the abstraction layers: digital itself is an abstraction of the physical world, and transistors actually have intermediate states that get engineered into 0s and 1s. Every layer of abstraction is lossy and ignores the complexity beneath it. So their approach is to wire the physics of the semiconductor directly to the neural network and skip the layers in between. His intuition pump is flocks of birds and ant colonies: individuals do something extremely simple, and complex behavior emerges from the whole. The field is called dynamical systems theory.

12:07 Metronomes on a board sync up on their own
Put several metronomes on a rigid board that can roll back and forth, and they will synchronize to exactly the same phase, simply because each one gives the board a tiny push. That's a pure physical dynamical system. Their question was whether such a system can compute. The answer is yes — they open-sourced an image generation model called UNO built on a set of such oscillators, and it trains and produces images. Define the system state as the phases of all the oscillators, condition on the output, and generating a plane, a car or a bird follows a different state space trajectory. It's the first demonstration that this class of system can be trained at scale and produce something useful.

14:08 Throwing away connections makes the system easier to train
Fully connected is n squared: 10 elements and 100 connections is fine, 1,000 elements is a million connections, and it doesn't scale. Their sparsity is deliberately discarding some fraction of connections and seeing whether the overall behavior can be rescued. The result isn't just that you can throw them away — after throwing them away the system behaves better and is more trainable, and that holds both in simulation and in real physical systems. Naveen calls this the rare case where more efficient, more scalable and better performing all hold at once, a holy grail nobody had cracked, provided you frame the problem correctly first.

15:09 The first physical dynamics computer has already generated images
This is Naveen's first public reveal: they built the first physical dynamics computer. The company only formally started in January of this year, with no team at the time; they sent the design to tape-out on June 1, and the chip is back in the lab with results — the first images generated by this kind of computer. On efficiency, generating an image costs about 500 nanojoules, versus millijoules for an ordinary GPU. A nanojoule is 10 to the minus 9, so that's several orders of magnitude. The reason is that it doesn't move information at all. Architecturally it's unlike both CPUs and GPUs: those are von Neumann machines, with memory and compute separated and data shuttled back and forth; in this machine compute and storage are the same thing, there is no memory interface, and every compute unit is itself a memory.

17:09 4D computing: three spatial dimensions plus one of time
They call the whole thing 4D computing: physically, die stacking uses all three dimensions, vertical and planar, and the fourth dimension is time in the dynamics. The objective function is intelligence per watt. There is a thermodynamic limit that can never be crossed; animal brains sit only one to two orders of magnitude from it, while today's computing systems are about 10 billion times away. Their plan is to hit the limits of 2D lithography within three and a half years, and the company's overall goal is to beat biology. Naveen expects the result to be a change in form factor: from gigawatt-scale mega data centers toward small data centers scattered everywhere, more local, more adaptive, and supporting billions of robots that dynamically combine to solve problems.

19:12 A thousand times cheaper means a thousand times more consumption
Naveen closes with the Jevons paradox: when the underlying cost of an asset falls, consumption grows by more than the price fell. Halve the price and consumption more than doubles; cut the price to a thousandth and consumption grows more than a thousandfold. So he doesn't think efficiency gains shrink the market — they create the largest market in human history. Chamath then asks about the ecosystem — tape-out, packaging and so on need a whole set of people to line up. Naveen's answer is a complete product within two years, in the form of an entire rack, sold as a new data center product: tokens in, tokens out over the network, but internally structured completely differently from existing computers.

item.title: Strategic Reserves Are Nearly Drained — the Oil Price Crisis Is Only Now Beginning
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-wsjournal-战略储备快见底-油价危机才真正开始/
item.description: Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to hit diesel and prices.
item.content:encoded:
Oil hasn't spiraled over the past six months because of three buffers: strategic reserves, sanctioned oil, and China buying less. All three are now being drained, and the real shock is only just about to hit diesel and prices.

Medium information density, but breaking down "why oil prices haven't risen" into three buffers and the pace at which they're being exhausted is more useful than reading headlines.

2:03 Close Hormuz and a fifth of the world's oil is gone
The moment the war began, Iran closed the Strait of Hormuz, cutting off roughly 20% of global oil supply. This was the move everyone treated as the "nuclear option" — nobody wanted to see it, because it's too bad for all sides. Once the strait closed, oil shot from around $70 a barrel to well over $100. But the market didn't spiral out of control from there; instead it found several buffers to hold prices down. The real question isn't "why did it rise" but "why didn't it rise more."

3:09 Three buffers, each less usable than the last
The first is the US Strategic Petroleum Reserve — emergency crude stored in salt caverns along the Gulf Coast after the 1970s Arab oil embargo — plus the commercial inventories held by refiners, which were at high levels before the conflict. The second is sanctioned oil: a large volume of "dark fleet" crude from Iran and Russia floating at sea, which in March the US temporarily allowed other countries to buy. The third is China — the world's largest oil importer, normally buying about 12 million barrels a day, roughly 10% of the global total, which earlier this year bought about 3 million barrels a day less, effectively leaving that oil to others. Together, these three held oil below $100 and the national average gasoline price just under $5.

6:12 Ceasefire talks slapped analysts in the face collectively
In June the US and Iran began talks and reached a ceasefire, and market sentiment flipped 180 degrees: from "extreme crude shortage" to "crude surplus," with analysts predicting oil would fall to $70 or even $60 a barrel. But the peace deal collapsed within weeks, Iran closed the strait again, and Trump declared the ceasefire over. So it was back to the state at the start of the conflict. This episode shows one thing: this round of prices contains a lot of bets on "the war ends soon," and that bet has repeatedly failed.

8:15 Six months of draining the buffers, and they're nearly dry
Commercial inventories have been drawn down, strategic reserves released — and reserves can't be released at will; the government only authorized a specific quantity. The US has taken more than 130 million barrels out of the strategic reserve, leaving about 280 million, which sounds like a lot but is approaching the authorized cap. Worse, this time there's an added refinery crisis: Middle Eastern refineries were struck in the war, and Ukraine, in self-defense, knocked out a large chunk of Russia's refining capacity — and Russia is the world's second-largest diesel exporter. Once a refinery is destroyed, it takes months to restore. So the problem now isn't whether there's crude; it's that there isn't enough refining capacity to produce the fuel the world needs.

9:16 Venezuela can't put out a fire this close
The Trump administration holds up Venezuela as the solution, and its reserves may be the world's largest. But reserves being there doesn't mean production capacity is there: to actually raise output you have to invest money, ship in rigs, hire people, drill, and then move the barrels out — that's a matter of years and billions of dollars of investment. As for other "miracle solutions," Benoit says there basically aren't any; you can only hope for "small miracles" — like China deciding to boost diesel output, or refinery repairs finishing early. But none of these take effect tomorrow.

10:17 Gas stations haven't blown up yet — diesel blew up first
US consumers haven't seen prices spike at the pump yet; what's really rising is diesel — the fuel that drives the heavy trucks moving consumer goods from one end of the country to the other. So the question becomes: will companies cut back on deliveries? When do they pass costs on to consumers? Once diesel rises, every kind of business has to factor it into its pricing. This is the real channel through which this shock transmits from energy markets into the real economy, and why "gas prices are okay" is a misleading comfort.

12:23 Two paths: absorb it yourself, or pass it on
Businesses have only two choices. One is to absorb it without raising prices: Jim Barber, a third-generation Pennsylvania farmer, has raised his beef price only once in five years, and even when the cost of hauling in hay rose 15% to 20%, he ate it himself, because he values his relationship with customers and believes the conflict will end soon and that holding on will be rewarded. A farmer's exposure to fuel is triple-layered — fertilizer, hauling in hay, and shipping his own goods out — so energy costs can be paid three times over or more. The other is to pass it on: Ambix, which makes plastic parts, uses resin, and resin comes from oil; some costs rose 30%, 40%, 50%. At first it resisted raising prices, but as the war dragged on it began passing the 60 cents its suppliers added straight to customers.

15:36 Six-dollar diesel in August, and the shock starts embedding in the economy
When energy prices eased this summer, many businesses had a spell of optimism, thinking maybe they were coming out of the woods. Then in August tensions flared again, fuel prices rose again, and recently diesel hit $6 a gallon. Owen thinks this is the moment when some businesses and economists began to realize "the price shock is truly embedding in the economy." Meanwhile, JPMorgan's commodities analysts said in their latest forecast that they no longer know how to model it — there's no baseline, because they can't see around the corner. On paper many economic indicators are healthy, but consumers feel terrible about prices, and nobody — oil executives, politicians, or CEOs — can say clearly how long this will last.

item.title: Optimism Is Not a Personality Trait, It's an Explanatory Style You Can Train
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-hiddenbrain-乐观不是性格-是一套可以练的解释风格/
item.description: Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.
item.content:encoded:
Helplessness is learned, and so is optimism. What decides whether a person gives up is not the blow itself, but whether he explains it as permanent, pervasive, or his own fault.

Seligman himself walks through the full chain from learned helplessness to learned optimism, and in the back half treats agency as a civilizational variable to be quantified — a rare angle.

9:36 The dog doesn't escape because it never learned that escaping was possible
In Solomon's lab, on day one the dog was strapped into a hammock and given Pavlovian shocks it could not escape no matter what it did; on day two it was placed in a shuttle box where running to the other side would shut off the shock, and the dog just lay there. Seligman's judgment was that what the animal actually learned was not "the tone predicts shock" but "nothing I do matters." That reading was in direct conflict with behaviorism at the time, because it required the animal to be a cognitive subject capable of thinking and integrating experience across time.

13:50 People can be taught to give up by noise too
Hiroto moved the same design onto humans: on day one, headphones played a harsh noise, and for one group no amount of button-pressing could turn it off, while for the other group pressing a button did turn it off. On day two they were given a four-foot "human shuttle box" — hand on one side, the noise sounds; move it to the other side, it stops. People who had been through uncontrollable noise the day before simply left their hand in place. Seligman stresses that the variable doing the work is not the trauma itself but whether there was control over the trauma — and they ran control experiments on exactly this point.

19:00 Helplessness became the model for depression
In 1970 depression was not yet a diagnostic category; there was only "manic-depressive illness." By 1975 the American Psychiatric Association's DSM had for the first time split out "unipolar depression," listing nine symptoms: passivity, cognitive difficulty, sadness, anxiety, sleep problems, food losing its taste, numbness, loss of pleasure, thoughts of death. Seligman compared the nine symptoms against the learned-helplessness literature that had accumulated, and found that eight of them could be reproduced in the lab; the only one missing was thoughts of death — probably because the experiments used noise rather than something more severe. This model later became the dominant model of depression, and the drugs that could break helplessness in the lab became mainstream antidepressants.

22:19 Five out of eight give up; a third do not
Across the whole helplessness literature the effect is statistical: on average five out of eight people or eight rats become helpless, and roughly a third do not. From the 1970s on, Seligman kept asking what was different about that third, and it became the turning point of his career. The answer landed on explanatory style: people who explain bad events as permanent ("I'm stupid"), pervasive ("I'm unlovable"), and their own fault become helpless; people who explain them as temporary, local, and not their fault recover quickly.

26:50 West Point's first week predicts who will drop out
The first six weeks after entering West Point are called Beast Barracks: woken at four in the morning to run ten miles, systematically put through the wringer, with the stated purpose being to "break them," and roughly a third of candidates quit. Seligman's team measured explanatory style on day one, and the ones who dropped out were the pessimists. The same pattern showed up in college grades (optimists outperformed their talent, pessimists underperformed it) and in insurance sales: MetLife lost 50% of new hires within a year and 90% within four years; they hired 140 "special forces" recruits whose optimism-scale scores were off the charts, and this group outsold the whole company and still had 75% on the job after four years, while the ordinary group was down to 10%.

34:17 Agency breaks down into three beliefs
Seligman defines agency as the opposite of learned helplessness, made up of three parts: efficacy, the belief that you can accomplish a specific goal right here and now; optimism, the belief that you can accomplish it not only now but in the future and the further future; and imagination, the range of possible goals you can picture — the wider the range, the stronger the agency. Full agency is: I can do it now, I can do it in the future, and I can innovate across many different situations.

36:22 The Axial Age's answer may have been "I can do it"
Between 1000 and 500 BCE, Greece, the Hebrew world, China, India, and Persia all underwent upheaval: the Buddha, Confucius, and Socrates appeared, and technology, medicine, art, literature, and the first political freedoms all erupted together. Seligman's hypothesis is that over those five centuries humanity discovered the concept of agency. The evidence is vocabulary: in the Iliad, Achilles does not decide to act on his own — Athena tells him to act; a hundred years later, in the Odyssey, Odysseus is already a wily, resourceful man who makes his own decisions, and the gods begin to exit the stage. By 500 BCE, every culture had produced a large vocabulary of human agency.

38:30 In the Old Testament, the verbs God commands with are declining
Seligman took the entire Old Testament and counted agency verbs: broadly, in the Pentateuch God commands and people obey, with only a few exceptions like "choose life"; the further along you go, into the Prophets and the Writings, the more words of human agency appear and the fewer words of divine agency. You can now have AI score each book for agency, and plotted over time it comes out linear — from the Pentateuch to the Babylonian exile around 300 BCE, agency increases, and it correlates linearly with human innovation, population, living standards, political freedom, and technology.

item.description: Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.
item.content:encoded:
Robert Moses stacked appointed positions into power, rewrote New York with parks and highways, and wrote racial bias into the city's fabric — his legacy is still being argued over today.

This episode is medium-density on information, but how Moses accumulated power through unelected positions, and the actual words from his 1945 Atlantic Monthly article, are valuable for understanding urban governance and how power operates.

1:01 Never elected, yet he held enormous power
Robert Moses was never elected to any public office in his life, yet he accumulated enormous power through appointment to various government positions. According to Encyclopaedia Britannica, his work includes 35 highways, 12 bridges, numerous parks, Lincoln Center for the Performing Arts, Shea Stadium, many housing projects, two hydroelectric power plants, and the 1964 New York World's Fair. He has been dead 45 years and remains a divisive figure, and his legacy may be argued over for another century or more.

6:10 His mentor taught him not to anger voters
Moses became chief of staff of the New York State Reconstruction Commission in 1919 and learned a great deal from Belle Moskovitz. Moskovitz understood deeply how to maneuver within government to achieve goals without angering those in power. One example: in an early draft of a report, Moses suggested cutting part of the workforce, and Moskovitz reminded him that every one of those people was a voter, that they could not be made angry, and that a way had to be found to cut costs without cutting that many people. This ‘don't anger the voters’ thinking ran through his later government work.

11:11 Parks were the means, highways were the end
When Moses took over the parks commission, most green-space plans merely preserved natural wilderness, but he envisioned adding more manicured landscaping and dedicated recreation areas. More importantly, every time he built a new park, he made sure the project included roads connecting the park to highways — that is where the parkway came from. From the start he planned a large state park system for Long Island, all connected by new roads. In just four years in the job, he added 13 parks to Long Island, about 9,700 acres in total, where previously there had been only one park.

13:14 His mother lent him $20,000 to save Jones Beach
Jones Beach was originally just a sandbar on the southern edge of Long Island, almost completely submerged at high tide. Moses wanted to turn it into a great park, and most of the government and the press considered it impractical. He began with large-scale dredging, pulling about 40 million cubic yards of sand from the seabed, raising the sandbar from two feet above sea level to twelve feet. But the project nearly died when the money ran out, and Moses did something highly unusual: he borrowed $20,000 from his mother, Bella, to continue the work. He later confirmed that if his mother had not put up the money, the contractor would not have brought the equipment back to finish. Jones Beach finally opened on August 4, 1925, in a dust storm, and an estimated 1.5 million people visited in its first year.

22:31 His only campaign, and he lost badly
Moses ran for public office only once in his life. In 1934 he ran for governor of New York and was thoroughly defeated by the incumbent Democratic governor, Herbert H. Lehman. Lehman received more than 2.2 million popular votes; Moses got fewer than 1.4 million. Reporting Lehman's victory, The New York Times wrote: ‘Meanwhile, his formidable and combative opponent, Robert Moses, will be free to continue his work as the great parks commissioner.’ After this defeat he never tried campaigning again, and instead continued to expand his power through appointed positions.

23:33 235 new playgrounds, only one in Harlem
Starting in the 1930s, Moses greatly expanded the city's playgrounds, building 235 new ones. But a pattern began to emerge: he ignored the needs of districts with predominantly non-white populations. Of the 235 playgrounds, only one was in Harlem. In the summer of 1936 he opened 11 new swimming pools: 4 in Manhattan (including one in Harlem and one in West Harlem), 4 in Brooklyn, and 1 each in the Bronx, Queens, and Staten Island. These pools had new filtration and chlorination systems, heating and underwater lighting, and were considered advanced, but they were also designed to be drained in the cooler months and used for other activities, from shuffleboard to roller skating.

24:35 ‘Tear down the slums, just build a road’
In a 1945 article in The Atlantic Monthly, Moses opened by describing how slums form: existing buildings overcrowded, speculators adding tenants, people packed into tenements like chickens. But the ‘cure’ he offered was this: clearing slums has in most cities been accomplished indirectly — not for public, semi-public, or private housing, but for parks, playgrounds, parkways, highways, boulevards, and other public improvements. He boasted that his ‘demolition-and-construction demon squad’ had torn down more old slums than all the housing experts combined, and that ‘we built nothing but broad highways, lined with landscaping and recreational facilities.’

33:43 Eminent domain is the only salvation
In the article Moses explicitly endorsed the use of eminent domain to acquire land. He wrote that buying large tracts of land at a reasonable price had become impossible, and that in such a situation, ‘eminent domain is the only salvation.’ Eminent domain had to be exercised by the city, state, or federal government for private limited-dividend or redevelopment companies. He also criticized unions as ‘a serious obstacle to financing slum clearance,’ accusing them of insisting on retaining hourly-wage rights, striking, and ‘resisting invention and improvement in the building field.’ He said this attitude was ‘without rhyme or reason’ and would not change until a better-educated new generation of union officials appeared.

item.title: Blame Is Not Revenge: A Philosopher Argues We Should Blame Less
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-phibites-责备不是报复-哲学家主张我们该少责备一点/
item.description: Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.
item.content:encoded:
Miranda Fricker argues that retributive blame makes no sense, and that the most valuable blame is "communicative blame" — aimed at getting the other person to genuinely understand the moral significance of what they did, and reaching shared moral understanding.

In 23 minutes it offers a workable moral framework: distinguishing retributive from communicative blame, and explaining why blaming less is not the same as abandoning responsibility.

0:04 There is no single definition of blame
Fricker points out that the philosophical literature holds a great many different views of blame: some say it is a hostile emotion, some a reactive attitude, some merely a judgment, some a rupture in a relationship, and some a form of protest. She suspects these views are not even talking about the same thing. She holds that the object of blame can be any agent — an individual, an institution, or even a collective as large as a nation — as long as it has done something wrong, it is a fitting object of blame.

2:05 Retributive blame has no logic to it
Fricker defines retributive blame as: you wronged me, I am at a disadvantage, so I am entitled to even the score by making you suffer a little too — "getting even" is its most apt metaphor. She says she does not believe this logic in interpersonal morality, and does not find it useful. She concedes she does not want to say anything specific about criminal punishment, but admits she is strongly inclined to think the retributive idea there is rather unpleasant. She believes genuinely useful alternatives exist.

3:08 Communicative blame wants shared understanding
Fricker holds that the morally most valuable model of blame is the one aimed at making the other person fully grasp the moral significance of their conduct. If you blame me for wronging you, perhaps I have not fully understood the moral weight of what I did; you put it into the conversation, and I either come to understand what I did or push back that it was "not that serious," and in the end the two of us reach a shared moral understanding of what happened between us. She admits this is an ideal, but one worth pursuing, and calls it "communicative blame."

5:11 Blame is at bottom a judgment of moral wrongdoing
After the functional analysis, Fricker gives her own definition of blame: blame is a judgment of moral wrongdoing, and that judgment is in some sense activated or driven by a disposition suited to holding someone responsible. She stresses that this is the context of moral blame. The definition is minimalist, and she thinks its advantage is that it transplants across domains — when she studies epistemic blame, for instance, she need not assume the blamer harbours hostile feelings toward the blamed, only that there is an epistemic fault and that the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding stance rather than passive observation.

6:11 An apology must be made to the right person
Fricker points to a key difference between apology and blame: communicative blame can be broadcast anywhere, and conveying the meaning of blame to a third party can be derived from conveying it to the person concerned — both promote shared moral understanding; but apologising to someone you did not wrong is not an apology at all. Apology is essentially second-personal moral address, and must be done to the right person. She also notes that apology's reparative power is tied to an ongoing relationship — if a stranger wrongs you at random, there is no need to chase an apology, and we all have to learn to let things go.

9:12 Sincerity is not all-or-nothing
Fricker rejects treating sincerity as all-or-nothing. She holds that in most apology practices a person need only be "sincere enough" to count as apologising, and sincere enough in the right way to be accepted by the particular person being apologised to. She cites the philosopher Jeffrey Helmich's notion of the "apology stance": an apology is a speech act that not only expresses but "enacts" the appropriate sorry inner state. She adds that an over-elaborate apology is merely irritating — an apology is a social performance, and must fall within the bandwidth of aptness to be accepted.

12:15 Responsibility is a social construction, not metaphysics
Faced with the minority view that genes and environment determine everything and no one is ever responsible, Fricker argues that this line of thought locates the threshold of responsibility in a metaphysical rather than a natural place. She understands responsibility as something that grows out of the practice of human beings living together, for the sake of social coordination and harmony, and to build shared moral consciousness. She borrows Peter Strawson's approach: whatever the metaphysics, in everyday life we simply cannot help praising and blaming. She holds that separating metaphysics from the practice of responsibility is itself a way of leading people astray.

19:20 Blaming less is a trainable choice
Fricker says that if blame is a judgment of fault, and the judgment issues from a responsibility-holding moral stance, then we can choose how much of human behaviour to bring into this "fault-finding" construction. She gives the example of lateness: some people are highly moralistic about others being late, others are not offended at all. She admits she prefers a world in which everyone is a bit more relaxed about lateness of up to 15 minutes, where it need not be constructed as a matter of respect — it is just "you were a little late," and that is all.

item.title: Chinese open-weight models lead, and distillation explains only one to two months of the gap

item.description: Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.
item.content:encoded:
Chinese models lead across the board on downloads and benchmarks, but distillation explains only one to two months of the gap — the real reasons are release cadence and task focus; US companies are already building products on Chinese models.

This is a state-of-open-models briefing for Congress: high data density, clear judgments, suited to anyone who wants to grasp the US-China open-model landscape quickly.

0:00 Open weights is not the same thing as open source
An open-weight model releases only the weights and a license; an open-source model also releases the training code and data. America's genuinely open-source models are led by nonprofits, such as the Allen Institute for AI's Olmo, OpenAthena's Marin, and EleutherAI's Pythia. Nvidia's Nemotron is more open than most open-weight models, having released a large amount of training data, but because it has not released all of it, it still does not count as fully open source. The distinction matters: when people discuss ‘open source’, what they are actually talking about is mostly open weights.

0:00 Chinese models have crossed the agentic capability threshold
GLM-5.2 and Kimi K3 achieved a step change in commercial viability, crossing a threshold in agentic capability similar to the one Anthropic's Claude Code crossed in December 2025. Chinese open-weight models overtook the US in these two key areas roughly 18 months ago. On Hugging Face downloads, China took the lead in July 2025, mainly on the back of Alibaba's Qwen. Data from the ATOM project, which the author maintains, shows China's download lead has grown to about 1.6 billion out of a total of 3.2 billion — twice that of the US.

0:00 The benchmark score gap is stark
On the Artificial Analysis Intelligence Index, as of September 14, 2026, the top three are Chinese models: Z.ai's GLM-5.3 and GLM-5.3-Flash score 45 and 42, and Moonshot AI's Kimi K3 scores 44. The US leaders are Thinking Machines' Inkling and Inkling Small, both scoring 26, and Nvidia's Nemotron 3 Ultra at 23. The top US models were released in June and July 2026, and refresh less often than their Chinese counterparts. Chinese labs are closest on tasks with well-defined demand, such as agentic coding, and lag further behind on open-ended scientific tasks like physics and biology.

0:00 Distillation explains only one to two months of the gap
Distillation is a technique Chinese labs use often, training their own models on the outputs of stronger models, but the author estimates that even if distillation were blocked entirely — say by deploying KYC tools at Anthropic and OpenAI — the gap between the strongest US models and Chinese open-weight models would widen by only 1-2 months. Distillation matters most in new domains, and it cannot easily produce a comprehensively strong final model. Chinese labs ship faster and with a narrower task distribution, which slightly inflates scores on public benchmarks, because all labs keep improving and later-released models naturally score higher.

0:00 US companies are building products on Chinese models
Harvey, Cursor and DoorDash use Kimi; Airbnb uses Qwen; Perplexity uses DeepSeek. A large number of young Silicon Valley startups use Chinese models to get a low-cost, flexible option. US startups sign enterprise agreements with Chinese model labs to license products for use — a new form of cross-border technology cooperation the author has not seen in his career. On OpenRouter, the Chinese model share has grown from about 70% to more than 80%, and weekly tokens processed have grown from about 1 trillion in September 2025 to about 80 trillion today. On OpenCode, Chinese models account for about 95% or more of inference volume.

0:00 Academia has already been taken over by Qwen
The author scanned papers in the five most popular ML categories on arXiv (cs.AI, cs.CL, cs.CV, cs.LG, stat.ML). In January 2023, papers mentioning any open model were 2%; by September 2026 they reached 50%. In April-May 2023, of about 12,000 new papers, 2,600 mentioned at least one open-model family, 5.5% mentioned Llama and 1% mentioned Chinese models. At Llama's peak in autumn 2024, 23% mentioned Llama and 7.5% mentioned Qwen. Today Llama is still mentioned by about 21% of papers, while Qwen has risen to 30%. Any Chinese open-weight model is mentioned by more than 40% of papers, versus 30% for the US.

0:00 US models are adopted more at equal capability
Research shows that US models are adopted disproportionately often at comparable capability and scale. OpenAI's gpt-oss, its first open-weight models after ChatGPT, became one of the most widely adopted open-weight models ever. Google's Gemma 4 is one of the few models whose adoption approaches Qwen's most popular small models. Nvidia's Nemotron, despite being more capable at the same scale, has seen middling adoption. This shows US models have brand and ecosystem advantages, but not enough to reverse the overall trend.

0:00 Open-model risk needs ecosystem-level preparation
The structural challenge of open-weight models is that there is almost no effective way to stop pieces of open-source software from falling into the wrong hands. If access to China's strongest open-weight models were restricted because of risk, the ones hurt would be US companies. HuggingFace once used a Chinese open-weight model to understand a cyberattack, because closed models refused the request. Managing open-weight model risk tends to come down to ecosystem preparation. Open models are becoming an essential tool for AI diffusion, and continuing to invest in US open models is the best path to staying ahead of these risks.

item.title: Poetry Is Not Democracy's Ornament but Its Pillar
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-mindscape-诗歌不是民主的点缀-而是民主的支柱/
item.description: Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.
item.content:encoded:
Banning books and telling teachers what they can't teach strikes at the root of free expression just like censoring the news; who a collective is and what it values takes shape through language — art is democracy's infrastructure, not its poster.

Not a literature class: a working poet who also heads the largest humanities funder in the country explains why close reading, naming and literacy are political capacities; the back half is harder than the opening.

5:32 The poet went to the scene instead of writing reflections
Rukeyser was not a poet who stayed in her study. At 19, while studying at Vassar, she felt she had to go south to sit in on the Scottsboro trial — staying at school was simply not an option; in 1936 she went to Spain to see the anti-Olympics mounted against the Berlin Games, and arrived just as the Spanish Civil War broke out; she also went to West Virginia to write about the Hawks Nest mine disaster — Union Carbide was digging a tunnel without wet drilling and without giving workers protective equipment, the workers were mostly African American, and nearly all of them died of silicosis, which Alexander says may be the largest corporate industrial accident in American history. The conclusion: writing lets more people know what happened, and connects people of different identities on shared human experience.

13:50 Art is a pillar of democracy, not an illustration
She breaks democracy down into a question of language: who a collective is, what it values, which voices it contains, all take shape through language, so without language there is no collective. When we talk about free speech we always fixate on journalism, but artists being censored, books being banned, teachers being told what they can teach — that moves the same foundation. Her wording is hard: art is not democracy's explanatory diagram, art is itself part of democracy — one of its pillars. And poetry does not just wave a flag for values; it is the thing itself. You can judge whether a democracy is healthy by whether art can still live in an unfettered space.

33:37 Close reading is critical thinking, and it can be taught
She describes close reading very plainly: a method, a practice, anyone can learn it, and its other name is critical thinking. Its use is not limited to poetry — you can use it reading the newspaper, reading the propaganda around you, whether that comes from above or from advertising and very, very powerful culture. Figuring out how others are working on you is a good thing. And in America, many people are nervous about poetry, feeling they ‘shouldn't be able to understand it’; her method is concrete: drop your shoulders, read it again, don't just read it on the page, read it aloud, then you read it to me — the same poem read by a different person, and you hear something different every time.
