42:37 Misnaming people is an anti-democratic weapon
She says one of the most powerful weapons against democracy is misnaming people, calling people by the wrong name. In America there is a saying, calling people out of their names, which means flattening people, using insulting labels, even smearing the behavior of an entire people as a whole — this is abuse of language, its purpose is to wound and divide, and it is coming from the highest levels of government. She stresses one thing in particular: it has real consequences. Conversely, naming things precisely, saying what you mean, saying who you are, and catching what others say — these are themselves the capacities democracy needs.

47:58 Grief has to be put into language to be held
Her husband Fikre died 14 years ago. She wrote a memoir shortly after his death, which surprised even her — she had never thought she would write one or show it to anyone; it was more a way of landing, of knowing what she was going through: too overwhelming, too unprecedented, and turning some of it into language helped her name the feeling. Writing about him years later was different in kind, became a responsibility: this person was her ‘my person’, who lived a brave, extraordinary, beautiful life and left hundreds of paintings, now shown in museums and galleries. She is wary of herself too: she hopes she is not wringing this experience dry.

57:30 Writing poetry throws away far more than it keeps
She does not start a poem from ‘I want to write a poem about X’, but from a word, an image, a phrase that is ringing there, and she can't say why, so she writes it down again and again. She has a day job — almost all poets do — so the real question is: while you're busy with something else, where do you put the thought down. Fragments accumulate slowly, and when she has time to sit down, she asks which piece is still vibrating, still alive. How much does she write versus throw away? Her answer is one word: Most. A serious writer throws away many times what they keep, and that takes a little courage, to keep writing even when it's wrong. What really excites her is the editing stage, because ‘the beast is there’, the outline is already visible.

1:02:17 The cost of college is a problem; learning is not
She directly rebuts the claim that the humanities have no prospects: critical thinking, close reading, extracting meaning from complex texts, communicating persuasively, imagining other people's lives, understanding multiple cultures — these are capacities useful in any career. She does not deny that the cost of higher education is a real problem that really needs solving, but she puts the emphasis elsewhere: what is more worrying is the attack on the university itself, interference in its mission, and the claim that ‘the university is not a valuable thing’ being repeated loudly. Her last line is sharp: creating an undereducated populace serves another purpose.

1:07:22 Those who cannot read are the easiest to control
‘free people read freely’ is a line from the poet and librarian Tracie D. Hall, and Alexander says she borrows it all day long. She reads those five words out of the African American tradition: under slavery, it was a crime for Black people to learn to read and write, and it was equally a crime for a free white person to teach a Black person to read and write — what was being controlled was not the text, it was the person. So the line holds two halves: free people read freely, and, free people are meant to read. If a person cannot read, cannot access a mass of information, they cannot understand their own life, and so lose the capacity to act on an understanding of how outside forces work on them. Where literacy is stripped away, there is only one logic: this is how you are easier to control.

item.title: Literacy Once Democratised Europe; Now It Is Retreating
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-econtalk-识字率曾让欧洲民主化-如今却在倒退/
item.description: Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.
item.content:encoded:
Writing cooled human communication from an emotional, face-to-face oral culture into a textual culture of evidence and logic; rising literacy once drove democratic revolutions, and screens are pulling public discourse back toward a pre-literate age.

Medium information density, but two mechanisms are worth hearing: "writing cools discourse" and "bad ideas are easier to whitewash on film"; the later section on pop music and reading is looser.

8:13 Literacy is historically extremely recent and fragile
Marriott stresses that we are so used to literacy that we forget how anomalous it is. By one estimate, in a certain ancient Mesopotamian city-state there may have been only 20 living people who could read and write; literacy in ancient Rome was around 10%. For thousands of years, reading and writing was not a cultural phenomenon but an esoteric code circulating within a wealthy scribal elite — some rulers were literate, some were not. The real turning point was printing: books could be reproduced in quantity, more people could read them, and books became more practical; Protestantism then placed extreme emphasis on the written word, pushing more people to become literate in order to read the Bible. These factors fed each other until the "Reading Revolution" historians identify in the mid-to-late 18th century.

11:19 The Reading Revolution really did change political form
Roberts pushes back: if literacy exploded, why doesn't the world look turned upside down? Marriott's answer is that the spread of literacy has a democratising effect — the more people who can access information and ideas, the more people participate in politics and criticise power. Early 18th-century Europe was ruled by absolute monarchs, and political affairs were essentially court secrets discussed among a small elite; by the late 18th and early 19th centuries, newspapers appeared, the standing of absolute monarchs declined sharply, France became a republic, the authority of the British monarch was far weaker than at the start of the century, parliamentary debates were reported, and public affairs were no longer discussed only in court. He calls this the great age of democratic revolution and democratic reform, and ties it directly to the spread of literacy.

16:32 Writing forces bad ideas into logical form
Marriott concedes books are imperfect, but argues that the way books organise information is more rational and more coherent than conversation, video or TikTok. Writing forces you to polish an idea repeatedly, externalising part of your mind onto the page and then testing it; the reader faces a fixed text and can reread and critically analyse it. More crucially, books restrict the means of non-logical persuasion — you cannot bypass argument with charisma, shouting or tears. He uses the Nazis as a counterexample: Hitler's Mein Kampf was unreadable even to Nazi elites, because Nazism simply does not hold together once it is required to be presented coherently as a written text; yet Riefenstahl's Triumph of the Will is treated as an artistic masterpiece, screened in film classes, and regarded as an extremely powerful argument for fascism. Bad ideas are easier to whitewash on screen than in a book.

25:05 The Republic of Letters filtered out trolls through writing
The 17th- and 18th-century European "Republic of Letters" was a community of thinkers, philosophers and scientists who wrote letters to one another and founded journals. The economic historian Joel Mokyr rates it enormously highly, even calling it the single cultural fact that explains the Industrial Revolution. Marriott's mechanism is this: if clever people sit alone in a village, their ideas can only be told to their neighbours, and scientific innovation struggles to accumulate; the spread of literacy let ideas travel further, more and more people joined the conversation, ideas flowed into a central pool, and thought grew more complex. Roberts adds that the key difference is not public versus private but who the participants are — conversing with Adam Smith, David Hume or Newton sets a high bar, a kind of "submission to something that cannot be enforced". Marriott concedes that the literacy barrier itself carries a benign elitism: you cannot burst in and shout like a troll on X, because nobody will pay attention to you.

34:49 The novel gives us a passage into other minds
Marriott argues there is a truth about life reachable only through prose fiction: it lets us see the inside of other people's minds. Reading is an active rather than passive process — you build images in your head from the words on the page, which is why it is immersive, why it feels like having lived another life. Film cannot do this, because it gives you the external world and cannot enter another mind directly; and writing is precisely the medium we use to express what is in our minds, mind communicating with mind. He also notes that oral poetry takes little interest in the subtle differences between human consciousnesses, and that this capacity to "inhabit another mind" appears only in prose fiction. Roberts does not fully agree, holding that great film can get close through dialogue, but concedes that film almost never captures the inner activity conveyed by something other than dialogue.

47:59 The post-literate commentator is more like Homer
Marriott writes that the post-literate commentator, unlike the print-era public intellectual, does not explain and analyse the world but is more like an oral storyteller, weaving strange and unforgettable stories for an entranced audience. Roberts considers this the deepest insight in the whole piece: faced with the mass of absurd, untenable statements online, people habitually interrogate them by the author's standards — "that isn't logical", "where's the evidence?" — but these people are simply not in that business. Their job is to entertain the audience; truth does not matter, what matters is a story that enthrals. Marriott goes further: presenting an argument logically, supplying evidence, driving to a rational conclusion — these are not in fact natural to human communication; in an oral culture, the more effective way to persuade someone is to entertain him, move him, get angry at him. Writing imposes an impersonal, more rational form of communication, and it is not a necessary product of human communication.

53:59 The richness of pop music also feeds on reading
Roberts cites an example from The History of Rock and Roll in 500 Songs: the opening of Jagger's "Sympathy for the Devil" is taken directly from Bulgakov's The Master and Margarita — the novel opens with two Russian intellectuals mocking God and faith, after which a suave gentleman appears, they take him for mad, and finally realise he is Satan. Marriott calls it an "annoyingly good" example and regrets not having put it in the book. He concedes it cannot be pushed too far — it is not that you must move Penguin Classics into the British Library to join a boy band — but Bob Dylan and Paul McCartney are both obviously heavy readers. He cites research showing that over the past 20 years pop songs have grown less complex in both lyrics and melody, partly because the environment favours the simple and the immediate: to go viral on TikTok, a song has to grab you within three or four seconds.

58:17 The future of reading will be deliberate, like fitness
Marriott stresses this is not a new phenomenon: statistics on the decline of serious reading go back to the 1950s and 1960s, television was the beginning of the screen age, and the remote control was the first scroll. Roberts quotes what his father said at the time — books have existed for centuries, television has been a mass medium for only 20 years, let's see whether it lasts — and concedes his father should have worried more. Marriott's consolation comes from an analogy with junk food and fitness: McDonald's arrived, many people got fat, but some realised that health could no longer be absorbed naturally from the environment and required deliberate effort, so they started running and going to the gym. He guesses cognitive health will follow the same path: if reading has a future, it will become more deliberate, less "I'm bored at the airport, I'll pick up a book" and more "I value this experience, so I sit down for half an hour to an hour every night". He admits this makes him a little sad, because reading will become more artificial, no longer the unavoidable part of life it once was.

item.title: A Glass of Water Has No Final Truth: Quantum Mechanics Forces Us to Give Up the Single Perspective
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-startweek-一杯水没有终极真相-量子力学逼我们放弃单一视角/
item.description: Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.
item.content:encoded:
Physicist Carlo Rovelli says the deepest lesson of quantum mechanics is not a new particle, but that the Enlightenment dream of a single objective reality independent of the observer does not hold — reality is multiple perspectives that enrich one another but do not converge.

A four-person roundtable crossing physics, poetry, drama and economics; high density of quotable lines but the argument is loose. Worth listening if you want a few perspectives that can change your judgment; skip it if you want hard information.

2:06 A glass of water has no final version
Rovelli opens with a glass of water the BBC provided: you look from one side, I look from the other, you wear glasses, I see a different colour. This glass of water can be a physical object (mass, velocity, position), it can be temperature and pressure, it can be the chemistry of H2O plus floating bits, it can be the global economy of being bottled in Italy and shipped to England, or it can simply be ‘we want to drink it’. His claim is: these perspectives are all real, none exhausts another, none contradicts another, and there is no ‘ultimate glass of water’. This is anti-Platonic — he does not accept a distinction between a ‘level of appearances’ and a ‘fundamental level’.

6:13 We have not yet digested quantum mechanics
Rovelli says what he is describing is not borrowed from philosophy but grown from inside physics. Physicists ran into quantum phenomena; quantum mechanics is a huge revolution, but ‘we have not yet digested quantum mechanics’ — the newspaper stories about experiments that ‘confirm what I learned in a textbook in the 1970s’ show precisely that we do not yet truly believe it. Take quantum mechanics seriously and what it says is this: the Enlightenment dream of ‘describing reality completely, determinately, clearly, independently of the observer’ does not hold. The observer here need not be a human; anything that interacts with something else counts.

8:19 The deepest level of reality is not more objective
Rovelli turns it around: the reality at the most basic level physics can reach is in fact not essentially different from the reality Lavinia deals with in poetry, or that James's characters deal with in economics — both are realities that allow different views, not a reality that is ‘absolutely objective underneath’. So quantum physics is not that hard; it has simply not been digested. The concrete physical phenomena are of course complex, but poetry is complex and economics is complex too.

10:25 Scientists have always used metaphors
Rovelli says the words Lavinia uses could be lifted line by line into his book. What is an electron? ‘It is a grain, a grain of sand, but it is not really a grain of sand.’ Why is an electric field called a field? Because it is ‘a bit like a field in the countryside’. We think through metaphor, by taking old concepts apart and piecing a new concept out of a bit of each. The goal is not to arrive at a final, perfect description of reality — a century ago we thought we could, but it does not work — but to gain a better understanding, a better way of navigating reality. He adds a crucial qualification: admitting that everything has a perspective does not mean all perspectives are equivalent, nor that there is no better and worse; it is only that the hope of ‘arriving at the final correct story about reality’ is empty — not unreachable, but meaningless.

12:27 Seeking the ultimate morality is itself wrong
Rovelli turns from ‘complexity’ to ‘value’: if you ask ‘what is the ultimate definition of good and evil, what is universal ethics’, he thinks this is itself a morally and ethically wrong approach. Our morals and values are powerful, important and indispensable not because they are outside us, but because they are inside us, and therefore equally perspectival. This passage connects directly to James Graham's play — whose first line is ‘what is a good life’.

15:30 Do not be afraid to learn a jargon
Lavinia Greenlaw argues for embracing jargon: not everyone has to learn it, but if you are genuinely interested in something, do not be afraid to learn its language — a mechanic has to learn the names of parts, a surgeon has to learn the names of parts, and a poet does too. It lets you see more clearly, and it lets you see where something has gone wrong. She admits jargon can be exclusionary, but ‘that depends on the context in which you use it’, and ‘you can perform difficulty, and poets and poems are probably quite good at that, but that is not what difficulty is for’. She gives the example of poems on the underground: before everyone looked at their phones, people would read a poem first and only then realise they were reading a poem — that kind of engagement is far more direct and confident than sitting down and being told ‘now you are going to read a poem’.

22:55 Friction is treated as a problem to be solved
James Graham says modern culture has fetishised ‘efficiency’ and strips out every layer of difficulty as friction. He gives a concrete image: emailing himself a script to save it, a prompt pops up — ‘this is a long document, shall I summarise it for you?’ — and his reaction is ‘how rude, I want you to sit inside it and read’. He connects back to Bloomsbury and Keynes: meaning is discovered precisely in the friction, in the difficulty, in the process. He also says the collapse of reading is despairing, because reading demands personal investment, and today that investment is treated as a problem to be solved rather than something to be celebrated.

26:05 War refuses to acknowledge complexity
Rovelli uses International Peace Day on 21 September, and the words of the UN Secretary-General and the Pope, to connect the perspectival argument to war: war is to a large extent driven by greed and power games, but it always wraps itself in a hypocritical narrative — there is only one truth, only one good, we are the good ones, they are the bad ones, we tell the truth, they tell lies and propaganda. So war is built on a total refusal to be prepared to accept complexity, perspectives, and worldviews different from our own. The host Adam Rutherford raises a counterexample on the spot: we also always need to pursue simplicity; if we embraced difficulty and acted scholarly all day, we might get nothing done and enjoy nothing. Lavinia's response pulls the topic back to rhetoric: language therefore matters more than ever, and poetry and poetics can teach people to argue.

item.title: Apple has no frontier model of its own, but wants to win again with a foldable
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-decoder-苹果没有自己的前沿模型-却想靠折叠屏再赢一次/
item.description: Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the event introduced no new AI features; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.
item.content:encoded:
Ternus's debut was about an intelligent personal hub, but the event introduced no new AI features; Apple's AI is propped up by Google's models, while its real bet is on a foldable and a pile of product categories that don't exist yet.

Mark Gurman is the most accurate reporter on Apple, and this episode strings executive turnover, the AI roadmap, the privacy controversy and foldable predictions into one line, with high information density.

5:09 The biggest difference between Ternus and Cook is willingness to make the call
Gurman says the event was almost interchangeable with the Cook era, with the only difference being that Ternus opened by laying out a view on AI. The mechanism he gives is management style: you bring an idea to Cook and he keeps probing with questions, in many cases not making a single decision, it's collective decision-making; you go to Ternus and he gives you a decision, gives you an opinion, you may hate the opinion, but he takes a position. Gurman stresses this is exactly the biggest difference between the two that came out of talking to insiders, and it explains why Ternus talked about AI first thing on stage.

8:20 The 2026 event had not one new AI feature
Gurman points out that Apple held a big product event in September 2026 and launched no notable new AI features, with the opening 15 minutes or so just retelling the past two years of Apple Intelligence. His explanation: Apple has gone as far on AI as it can and can only tell the best story with the cards it holds; and Apple has no AI-centric device, so it has to prop up the iPhone as its AI device until a killer device appears and it can switch narratives.

13:29 Under Cook, Apple became an institution
Gurman distinguishes the Cook era from the Jobs era: in the Cook era people's relationship with Apple is a relationship with an institution, one that spans the globe, is enormous in scale, like IBM; the Jobs era was one new product after another redefining categories. He also corrects the host's judgment on Vision Pro — every time he writes that Vision Pro is on life support, he gets dozens of reactions close to death-threat level, because some people have built businesses around spatial computing, and some consumers paid four thousand dollars for it.

20:45 Apple took five years to replace the old guard one by one
Gurman reconstructs the rhythm of this handover: in 2023 Cook began saying at every executive meeting that succession had to be taken seriously; at the time the top ranks either had five hundred million in the bank or were billionaires, and were close in age. So they lined up an order and went one by one — at the end of 2024 CFO Luca Maestri retired, replaced by Kevin Parekh; in 2025 COO Jeff Williams retired, succeeded by his deputy; in 2026 the general counsel changed, with Jennifer Newstead poached from Meta; and only at the end of 2026 did Cook hand the baton to Ternus. Gurman calls this retention strategy Hotel California: you can never leave.

28:07 The chip chief was kept by handing him a title on the fly
Gurman says the second most important person at Apple now is the hardware head, who built Apple Silicon, Apple's key differentiator. In late summer or early autumn last year, he went to tell Cook he was quitting, right during the preparations for Ternus's succession. Cook had him stay to take part in the transition and promised him the title of chief hardware officer, which Apple had never had, after Ternus took over, letting him keep his existing team and also take over Ternus's side of the business. Gurman judges this is not a long-term arrangement, and that this person already wants to leave again — he conquered the Mac, ditched Intel and Qualcomm, and Apple has no next goal, so he may leave within a year or two, at which point the hardware engineering team will have to be split up again, because no successor carries his industry weight.

33:15 Willing to spend tens of billions on a modem, yet says it needn't own AI
What Gurman finds most absurd is executives saying in interviews over the past year that "we never owned search, we don't need to own AI." He counters: these are two completely different things, and Apple spent tens of billions to own an already commoditized cellular modem, acquiring and fixing Intel's modem business — willing to do that for a modem, yet unwilling to own AI, which is absurd. The internal idea was originally to partner with Google as a stopgap until it could build its own models, but Gurman says he has seen no evidence that Apple is restarting its own model effort, making big AI acquisitions, or paying AI researchers high salaries.

48:53 The watch's all-day transcription stepped on the privacy landmine
Gurman's reaction to the Apple Watch's all-day listening feature was "I can't believe they did it." The feature only transcribes, doesn't record or store, and a double tap shows you the last 15 seconds of what someone said to you, without their consent. He says Apple knows the next-generation interface needs a degree of always-on capture, but the societal privacy problem isn't solved: technical white papers, private cloud compute and encryption can't hold back the social-level backlash. He thinks Apple could have put audio and visual intelligence together next year and told one coherent privacy story; as it is, it's boiling the frog slowly.

57:05 Foldables will become the new normal within a decade
Gurman offers a bold prediction: foldables will become the new normal within a decade. He draws an analogy with smartphone penetration — at the end of 2006 smartphones were about 6% of the market, now 85%, and it crossed half within five or six years; the iPhone itself wasn't that source, but it pulled everyone into the smartphone game, and he thinks the iPhone Duo will do the same for the phone market. He also mentions the iPhone's number migration feature, hinting that the future may be a combination of a foldable for work and a smaller, lighter phone for weekends with family.

item.title: The Real Bottleneck in the Treasury Market: Not Size, but Not Enough Intermediaries
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-macromusings-美债市场真正的瓶颈-不是规模-是中间商不够用了/
item.description: Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders, but the latter collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.
item.content:encoded:
Primary dealers' balance sheets long ago stopped keeping pace with the growth of outstanding Treasuries. Market makers gave way to high-frequency traders, but the latter collectively retreated in March 2020 — that is the core of the Treasury liquidity problem.

A front-line New York Fed operator explains Treasury market structure, including empirical data from two 2025 papers and the latest TBAC developments. High information density.

11:26 The Treasury market is so big it must attract new buyers
Golay gives the scale: CBO counts $30 trillion in outstanding Treasuries at the end of 2025, projected to grow by another $26 to $27 trillion over the next decade. The market splits into two parts — the cash market (direct buying and selling of Treasuries, partly through inter-dealer broker electronic trading, partly dealer-to-client) and the repo market (borrowing collateralized by Treasuries, mainly intermediated by dealers). A market this large and growing necessarily has to attract different types of investors, including price-sensitive high-frequency traders and hedge funds.

14:31 High-frequency traders went from zero to the main force in electronic markets
Golay calls these firms principal trading firms (PTFs), mostly employing high-frequency strategies and trading on electronic platforms. Twenty years ago they were not in the Treasury market at all; today they may account for the majority of electronic cash market trading. The turning point was the 2014 flash rally — a large yield move that no one could explain — which led the official sector to truly understand the growth of PTFs in electronic markets and sparked the IAWG's work to study market structure and obtain better data.

16:33 Primary dealer balance sheets have not kept up with the growth in outstanding Treasuries
Golay cites a chart from a Darrell Duffie paper: the size of primary dealers' balance sheets relative to their Treasury intermediation has completely failed to keep pace with the growth in outstanding Treasuries. Part of the reason is post-2008 reforms, and part is simply that the growth in outstanding Treasuries itself has been too fast. The result is that the market has had to attract more price-sensitive types of investors. She also corrects a common impression: it is not that PTFs always retreat during volatility; in other volatile periods the official sector has observed increased PTF activity. But in March 2020, everyone retreated.

19:42 The essence of all-to-all is bypassing dealer matching
All-to-all trading is literally that: any participant in the Treasury market can trade with any other participant. This is not new in the equity market, but the Treasury market is largely over-the-counter and dealer-intermediated, so it is not the case there. Golay points out that entering the March 2020 crisis, dealers already had a lot of Treasuries on their balance sheets, and when the wave of selling hit, there was no intermediation capacity left. If counterparties could be matched without going through a dealer, perhaps that could ease things. But she explicitly says that at the time most people were selling, and it is hard to imagine all-to-all perfectly solving that situation — it is just that every incremental improvement helps.

22:51 All-to-all is stuck on the lack of counterparty matching
One of the paper's core findings: in the off-the-run market, if you look at a 15-minute window, almost no one wants to buy the same off-the-run security you want to sell. Extend the window to a day, and the match rate rises to 60% to 70%. Golay mentions possible innovation directions, such as an end-of-day batch auction, and some institutions already have such capabilities. But to date, no case in this area has truly succeeded. She also mentions that expanding central clearing could push the transition to all-to-all, because you would not need to establish bilateral clearing arrangements with every counterparty — just connect to a central counterparty.

29:06 Off-the-run is 97% of outstanding but a liquidity desert
Off-the-run refers to older Treasuries, ranging from those issued three months ago to 29- and 30-year bonds, accounting for about 97% of outstanding Treasuries. The March 2020 dash for cash selling was mainly off-the-run, and the off-the-run market is dealer-intermediated, with no all-to-all. Golay and colleagues at the Board of Governors and the New York Fed used TRACE data collected by FINRA for empirical work, and the transaction-level data is visible only to the official sector. The conclusion: the older the Treasury, the worse its liquidity — larger price impact, lower volume, wider bid-ask spreads.

31:15 The cheapest-to-deliver can revive liquidity
Another finding of the paper: when an off-the-run Treasury becomes the cheapest to deliver into a Treasury futures contract, its liquidity becomes better than similar off-the-run securities. This shows that part of the off-the-run problem is trading activity itself — with trading activity, liquidity improves; without it, liquidity deteriorates. On policy implications, Golay mentions that Treasury buybacks can create trading activity around off-the-run securities and improve liquidity; central clearing makes clearing smoother; as for reducing the number of issuance times and making individual issues larger, the paper has no definitive conclusion, because investors also like the finer granularity of monthly issuance.

36:33 TBAC put the brakes on expanding transparency
At a recent TBAC meeting, some members suggested expanding transparency of Treasury trading data: there is already market-wide aggregate statistics and transaction-level data for on-the-run securities; it was suggested that transaction-level data for Treasury bills could be considered for release, as well as more frequent on-the-run data. But TBAC expressed caution about expanding transparency in other areas, including the off-the-run and TIPS markets. Golay says this is interesting because data transparency is precisely the focus of the IAWG's recent work, and it was listed as a priority in 2021. She personally believes small incremental transparency is beneficial, but understands that in less liquid markets, releasing too much information can make intermediation very difficult.

item.title: Stanford Has a Secret Course That Teaches 12 People How to Extract Value From Other Humans
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-grayarea-斯坦福有一门秘密课程-教12个人如何从他人身上提取价值/
item.category: The Gray Area with Sean Illing
item.description: The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.
item.content:encoded:
The course isn't in the catalog, admits only 12 students a year, and is taught by a Silicon Valley CEO about extracting value from people. The author says students lying isn't an accident — it's what the machine has rewarded all along.

Not a vague critique of Silicon Valley but a specific investigation with course names, dollar figures and people's names; if you care about early-stage investing and talent pipelines, the detail density is high.

5:12 You can raise hundreds of thousands before you have a company
Pre-idea funding was the newest layer of the game when Theo arrived on campus: give an 18-year-old who just got there hundreds of thousands, even millions, of dollars, sign a one-page SAFE check, agree that "if you start a company later, come back to us," and otherwise the money never has to be repaid. For a VC that's pocket change; they don't actually believe in these hyped-up teenagers, and they don't need you personally to succeed — they just need one overnight hit. Meanwhile students are encouraged to make enormous promises and then discover again and again that no one follows up: lie, and nothing happens.

13:22 The secret course teaches extracting value
Stanford has a course that isn't in the catalog, called How to Rule the World, taught by a Silicon Valley CEO who styles himself a professor, admitting only 12 students a year — merely knowing it exists is a status symbol. Its central assignment is extracting value from people, with a strong whiff of the ends justifying the means. One woman Theo interviewed said the course taught her how to lie to VCs to raise money — she later raised millions, dropped out of Stanford, despite having already been caught cheating in a computer science class; months later she put out a glossy launch video for a technology that didn't exist, and Silicon Valley still cheered her on, she moved into a mansion, and she was invited back to Stanford to speak.

26:46 Ethics isn't a premise; you only count as caught
During ethics week in the intro computer science course, the professor covered a case where a software defect killed four people on a radiation therapy machine, and the TA asked who in the room cared about ethics — Theo was the only one who raised his hand. Weeks later a classmate told him he was taking a business ethics course, and "we're all just there to figure out how they got caught." He didn't sense these people needed to pretend to care; when Sam Bankman-Fried was under house arrest in the house on the Stanford campus where he grew up, students made pilgrimages, threw parties themed around him, and said they wanted to replicate his success minus the final fall. A colleague's summary of the money that mysteriously vanished at Tree Hacks: it's all just a little bit of fraud.

38:01 The real reason the president fell wasn't the data
Board members who ousted Marc Tessier-Lavigne later told Theo that one of their heaviest reasons was his posture — a highly aggressive public stance when challenged, deny, deny, deny, plus the threatening letters sent by the lawyer he hired, Steve Neal, which embarrassed the university. Theo found no evidence he personally falsified data: the problem was in the labs he oversaw, where subordinates committed fraud on papers he co-authored, including the 2009 paper claiming to have found the cause of Alzheimer's, while internal company results before publication showed its central finding was "at best unreliable." He was asked to retract and refused, dragging it out for a decade. What drove him out was image management, not the data.

39:01 The mansion closed four days after he was ousted
Four days after the board unanimously removed him, Tessier-Lavigne closed on a 7,600-square-foot mansion in "America's most expensive zip code," valued at over $10 million; eight months later he announced he had raised $1 billion for a new company doing AI biotech. Of the two VCs that led the round, an investor at one messaged Theo two months later to rib him, followed by a winking emoji; an investor at the other offered him money to start a company. Theo says it's the most Silicon Valley thing you can imagine: everything can be monetized, even taking down a university president turns into an invitation.

45:44 Duck syndrome: paddling like mad under the surface
Duck syndrome is Stanford's own coinage: students glide across the surface elegantly, making everything look effortless, while underneath their two legs paddle like mad just to keep from sinking. Katie Meyer was its best illustration — women's soccer captain, led the team to an NCAA title, headed to law school, didn't drink, didn't smoke, didn't speed. Months before graduation, late on a Friday night, after every student support office had closed, she received a letter: because six months earlier she had spilled coffee on a football player (she said it was an accident, he said it was on purpose), her degree was suspended. That night she took her own life. Twelve schools later paid tribute to her; Stanford was not among them. The women's soccer team she had just captained held a mental health night and didn't mention her name.

52:01 A legendary professor's fraud case, and the school says it never heard of it
Stan Cohen was the first geneticist to transplant a gene from one living organism into another, and his 1970s recombinant DNA technique gave rise to the model of universities profiting from patents; in its final valid year that patent contributed 62% of all Stanford patent revenue. In his freshman year Theo found that Cohen had been found liable for fraud by a court: he promised investors a drug target that might cure Huntington's disease and said the drug was already approved to treat another condition, without telling them it had been permanently banned by the FDA in 1976 because it was lethal. He was ultimately ordered to pay $29 million and paid it. Theo asked the university, and the university replied that it had never heard of the case and had no involvement at all — even though Stanford owned the relevant intellectual property and had been subpoenaed.

55:04 Raising money is easier than an internship, and that itself is the signal
The saying circulating in Stanford's inner circles is that raising money for a startup is easier than getting an internship — Theo says that's absurd, it shouldn't be that way, but that's the status quo. He describes the moment as a game of AI musical chairs: everyone is waiting to see who's still standing when the music stops and who's holding the bag. He isn't worried about cash-flow-positive companies like Meta and Google; he's worried about the companies clinging to the AI narrative that have no technology of their own, no revenue, and no ability to generate revenue — they can't hold on and will definitely collapse. But he also cautions that Silicon Valley hasn't held power for long, that it's a very immature power system that hasn't grown guardrails, transparency or accountability, and that one collapse doesn't necessarily mean a reckoning.

item.title: America's Manufacturing Hollow-Out Isn't a Capability Problem, It's a Financial-Return Problem
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-oddlots-美国制造业空心化不是能力问题-是金融回报问题/
item.description: Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing their competitors' industrial capacity.
item.content:encoded:
Chris Power says the US manages industrial policy like a hedge fund's financial statement while China manages it like national security; tariffs are only an imperfect corrective tool, and the core issue is getting American consumers to stop subsidizing their competitors' industrial capacity.

Two frontline hardware founders lay out the real bottlenecks of American reindustrialization: not technology, but trust, cost, and how you define a supply chain. High information density; the back half on tariffs and subsidies is the most valuable part.

2:02 The reserve currency is the first step of decline
Chris Power gives a four-step cycle: a great power first has a generative population and the best industrial capacity, then wins or prevents a war, then becomes extremely lazy, and finally outsources the very things that made it successful. He says this cycle repeats roughly every 150 years — the Dutch gave way to the British, the British gave way to the Americans, and each time industrial power was re-traded for financial power, the world's reserve currency changed hands. This judgment was the starting point for him founding Hadrian: you think you're Mike Tyson at his peak, and your opponent thinks you're the Mike Tyson right before Buster Douglas knocked him out.

9:10 90% of the factory is a software problem
Chris Power says the biggest misconception people have about advanced manufacturing is seeing someone moving things in a factory and assuming it's a humanoid robot problem. In reality, 90% of advanced manufacturing is smart people sitting at computers doing digital engineering, or operating an extremely dumb computer on the shop floor. A welder or machinist has to stand in front of the machine because the system isn't closed-loop — they're doing trigonometry in their heads, judging whether the tool is about to break. That's why Hadrian positions itself as a software company: its work is breaking physical tasks into high-judgment fixturing, then handing execution to robots, CNCs, or welding systems.

14:14 Software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware in LA
Tom Mueller says Southern California's aerospace talent ecosystem is recovering — three or four years after SpaceX was founded in 2002, the aerospace employment curve in the South Bay started turning up. He lists what this area is doing all at once: nuclear companies, drone companies, defense companies, 3D printing companies, plus Anduril in Orange County. The two companies poach from each other and compete for talent, and Northrop Grumman is right across the street from Impulse. Tom's summary: software is done in Silicon Valley, hardware is done in LA.

15:17 Vertical integration is for learning the problem, not saving money
Tom Mueller explains the real logic of SpaceX-style vertical integration: you have to build the first development engine or spacecraft yourself, because in the prototype phase you need to learn every assembly and machining problem. If you hand it to a machine shop from the start, the drawing has problems, the parts come back and don't fit, and you learn nothing. Once the design converges, then you outsource. Chris Power adds that every company should keep 10% to 15% of in-house capacity, because there's always a "hot pot" moment when you need a genius to make something in an hour to hit a flight milestone — but scale has to happen outside.

16:18 Outsourcing decisions run on trust, not finance
Chris Power says what's bought and sold in manufacturing is trust. Hadrian's vertical integration strategy is to outsource as much as possible to every reindustrialization startup and small business, because there are too many projects to run. But they will vertically integrate the links where they "don't believe you can deliver on time" — that's not a financial trade-off, it's preferring to spend an extra two million dollars on equipment and hiring a team rather than betting risk on a legacy foundry that has been late on every submarine program for the past thirty years. His exact words: most of America is incompetent at trust and scheduling.

19:20 In World War II, America was China
Chris Power uses World War II as an analogy: German engineers crushed America on engineering, but America ground them down with McDonald's-style mass production and better logistics. He says America played the role in World War II that China plays today — not winning on the best engineering, but on producing the most. Now the situation is reversed: US missile stockpiles run out in seven days in war games, and China built 2,600 ships while America built six. His conclusion: you can have the best Raytheon missile, but if you can't mass-produce it, you have no options.

21:23 The robot bottleneck is the velocity of training data
Chris Power says the robotics race ultimately comes down to software, and software — especially AI — now comes down to the velocity of training data, which in turn depends on physical-world deployment, meaning mass manufacturing. So this isn't a friendly competition between American companies over "whether Tesla sells a few more Optimuses or Google wins" — it's a civilizational-level confrontation. Tom Mueller adds from the space angle: building on the Moon and Mars requires robot legions rather than humans, because the environment is too dangerous and too expensive; good robots need three things — dexterous hands, vision, which is basically solved, and an AI brain.

29:40 Tariffs are an imperfect corrective tool
Chris Power says manufacturing has four inputs: energy, labor, cost of capital, and export tariffs. He has run the numbers: even if you set Hadrian's labor cost and energy cost to zero, importing components from China is still three times cheaper than buying raw materials in America and making them yourself. He argues China has run industrial policy as national security since 1985, subsidizing energy, labor, capital, and export tariffs, while America manages industrial policy as a hedge fund's financial-statement return. The problem with tariffs is enforcement: ban China but not Singapore, and Chinese companies route through Singapore; differences in the definition of raw materials versus assembly also end up hurting American companies that import components from Mexico.

item.title: He Cooked the Chickpea Pasta Into Mush, Then Survived by Telling People to Steep It Like Tea
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-howibuilt-把鹰嘴豆意面煮成糊后-他靠-像泡茶一样泡-活了下来/
item.description: Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.
item.content:encoded:
Banza's first scaled-up production run failed across the board — 20,000 boxes of pasta fell apart the moment they hit boiling water. They didn't destroy them. They slapped on a sticker that said ‘steep it like tea’ and shipped — because not shipping meant losing the retailer forever.

The founder's account is unusually dense with failure detail: three scrapped production batches, a kidney stone, being thrown out of the factory, a 30% week-over-week decline. Worth hearing for anyone who wants to know how you survive a near-death moment.

5:14 The starting point wasn't a business insight, it was a sinus problem
In college Brian's fridge held nothing but hummus, eating was just ‘fuel’ to him, and he cycled between antibiotics and steroids for so long he was nearly facing surgery. It was his father, an orthodontist, who got him to try an elimination diet, and that's how he found that wheat-based foods triggered his sinus inflammation — one beer and the next day he couldn't breathe. The ENT told him: I don't know what you're talking about, but if it works, keep doing it. That private problem became the product definition: high-protein, high-fiber, gluten-free pasta, doing what Chobani did for yogurt.

10:26 The first recipe had chia in it and was too sticky to look at
He bought Bob's Red Mill chickpea flour on Amazon and followed blogs for combinations. Version one was chickpeas plus eggs plus chia — the chia made it so sticky the result was ugly. With no rolling pin he used a wine bottle; with no pasta cutter he used a knife, dusting flour on the table as he cut to keep it from sticking. Version two dropped the chia, leaving just chickpeas and eggs, and was clearly better, but to make it usable for more people he added tapioca starch and xanthan gum back in and committed to the vegan route. His first capital expenditure was an Atlas Mercado hand-crank pasta machine, about $30 on Amazon. He got up at 5 a.m. every day to make pasta, put on country music, and his roommates thought he was insane.

20:49 Going from 200 pounds an hour to 1,000 magnified every mistake
They first found a tiny gluten-free factory in Michigan that could only do 150 to 200 pounds an hour — wildly inefficient, but they could learn as they went. To get into 190 Meijer stores and 2 Eataly locations, that capacity wasn't enough, so they found what was then the largest gluten-free pasta factory in the country, outside Los Angeles. The problem: that plant had only ever run rice and corn pasta, never legumes. Scaled up to roughly 1,000 pounds an hour, the pasta looked fine coming out and turned into total mush the moment it was boiled. Each trial run was 8,000 to 10,000 pounds, and a failure meant the mold costs and ingredient costs were gone, while they had only a little over $100,000 on hand.

26:02 He got thrown out of the factory for asking the operators
After several failed trial runs, Brian went straight to the line operators to ask what was actually going wrong, against the other side's objections. A worker said ‘this corn smells weird,’ and he answered: that's not corn, we're not making corn pasta today, it's chickpeas. He realized on the spot that communication had broken down completely, and right after that he was escorted out of the plant. At the same time the distributor was threatening him: if you don't fulfill this purchase order, you will never work with this retailer again. He later estimated this shipment would cost nearly every dollar they had.

28:07 The fix was: don't boil it, steep it like tea
With nowhere left to turn they started testing: boil one minute, two minutes, three minutes, then stop boiling altogether — bring water to a boil, turn off the heat, and let the pasta sit in the hot water. What came out of steeping was better than what came out of boiling, or at least it didn't fall apart. Brian says he wasn't proud of the product, and it bothered him to sell it under his own brand, but he knew it was life or death. The packaging was already printed, so they could only add a sticker reading ‘Banza is easier to cook than regular pasta — steep it like tea,’ and then had people hand-apply it to 20,000 boxes. Once that shipment went out, they immediately pulled out of the big plant and went back to the small Michigan factory.

35:18 The box is orange because every pasta box was blue
They noticed that nearly every pasta package on the shelf at the time was blue — Brian put it as ‘you'd think they'd colluded.’ Orange contrasts most strongly with blue, and orange was also the color he'd loved since watching Nickelodeon as a kid, so it became the brand color. They made trade-offs on the packaging copy too: putting ‘chickpeas’ front and center would scare off a lot of people, and so would gluten-free, so the gluten-free certification went on the side while the front led with high protein and high fiber — making consumers feel this was ‘a product for me’ rather than ‘not a product for me.’

41:31 The glyphosate report cut weekly sales by a third
Moms Across America published a report saying glyphosate residue had been detected in Banza products. Brian saw the Google alert during a one-on-one meeting; he says his heart sank and his mind jumped twenty steps ahead. He wanted to verify first, so he only put out a statement saying ‘we are investigating’ — which was nowhere near enough for the most panicked people. The lab results were delayed again and again, dragging on for three weeks. The final published result was 98% below the allegation, but not zero — still a very low level, and below the EWG's risk benchmark. He decided to make the supply chain 100% traceable and to join the Detox Project's certification program.

52:15 Natural channel recovered far more slowly than conventional
The sales recovery was a mixed bag: some channels came back better than before, but the natural channel recovered much more slowly — and that was exactly the customer base with the best repeat purchase rates and the highest sales per store. Brian says this actually makes sense, because natural channel consumers are the most susceptible to this kind of information. What he does now: he keeps alerts on for anywhere Banza and glyphosate are mentioned together, and personally goes onto Reddit to reply and add context, with the goal of making it impossible for the story to be seen without its context. He also admits he should have acknowledged what was happening faster and more visibly at the time.

item.title: AI Won't Replace People — What Replaces Them Is Work That Was Never Written Down
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-twentyvc-ai-不会取代人-取代人的是没被写下来的工作/
item.description: Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that map of work is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.
item.content:encoded:
Models are interchangeable; what's actually valuable is the manual a company writes of how work gets done — that map of work is the irreplaceable asset of the AI era, and the only precondition for a company to train its own models.

Daniel Dines breaks down the real bottleneck of AI inside the enterprise from UiPath's front line, with a high density of counter-consensus claims — useful for anyone trying to judge the pace of enterprise AI adoption.

6:17 AI does not change its own weights on the job
Daniel argues the biggest difference between AI and humans is not reasoning ability, but that AI does not change its own weights on the job. A human is changed by a job; AI just writes things into a notebook. He gives the example of two chefs: one who has cooked Japanese cuisine for 20 years, one who has cooked Italian for 20 years. Give them the same recipe and what they produce is completely different. This is not something you can replicate by writing the company down on paper, because human judgment comes from years of being reshaped by the work. So when it comes to the line about "millions of Einsteins in a data center," Daniel thinks what Dario meant is millions of entities with partial reasoning ability — not Einsteins who can learn on the job the way a person does.

16:29 Probabilistic tech shouldn't do work that demands precision
Daniel raises another limit on AI: precision. Every step AI takes is probabilistic, and even if each step is 99% correct, after 100 steps the overall success rate may be down to 60%. So if you have AI do long multiplication over and over, it will eventually get it wrong. His conclusion: the fact that a tool can do something does not mean you should use it to do that thing. ChatGPT looks like it is doing arithmetic, but behind the scenes it is calling a computer tool — the precision is not coming from ChatGPT. Extend that logic to the enterprise: all work that demands precision should run on precise technology, and there is no reason for it to run on probabilistic technology.

18:34 Deploying AI hasn't gotten easier; deploying automation has
Daniel points to an asymmetry inside the enterprise: deploying AI agents is no easier than it was two years ago, but deploying automation has become much easier, because you can use coding agents to generate the automation. He lists ChatGPT, chain of thoughts and coding agents as the three main milestones. A coding agent works at "design time"; people use it to build automation that runs precisely every time at "execution time." And when automation breaks because an upstream system changed, AI can come back and fix it. The result is that AI is generating the software that runs the company, and that software cannot change its behavior in real time — it can be audited, tested and read by a person. This is the pattern he believes is taking shape in the enterprise right now.

23:46 Blind layoffs cut exactly the people AI needs most
In his book Daniel introduces the concept of the "credentialed middle": companies used to hire for deep domain credentials in some field, and that is precisely the kind of expertise AI helps with most. His judgment is counterintuitive — you will be inclined to cut the people who are not the biggest experts in the domain, but those are exactly the people you will need to supplement expert work with AI. He gives the example of a law firm: it used to hire 25 interns a year, this year it hired only 4. He agrees most roles will need fewer people, but the key question is "which people." His criterion: keep the people with the most initiative, who can maintain client relationships, who can mentor newcomers, who carry the company culture — because AI cannot show initiative in the human sense.

25:51 What decides whether AI can take over is how clear the framework is
Harry argues that work like finance and accounting is highly verifiable, and therefore easy for AI to replace. Daniel disagrees outright: it is not a question of verifiability, but of whether the work is framed by a framework someone else has already defined. He says finance is precisely a domain where the framework is unclear — when an invoice or an order comes in, there can be different ways to handle it, such as whether Nvidia would ship to OpenAI first, and that rule may never have been written down at all. If the rules are not captured by a framework, AI cannot learn them. So a company must first hand AI the "map of work": all workflows, all exceptions, all processes, all systems. This is also what he keeps stressing: models are interchangeable, and the map of work and the processes around it are where the real value lies.

29:01 Interview employees with agents and draw the work as a map
UiPath has launched a technology called cartography, as a discipline that helps companies surface how work actually gets done. Concretely, it uses a product called a cartographer agent to interview real business experts and have them record what they are doing, while the agent follows up in real time: why did you change how you handled this invoice because the zip code was different? Why did you take the other path? That is how exceptions get dug out one by one. Then it aggregates data from multiple people to generate a real-time process map. With that "map of work" in hand, you then use coding agents to design how the process should be transformed, and ultimately, through "printing software," push the process from purely manual point A toward a state with fewer people operating systems and more automation and agentic AI operating systems.

34:15 Vibe coding is easy for prototypes and hard for production
Daniel admits UiPath tried vibe coding, and at first it looked astonishing, but pushing it into production hit a wall: connectors, permissions, auditing, security — all of it has to be maintained. He gives his own example of writing a procurement tool: it was initially written entirely by AI, but the database schema was completely wrong and someone had to rebuild the structure. His conclusion is that going from prototype to production is where the real work is, not writing the code itself. In the end you will very likely spend as much as, or more than, the tool you replaced, while also consuming the bandwidth of your best people. So he does not think systems of record like Salesforce will be replaced by vibe coding.

45:34 The opportunity in legal AI is in process, not model calls
Harry does the math: the US legal industry is a $300 billion market, and if 30% of the labor can be replaced, that is $90 billion in revenue. Daniel counters that the $90 billion will not convert into token revenue — maybe only 10% of it, so a $10 billion token opportunity. His judgment: for legal opinions, both open-source models and frontier models are good enough, and what is actually valuable is the custom workflow built around the legal process. If Harvey and Lagora just call a model once for you to get a legal opinion, that will not be a hundred-billion-dollar market; but if they really draw the work as a map, build out the workflows and give you a legal department, the value is far greater.

item.title: Even Legal-Cannabis States Can't Escape: A Federal Ban Is About to Empty the THC Shelves
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-indicator-大麻合法州也躲不过-联邦禁令要清空-thc-货架/
item.description: A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even states where cannabis is legal will feel it through the loss of a cheap substitute.
item.content:encoded:
A loophole in the 2018 farm bill let hemp-derived THC grow into a $28 billion industry, and now Congress wants to close it — even states where cannabis is legal will feel it through the loss of a cheap substitute.

Eight minutes explaining how a regulatory loophole grew into an industry and how it gets cut off in one stroke — for anyone watching policy risk and compliance arbitrage.

0:00 Legal-cannabis states can't escape a federal ban either
Half of US states have legal recreational cannabis, but the reason THC drinks, vapes and gummies can be sold openly in states that ban cannabis is a loophole left by the 2018 farm bill: it allows low-concentration THC from hemp. After lab processing, that low concentration is enough to mimic a cannabis high, which is how you get Delta 8, Delta 9 — and, as the show jokes, by now Delta 11. Congress now wants to close the loophole, and with a stricter ban. The key point is that it's a federal ban, so even if your state has legal cannabis, you get hit.

1:00 What's being banned is a $28 billion industry
The show puts the size at $28 billion and says the industry could disappear before the end of this year. Tennessee has already gone first: since July it has banned most THC hemp products, and a local reporter describes himself as already living in a ‘post-hemp world’. State legislators even beat Congress to it, banning full-spectrum CBD and smokable flower first. For retailers, farmers and processors, this isn't a policy debate — it's a choice that has to be made before year-end.

3:07 Farmers are going back from hemp to blackberries and corn
Tennessee farmer Lee Crabtree's farm used to grow mostly CBD-variety hemp, and the new state law makes selling those products illegal, so he's gone back to traditional seasonal crops like blackberries and corn. The family still has the industrial kitchen from its CBD food days, and now his wife Stacy uses that big stainless-steel counter to cut grapes for chicken salad and sell it at the roadside farmers market. Lee says income is down, and if the traditional crops don't sell, he'll have to go find a job. This is what the ban looks like landing on one specific household.

5:08 The regulator's case: consumers don't know what they're drinking
Tennessee Republican state representative William Lamberth uses a drinks analogy: someone buying a Sprite expects a Sprite, not a beer; someone buying a beer expects a beer, not a tequila; someone buying a tequila expects not to get a Sprite. He says the goal is for consumers to know exactly what they're buying. But farmers, even when they agree with the logic, worry the law overcorrects. The show also gives the other side: big companies are laying people off, and some are simply moving across state lines — for example Emily Schaeferich's company Burning Acre moved from Columbia, Tennessee to North Carolina to keep growing, and she admits ripping up the entire retail, manufacturing and wholesale supply chain ‘definitely costs a lot of money’.

6:10 Moving to another state may be a wasted move
Hemp economist Beau Whitney calls the nationwide ban taking effect in December an ‘extinction-level event’. His mechanism: cannabis can only be grown in certain states, while hemp can be grown and shipped anywhere, so hemp businesses can build supersized capacity, push costs down and ship nationwide; cannabis, by contrast, needs a separate supply chain per state and can't get hemp's economies of scale. The result is that hemp-derived foods are far cheaper than their cannabis equivalents. So even in states with legal recreational cannabis, consumers will feel squeezed by losing the cheap substitute.

7:13 The ban takes out state tax revenue
The show pulls out economies of scale on its own to explain: the more of the same good you produce, the lower the unit cost, and the savings can be passed on to consumers. That also explains why hemp-derived foods are cheaper than cannabis products. But consumers aren't the only ones affected. For many state budgets, losing the hemp industry means losing a sizable source of tax revenue — in Tennessee alone, a $54 million budget hole. Beau Whitney also says it could put hundreds of thousands of jobs at risk.

7:13 The delay just moves it from November to December
The White House has urged Congress to delay or amend the ban, the Senate currently supports it, and the House voted earlier this month to delay it too. But these moves only push the effective date from November to December — a one-month delay. For companies that have already moved across state lines and rebuilt supply chains, a month changes nothing — they may have just moved the whole business only to find the industry destroyed in December.

8:14 Those staying behind switch to fiber hemp
Tennessee farmer Bill Corbin, in Springfield, is preparing the first fiber hemp crop for the French company Hemp-It; this kind of hemp is used for rope, packaging and auto parts. He says there isn't a single person in the industry who didn't know this day was coming, that he thinks the industry was unsustainable to begin with, and he agrees with legislators' efforts to suppress recreational use of hemp derivatives. But he worries about medical consumers: he himself is older and has arthritis, relies heavily on full-spectrum CBD, and the products left after the ban may not be strong enough for older people or those trying to avoid opioid painkillers.

item.title: The Bat Doesn't Know What It's Like to Be a Bat Either
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-pel-蝙蝠自己也不知道当蝙蝠是什么感觉/
item.description: The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.
item.content:encoded:
The bat argument rests on a private inner core that can never be reached; Dennett says that core doesn't exist, and that a bat isn't even a "what it's like" to itself.

The second half of episode 400, and listenable on its own. The first half is about theories of consciousness; the second half unexpectedly slides into animal ethics, and the four of them never do settle their disagreement.

1:07 A bat having an inner world is not the same as its being conscious
Christopher summarises Dennett's response: he flatly denies Nagel — we can talk about what it's like to be a bat in all sorts of ways (by first ruling out the things a bat doesn't do, for instance), and with enough information we can eventually get there, because "what it's like to be a bat" just is the discriminative, dispositional states the bat has. Dylan supplies the step Dennett actually rejects: drawing on von Uexküll's Umwelt and Innenwelt (surrounding world and inner world), Dennett grants that the bat has an inner world, which isn't crazy; what he won't accept is going straight from "has an inner world" to "therefore consciousness exists," and that is exactly the step Nagel uses to prove consciousness exists. Our mode of access is heterophenomenology: treat the bat's behaviour and physiology as a text in need of interpretation.

5:37 Consciousness is not an all-or-nothing property
Christopher reads out a passage from Dennett: are language-less animals not conscious at all? Dennett says the question shouldn't be taken as a matter of course, because it presupposes "something we've had a great deal of trouble getting away from" — that consciousness is an all-or-nothing property that splits the universe into two utterly different categories: things that have it and things that don't. That dichotomy is what Dennett wants to dismantle; what he wants is consciousness in degrees. Christopher then offers his own version: he doesn't want to accept property dualism, he wants to deny the hard problem, because subjectivity can perfectly well have a biological and evolutionary explanation — agency and subjectivity co-evolved; a physical process organised from the inside "feeling like something" is a real biological phenomenon.

12:57 The bat doesn't know what it's like to be a bat either
Seth pushes the argument to its extreme: it isn't "we don't know what it's like to be a bat," it's that there is no "what it's like to be a bat as seen from the bat's side" at all; the bat itself doesn't know either, because it lacks the machinery to string experiences into a narrative and give them names. Dylan immediately marks out the cost of this inference: if anything with dynamic activity has its own experience, then atoms count too, and that's panpsychism. Christopher says you don't have to go as far as atoms, but concedes that the direction really does sound like panpsychism — he'd rather use a threshold: you need a feedback loop of sensing and acting before you can talk about a new mode of being.

14:35 Even plants have a perspective in some sense
Mark digs up a line from Dennett's book: the perspective of a conscious observer is a refined descendant of the primitive perspective of the first replicators, which "divided the world into good and bad" — on that account even plants have a perspective in this sense, and "perspective" thereby becomes a metaphor. Christopher then offers gradualism: from sponges to mantis shrimp to humans, subjectivity accumulates layer by layer and gets thicker and thicker, with a fuzzy threshold in between. Dylan wants to nail the threshold down harder: you can't use "complex" as the criterion, since the weather is a complex self-maintaining system too; the difference is that living things can replicate themselves and have a wholeness, so the only thing the Earth lacks is its own replication.

19:47 You are a bunch of things, not a soul
Mark finds Dennett's 1994 reply collection Get Real, which uses the snake as an example: the snake has no central representation of "mouse," it just responds to prey through three separate sensory systems. Dennett's point is that the perceptual system we take to be a single whole is really a bundle of little homunculi each making its own discriminations; you are not an Aristotelian form, a soul, an organisation that runs you — we are all a bunch of things. Christopher objects: failure to integrate information processing doesn't mean there's no self — the two hemispheres of a split-brain patient are also separate, and we don't therefore say he has no self; the snake may still have a more ancient, minimal sense of boundary and evaluative experience.

27:39 Reducing experience to discrimination looks a lot like behaviourism
Christopher says he agrees with Dennett 99%, and is stuck on the 1%: when Dennett wants to reduce a person to dispositional states, saying that experiencing red is nothing over and above being able to discriminate red from non-red and being in that discriminative state, it sounds like behaviourism. Seth offers a defence: even if the substrate is just discriminative states, subjective experience, the self, is a composite stitched together out of memory, imagination, representation and symbolic language — it weaves scattered discriminative states into a story with descriptions, meanings and colour, and that story is me. Christopher agrees about the narrative self, but points out that the bat lacks the metacognitive capacity to construct such a self.

38:54 You can club an iguana, but not a rabbit
Mark says "everyone is a world" is a good moral fiction, but he doesn't know how to apply it to animals: Florida has too many iguanas, and he encourages everyone to go out and club them, which he says is completely fine and humane; swap in a rabbit and he won't accept it. Seth offers an evolutionary explanation: our feelings about animals domesticated over tens of thousands of years, wild animals and reptiles were never the same to begin with, and this doesn't conflict with "the self is a narrative centre of gravity." Christopher anchors it in valence: animals are not reflex machines, they are situated perspectives that evaluate, and that is the reason they enter moral consideration — he says that after reading Lars Chittka's The Mind of a Bee, the way he deals with bees changed.

46:10 Take away caring and nothing is left of pain
Mark turns to where Dennett talks specifically about pain: what is the functional relation of pain? If you take away "caring about it, wanting to get away from it," take away everything else, and leave only the sensation of pain, then nothing is left — your not liking pain is itself part of the pain. Mark says this is exactly Dennett's attitude to the philosophical zombie: imagine a being whose biological makeup, reactions and even internal relations are exactly like yours, but the light of consciousness never came on — Dennett thinks this is so absurd that it's hard even to explain to scientists.

item.title: Beijing's Central Axis Is Not a Relic — It's a City Operating System Still Running
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-historyhit-北京中轴线不是古迹-是仍在运转的城市操作系统/
item.description: The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.
item.content:encoded:
The Ming rebuilt Beijing from a blueprint written two thousand years earlier, and the central axis still dictates the symmetry and growth of a city of twenty million — even the Olympic Bird's Nest sits on that line.

Medium information density, but its strength is restoring the central axis from tourist attraction to a planning logic still in force — suited to anyone interested in cities and organizational design.

7:13 A manual from two thousand years ago is still in use
When the Ming set out to rebuild the capital, they dug up a technical manual more than two thousand years old, the Kaogong Ji (“考工记”). It specified a city four to five kilometres on each side, three gates per side, the palace at the centre, an ancestral temple on one side, the court in front, the market behind, and a Temple of Heaven in the southern suburbs. The historian Jeremiah Jenik says the logic behind this layout was cosmic order: there is a fixed point in the sky, the North Star, so there should be a corresponding fixed point on earth, and the most fitting fixed point is the emperor himself — placing yourself in the palace at the exact centre of the city is placing yourself inside a cosmic order that revolves around you.

9:16 They actually built it to the drawing
The most astonishing thing is not that the Ming dared to use a blueprint over a thousand years old, but how closely they built to it. Overlay the Kaogong Ji plan on the model at the Beijing Planning Exhibition Hall and the two almost coincide. So Beijing today is still a twenty-first-century city running around a fifteenth-century heart, and that heart follows principles laid down nearly two thousand years ago. Compare London, which grew organically along the Thames: Beijing had the blueprint first, the city second.

11:20 The central axis is a spine, and the city grew out of it
From north to south, the axis strings together the Bird's Nest, the Drum and Bell Towers, Jingshan, the Forbidden City and the Temple of Heaven, ending at Yongdingmen in the south. The episode likens it to a spine: everything is planned and expanded outward from this line. Running true north-south and aligned with the heavens, the line has been Beijing's most distinctive feature for six hundred years, and it determines the shape of the city today.

12:22 The right to tell time is the right to rule
The Drum and Bell Towers were the city's timekeeping centre, and the bells are said to have carried twenty kilometres. From 1272 all the way to 1924 — the year the last Qing emperor left the Forbidden City — the time struck here was Beijing's official time. The drum was beaten one hundred and eight times every two hours; it was the first sound Beijingers heard in the morning and the last they heard at night. The episode says it is almost as if the emperor were not merely marking time but claiming ownership of time itself.

15:32 Jingshan was piled up from the rubble of a previous dynasty
Jingshan is not a natural hill; it was built by hand under the Yongle Emperor according to feng shui principles. An ideal palace faces south, with water to the south that bends and flows to bring qi and life, and a mountain to the north to block the evil qi coming from that direction and display majesty. Beijing lies too far from the Yan Mountains to the north, so the Ming used rubble from the old Mongol palaces and earth dug out of new water channels to build a symbolic mountain inside the city.
