18:52 The Forbidden City was a super-project of nationwide mobilisation
Ten thousand logs were shipped from 1,800 kilometres to the southwest, golden bricks from Suzhou 1,100 kilometres to the south — 18 million bricks fired in all — and gold leaf from Nanjing. One million labourers plus more than 100,000 craftsmen built it in fifteen years. From the 1420s to the early twentieth century, twenty-four emperors lived here. Today it receives more than 15 million visitors a year, making it the most visited historic site on earth.

22:55 A nail-free timber structure survives a magnitude 9.5 quake
These buildings are almost entirely wood, and what lets them stand for centuries is the dogong (斗拱): the dou are the bearing blocks, the gong slot in, and they interlock very tightly. Wood shrinks and warps, and this system lets it flex and deform while holding the whole structure together; in an earthquake every small piece of wood can slide a little, without shearing the blocks or popping screws. Scientists have calculated that this construction could withstand a magnitude 9.5 earthquake, the strongest ever recorded.

23:57 It was struck by lightning within a year of completion
The Forbidden City was not fireproof. Less than a year after it was completed in 1421, the three great halls burned to ashes after a lightning strike. Afterwards 308 bronze vats were installed to store water against the next fire. The detail makes the point: no matter how precise the planning, it cannot stop a single point of failure — you can only add redundancy after the fact.

item.title: Germany's CDU Falls Out of a State Parliament: The Era of the Centre Is Over
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-goodfight-德国基民盟跌出州议会-中间派时代已经结束/
item.description: The CDU won less than 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.
item.content:encoded:
The CDU won less than 5% in Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, shut out of a state parliament for the first time since the Federal Republic was founded. Merz has lost his authority, and the populist far left and far right command an overwhelming majority among voters under 35.

This is a piece of German domestic political commentary, not an interview. Information density is moderate, but it lays out the judgment that "populism has become the mainstream" very clearly. Suited to anyone following the direction of European politics.

0:00 The CDU is shut out of a state parliament for the first time
In the Mecklenburg-Vorpommern state election, the CDU won less than 5% of the vote and therefore holds no seats in the state parliament — the first time this has happened in the history of the Federal Republic. In the same election the AfD took roughly 38%, once again becoming the state's largest party. The author calls this the "final nail in the coffin" for Merz: he may cling to the chancellorship for a few more weeks or months, but his authority is gone, his capacity to shape the country thoroughly exhausted — in political language, "a dead man walking."

0:00 The CDU's decline came later than the SPD's but is just as fatal
The CDU is the most important party in postwar German history, governing the Federal Republic for 53 of the past 77 years, and from Adenauer to Kohl to Merkel it left its mark on every aspect of the country. The author notes that in the early 2000s everyone was talking about "the crisis of social democracy," as the SPD fell from above 40% support to record lows; in hindsight, the fate of the centre-left big tent was merely a leading indicator of a broader crisis of the entire political centre, and the CDU then walked the same road. The era of what Germans call the Volksparteien — catch-all parties capable of mobilising most of the vote — is effectively over.

0:00 Populists are not a fringe phenomenon but the most important political force
The author says this has been the most-asked question of the past decade: "Will the populist wave last, or is it about to peak?" In the summer of 2016, when Trump became the Republican nominee and Britain voted to leave the EU, the answer seemed obvious to him; now the answer is undeniable — the populists are here to stay. What looked abnormal a few years ago has, like it or not, become the mainstream. Populist politicians now hold power in the United States, India, Turkey and much of the democratic world, and have a high probability of taking office in France and Brazil in the coming months. Even where they remain in opposition, they are already strong enough to destroy any sense of business as usual.

0:00 The rise of one extremist party feeds the other
In the Berlin state election, Die Linke took 26% of the vote and emerged the big winner. The party descends from the SED, which ruled East Germany with an iron fist, and after reunification initially appealed mainly to older voters nostalgic for the security of the communist system; in recent years it has remade itself in the image of the global illiberal left, which the author considers roughly comparable to Zack Polanski's Greens in Britain or the more extreme parts of the DSA in the United States. During the campaign, some of the party's supporters were filmed chanting "Yalla, Yalla Intifada!"; on election night, the head of a notorious crime family turned up at the party's election celebration and cheerfully told the media he felt an affinity with it. The party's leader is now very likely to become the next mayor of Berlin, which would be the first time an heir to the SED has taken power in the capital.

0:00 Voters under 35 have swung to the two extremes
Another notable feature of the two elections was the age distribution. The SPD and CDU, which once dominated Germany's political landscape, now draw most of their support from pensioners. Among voters under 35, Die Linke and the AfD hold unassailable majorities in both Berlin and Mecklenburg-Vorpommern. From this the author concludes that the coming years will bring an even sharper tilt toward the extremes. It also explains why the collapse of the centre is not a one-off election accident: the structure of the electorate itself is pushing the scales toward the two ends.

0:00 Mecklenburg-Vorpommern's left coalition is just an election accident
In Mecklenburg-Vorpommern, because a batch of other parties all failed to clear the 5% threshold for entering parliament, a broad left coalition just barely won enough votes to govern. But the author stresses that this was an election accident unlikely to be repeated — a few thousand votes either way and the state would be completely ungovernable. The point matters: when centrist parties fall below the threshold, they don't just lose their own seats, they push the governability of an entire state to the edge of a cliff.

0:00 Don't surrender, and don't deny the problem is real
The author explicitly rejects two responses. The first is to urge the centre to surrender: if the political middle can't hold, moderates might as well defect to the extremists on "their own side." He thinks this is wrong — neither Die Linke nor the AfD can solve the real problems Germany faces, and despite their vast differences the two have conspicuous similarities, from their coyness toward Moscow to their persistent inability to purge antisemites from their own ranks. The second is to keep denying reality: for a decade the centre has attributed the extremists' success to foreign interference, social media algorithms, some candidate's tactical blunder, or the stupidity, sexism or racism of voters. The author says these ways of blinding yourself to the facts in front of you may be comforting, but they are just as dangerous.

item.title: Going global: don't wait until you're big to go to the US and Europe — go there first to get big
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-beiwanglu-出海别等做大了再去欧美-先去欧美才能做大/
item.description: Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to the US and Europe once they're big, but it's the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.
item.content:encoded:
Wei Zhe says many companies think they'll go to the US and Europe once they're big, but it's the reverse — you go there to become big. Get the region choice wrong and the later product 3.0 and channel pyramid won't stand up.

Wei Zhe compresses ten years of overseas investment experience into four choices, counterintuitive but each backed by cases and numbers, especially the second half on AI transforming organizations and pricing, which has the highest information density.

1:30 The old cross-border mega-seller path is dead
Wei Zhe says the ‘cross-border mega-seller’ popular in Shenzhen is a distribution-type mindset, with dozens or hundreds of accounts; he has seen companies with over a thousand accounts and hundreds of thousands of SKUs. Ten years ago these companies made money faster than other paths from a profitability standpoint, and many investors liked them. But distribution-type companies are essentially traffic-type companies: the more stores, the more likely to get traffic. When platform goods aren't plentiful, distribution isn't opposed; once goods are plentiful enough, using distribution to grab traffic is bad money driving out good. More critically, three red lines: goods not matching descriptions harms consumers, fake orders harm other merchants, and inserting small cards to build private domains harms the platform. Amazon's flywheel places great importance on consumer experience, and these behaviors hit exactly that protective wall.

4:38 Four choices, region comes first
Wei Zhe says it's not just cross-border e-commerce; all of life is about choices being more important than effort. He gives four choices: region choice, channel choice, product category choice, brand positioning choice. On region choice, he has always advocated seizing the US and European markets first, because of strong paying power, high internet penetration, and more importantly, the brand can build momentum. This isn't their invention; when Japanese and Korean brands went global back then, they all seized the US and Europe. On category choice, they change their recommendation every three years: the earliest three years supported products common to China and abroad, where domestic supply chains didn't need modification to sell overseas, like Anker's power banks back then, almost identical except for voltage; the second three years recommended overseas-exclusive products, because Chinese supply chains all went overseas, and common products had no differentiation; the most recent three years is product 3.0 — electric, with chips, with algorithms.

12:29 It's not that you go to the US and Europe after getting big, it's that you go there to get big
Many companies tell Wei Zhe ‘I'll go to the US and Europe when I'm big’, and he says it's exactly the reverse: you go to the US and Europe to get big. He gives the example of Cupshe, a swimwear company: a husband and wife, stocked $50,000 worth of goods, and their first stop was the US. $50,000 is sales goods, actually very little, so there's no minimum threshold. He recently looked at AI smart hardware, starting from Kickstarter crowdfunding platforms with a thousand or ten thousand products, even collecting pre-payments before placing orders, with no capital — this is also a great way to test the waters. He even advises big companies entering the US and European markets to learn from small startups. They always say the needle must be fine enough to pierce through; both big and small companies should first do well in the four singles: single market, single category, single channel, single brand.

20:36 After AI, good companies don't just find demand, they create it
Wei Zhe says with AI, excellent companies don't go looking for demand; they should lead demand and create demand. He gives the example of a Chinese company making astronomical telescopes: originally not electric, they electrified it, with chips and algorithms; the algorithm is actually simple, with GPS positioning, and the map of the universe's movements is regular. He, not originally an astronomy enthusiast, would buy one; at his home in Silicon Valley, with one tap, it automatically aligns to Orion for you, tells you 3 a.m. is the best time, you press it and go to sleep, and the next day it takes the photos for you. This lets everyone become a good astronomy enthusiast. Another example: a cross-border class student making curtains, after electrification they didn't sell well in the US because American electricians are expensive, so he put solar panels on the windows, turning electric curtains that need an electrician into DIY ones; originally always one or two hundred million, now four or five hundred million, with profit of one or two hundred million.

24:48 In the AI era, still using subscription fees means you're behind
Wei Zhe says in the AI era, if you still think in terms of subscription fees, you're behind again; they are all advising companies to do back-end charging, software charging, called tokenized. A monthly subscription fee is the dumbest way, a bit like advertising charging by time instead of by usage. This time AI has brought out the most ideal charging model in all of human education: paying according to your usage of AI software, services, or content. He gives an example: Bessie, if you take two weeks off this month, isn't subscribing for a month wasting two weeks? They suggest that AI-transformed hardware should be charged like AI, not going back to the old SaaS monthly $9.9 subscription model. An AI reading platform he looked at charges by how many articles you read, and doesn't charge if you don't read; the same for smart bike trainers, after recharging, one dollar per ride, two dollars for two hours.

27:28 Adding AI is more worth favoring than AI adding
Wei Zhe has a viewpoint called AI plus or plus AI; he reverses the phrase, favoring plus AI more than today's favoring AI plus. The difference is: plus AI is hardware humans have already accepted, and you AI-ify it; rather than creating a previously unseen hardware because of AI. It's very hard for humans to accept a completely new hardware. For example, Oura makes rings, because you first accepted rings; some make you hang a camera under your neck, which I find harder, I haven't accepted that hardware. So they are very optimistic about adding AI to already-accepted hardware. They invested in a capacitive stylus that is number one globally, because everyone already writes on a Pad, it doesn't add an extra pen for you, it just AI-ifies your pen. He also especially wants to transform a top-two overseas fitness equipment company, replacing the fitness coach on the screen with AI-generated ones, you want a male, it's male, you want a black person, it's black, and with two cameras it can provide AI fitness guidance.

29:43 Channels aren't flat, they're a pyramid
Wei Zhe says channels aren't multiple channels multiple paths, each channel parallel or even competing; excellent brands all have a channel pyramid. Like luxury brands and traditional brands, there must be different channel strategies, pricing strategies, and which channel to launch new products in first all have讲究. What is a light-goods channel, what is the main waist volume-running channel, the pyramid design differs for different categories and brands. He gives Anker as an example: making power bank mecha seems a bit low, to enter the consumer electronics high ground, Soundcore earphones must enter Apple flagship stores; whether it really sells a lot isn't important, but it can transform the brand, Apple is the pyramid's apex. Pop Mart must open on London's Oxford Street, even if it doesn't make money, how much can it lose, but it must be propped up there. He says some companies treat Temu and AliExpress as parallel channels for selling goods, which definitely won't work; AliExpress is a light-goods channel, when Amazon delists you, you dump it in that channel, you can't sell on Amazon and here too, consumers get confused.

36:14 R&D is 1, marketing is 0
Wei Zhe says he really dislikes spending heavily on marketing. Many Chinese brands going overseas or cross-border e-commerce are very willing to add 2% of revenue to marketing expenses, but consumers don't get it. He says, do you dare to add 2% of revenue to R&D expenses? He has met many bosses with 1 billion or 2 billion scale; a 1 billion boss says 20 million for R&D, I don't know what for. He says, see, there's the problem, you don't know what for. Your 2% thrown at marketing expenses makes the platform happy, consumers don't get it; but 2% thrown into R&D, consumers get it. He has always firmly believed that good products speak for themselves, marketing is just, your R&D is 1, marketing is 0, if you have something good you can amplify it, if you don't have that 1, never put many 0s. He gives three judgment signals: first, dare to find a benchmark company, definitely a mid-to-upper brand, and you crush it by doubling performance; second, you sell at the same price as it; third, you sell online, and offline channels come to you.

item.title: The AI Office Hype Hasn't Cleared, and the Personal Agent War Has Already Started | Breaking Down Town, Instinct, Grok Bot and Muse
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-luanfanshu-10万用户估值100亿-个人agent的估值跑在产品前面/
item.description: Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.
item.content:encoded:
Instinct has fewer than 100,000 users and its product isn't officially launched, yet its valuation went from $50 million to $10 billion in half a year — in this round of personal Agent heat, capital grabbing a ticket matters more than real demand.

Four frontline product people break down four routes — Town, Instinct, Grok Bot, Muse — and also explain why that batch of products like Xiaolongxia became martyrs. Information density is high, but the second half is worth more.

0:00 100,000 users prop up a $10 billion valuation
Instinct only began small-scale invite testing in February this year, and by the end of August it still hadn't reached 100,000 users, yet its valuation went from $50 million at the start of the year to $500 million in August, $2.5 billion at the end of August, and this month the new round being quoted in the market has already reached $10 billion, with Sequoia and Benchmark both in talks to lead. The founder is a 23-year-old unknown with no big-company experience, no technical patents, no industry background. Pan Luan (潘乱) put it bluntly: what capital is buying is neither the founder nor the product, it's the story of the next OpenAI, and it can pay the price of the next-generation personal operating system to grab a ticket.

15:16 The line between tool and person is proactivity
The biggest difference between this wave of Agents and the last is that it is no longer another tool, but a person. Two differences between a person and a tool: first, long-term understanding — a tool needs the context explained again every time, while a person understands what kind of person you are like a friend or colleague; second, proactivity — setting up an automation task in Manus still depends on prompts, on you spelling out the rules and intent, and that isn't proactivity. True proactivity is subjective initiative — like the colleague who understands your goal in doing something and comes over on their own to say, "I have a plan, should we discuss it?"

18:09 Office Agents organise by project, personal Agents by person
The most core difference is the dimension along which context is built. Cloud Code builds context along a mission or project dimension, and switching to the next project means starting over; this wave of personal agents builds context centred on you as a person, knowing your profile, preferences and past history. Open Codex or Manus and the list on the left is all the tasks and projects you've sent out; open Grok Bot and beside you are AI companions you can drive together. In personal scenarios people care less about model capability and the harness layer, because individuals don't have that many complex tasks — it's office Agents that care a lot about task completion rate.

30:28 Town trades email for the user's right to delegate
The four products are trying to solve the same problem, just with different approaches. Town has a mobile app, but 70% of its data traffic is on PC; it focuses on the email scenario, solving one high-frequency scenario well before expanding. It understands which emails you send and receive often, auto-archives, learns your writing style, drafts replies for you, and sends automatically after you hit confirm. It goes deeper in the email scenario than any other agent, and overseas it has already achieved fairly viral spread, especially in school-related scenarios. In one sentence: use a high-frequency scenario to build user trust, and acquire the user's ultimate right to delegate bit by bit.

39:33 Poke didn't break out for lack of technology
Poke and Instinct are both agents that live inside IM and don't make a standalone app, but Poke didn't break out. Suki believes it wasn't a technical limitation — Browser Use was already very mature by the end of last year, and Poke could absolutely have done it at the time; the difference was team strategy: Instinct went deeper in the agent direction, taking the full-delegation route, able to access credit cards, screen and microphone, booking flights and buying things for you — things users had never seen, which produced viral spread; Poke put its energy into content push accuracy, taking the proactive-push route, with email notifications arriving even earlier than the inbox itself, but it didn't take the step of "getting things done for you."

42:39 Cloud Agents must handle three environments
Mark says building a cloud agent was a painful lesson: a local agent and a cloud agent are completely different things. To do personal AI you have to be usable anytime, anywhere — you can't be unreachable just because the computer screen is off. The cloud has to handle three environments — the user's device, the cloud service, and the agent's execution environment — and task state, task interruption and recovery, and context passing between the three are very complex systems. They started in February, and just getting the agent to run stably on the cloud took at least two months; setting aside detours, polishing a sincere piece of work takes at least three to four months.

50:39 Hiring an assistant and being a middleman are two businesses
Town started out doing corporate tax filing, and after pivoting it leans more toward enterprise scenarios; the relationship is more like paying for a personal assistant, which naturally filters for people willing to pay, with a typical profile of white-collar workers who are extremely busy and have no time or energy. Muse is more like a middleman, a shopping guide, a broker — although it has a paid subscription, the main projected revenue source is still commission from matchmaking transactions, leaning toward mass users and blending into everyday WhatsApp chats. Two completely different logics, and the scenarios they cut into and the users they filter out are different too.

1:14:07 Your saved folder may be noise to an Agent
The story Zuckerberg told when launching Muse was: extract what you like to eat from ingredients saved on Instagram, generate a shopping list, adjust the menu by dinner party headcount and dietary restrictions, then complete the shopping and relationship maintenance — turning years of interest profile into money, going from a discovery platform to a decision-and-transaction platform. But Suki suspects this is to save face for the free business narrative: helping users complete transactions is absolutely not among the top scenarios users want to solve; users would rather solve the annoying things they don't want to do themselves. There isn't that much high-quality context in saved folders — the truly high-quality context comes more from offline, IM and email, and Douyin and Instagram saves may themselves be noise to an agent.

item.title: Ten Years of Parenting Taught Me: When Kids Don't Listen, the Problem Isn't the Kid
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-parentmojo-育儿十年才懂-孩子不听话时-问题不在孩子身上/
item.description: On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as gospel—from forcing a child to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth—each learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.
item.content:encoded:
On the podcast's tenth anniversary, the host revisits ten parenting beliefs she once held as gospel—from forcing a child to take medicine to treating an expert's framework as truth—each learned first in a book, then relearned in a real conflict.

For parents who want to reflect on parenting methodologies. Medium information density, lots of personal narrative, but the ten reflections are clearly structured, and the second half—on "the village" and the couple relationship—is more valuable than the first.

6:00 Forcing a child to take medicine wins the behavior, loses the relationship
The host recalls that when her daughter was three and refused antibiotics, she held her down and forced the medicine in; the daughter threw most of it back up. That night her husband Alvin stayed with their daughter in the bathroom for an hour, calmly saying the whole time, "I'm willing to do anything, but we're not leaving until we figure this out." In the end the daughter finished the whole course herself, with small sips of medicine, small sips of water, and a small piece of chocolate to take away the taste. The host says the difference wasn't that her husband was more patient, but that he wasn't solving a behavior—he was understanding what would actually help the child do this thing. What the child needed was autonomy over the process and to feel she was on the same team as her parent, not being held down to do something.

9:19 The authoritative parenting framework was based on just 146 white kids
The host says she uncritically accepted the conclusion that "authoritative is the best parenting style" early on, because every blog and study said so. It wasn't until she did the episode on corporal punishment that she found a paper co-authored by Diana Baumrind defending parents' ability to spank their children, and started digging. She found that this framework—cited more than 26,000 times and defining sixty years of parenting research—was originally based on just 146 white, middle-class preschoolers in the town where Baumrind lived. She sees this as evidence of her own insufficient critical thinking, and says she now asks at the macro level, "Does this theory make sense?" and at the micro level, "Does it fit this specific child in front of me?"

17:41 Not punishing kids doesn't mean being walked all over
The host says she once believed that without punishment and consequences children would run wild—she even remembers thinking in the shower when her daughter was four months old, "How do I discipline her without becoming a mean mom?" Clinical psychologist Dr. Houri Parsi admitted in the membership community that she too had once treated "obedience" as the goal, and that every tooth-brushing was a battle. Once, to record for the host, she deliberately avoided threats, punishment, and rewards, and simply asked her two-year-old son, "Why don't you want to brush your teeth?" He couldn't put it into words—he just called out "Mama" and buried his head in her chest. She realized what he wanted was time alone with her. She put the toilet lid down, sat down, held her son, and sang a song with him; then he brushed his teeth himself, all in under five minutes.

21:31 "I need you to take out the trash" is not a need
The host says looking back, she didn't understand what a "need" was—she thought saying "I need you to take out the trash" to her husband was a perfectly logical sentence. Before their daughter was born, the two almost never argued; they rode mountain bikes in summer and skied in winter, because the ad agency they worked for represented resorts and paid wages in vouchers. After their daughter was born, everything changed: during his three weeks of paternity leave, her husband would get her anything she asked for, but the rest of the time he was training for a hundred-mile ride and watching the Tour de France. She says it was learning that she had needs for "collaboration, partnership, and having her effort seen" that actually unlocked the problems between them; before that, she had accumulated a large amount of resentment she didn't know how to handle.

24:01 When you're triggered, the problem isn't the person who interrupted you
The host says her biggest trigger is being interrupted—the moment her husband interrupts her, she flies into a rage, most recently over how much postage to put on a package. She always thought the cause was simply that her husband interrupted her, and that if he just stopped, everything would be fine. In July 2018, while recording an episode with intergenerational trauma expert Dr. Rebecca Babcock-Fenerci, she traced it back on the spot to her father, a special education teacher who treated 16-year-olds like 10-year-olds and for a period lectured her every night. Later, in the car, she interrupted her daughter, and her daughter said, "Don't interrupt me, Mama," and her husband looked at her and said, "She is you." She says that was the moment she realized it was never just about the two people in front of her, and from that she developed the "Tame Your Triggers" course, which grew from a one-month module to ten weeks.

30:27 The handmade book she made while pregnant was full of expectations for her child
The host describes a book she made while pregnant: three covers, one in the middle and one on each side, opening in both directions, brown book cloth with a beige spine, with "me" cut out of the board on one cover and "you" embossed on the other when flipped, the concept being "you came out of me." On the "me" side she wrote her own feelings and thoughts; on the "you" side she wrote to the not-yet-met Carys. She reads out the earliest batch of "expectations for you": I hope you're smart, or at least average; I hope you're the kind of child who shakes hands instead of hiding behind my legs; I hope you like both roughhousing and pretty things; I hope you don't cry all the time; I hope when you fall you get up yourself and say "I'm okay." She says looking back now, the biggest mistake was not knowing how to simply be with a person, allowing them to be their whole self and witnessing that, without carrying ideas about how they should be.

33:14 Kohn's principle two: reconsider your demands first
The host says she once thought she'd play the role of "enforcer," even writing in her pregnancy expectations list, "I hope you can love me as much as I love him." She says RIE loosened the soil for her, but what really planted the seed was Alfie Kohn's Unconditional Parenting. She shares a few of its principles: Principle Two is to reconsider your demands—"maybe when a child doesn't do what you ask, the problem isn't the child, it's what you're asking"; Principle Five is to change the way you look, not just the way you act—when you see a child doing something you asked them not to do, your first reaction should be curiosity about what they're struggling with, not how to make them stop; Principle Ten is to "attribute to the child the best motive consistent with the observed facts," and she says when she quotes it she changes the ending to "consistent with the observed behavior," because "there are no facts, only what we observe."

39:07 The couple relationship isn't a different subject—it's the same one
The host says she long believed the couple relationship and the parent-child relationship were completely different things; when she started the parenting membership eight years ago, she asked Dr. Laura Froyen to write the co-parenting module because she had no idea how to handle a partner relationship. She says her parenting shift toward collaboration was relatively easy because she had no ten-year-old habits with her daughter; but with Alvin, after ten years together, they had never learned how to disagree, because most of the time they were doing hobbies they loved, and she didn't mind doing most of the housework. It wasn't until she took Gottman training that she realized this was almost the same as what she'd been doing with her child all these years—though she also thinks the Gottman method itself has several key flaws. She recruited couples from the membership to record real arguments, using modified tools; one couple where the husband had refused to discuss a toxic issue—after his wife listened for ten minutes with a genuine intent to understand him, he was willing to talk, and in the same session they reached an agreement to move forward.

item.title: NPR's comment section was flagged as bots. It was a group of middle schoolers.
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-21-tal-npr-评论区被当成机器人-其实是一群初中生/
item.description: NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had banned them from social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.
item.content:encoded:
NPR staff saw gibberish flooding a comment section and reported it as bots; a younger colleague recognized it as kids whose parents had banned them from social media, using a Spotify comment section as a group chat.

Four separate stories, medium information density, but the generational misreading in the first story and the mother-daughter conversation about braiding in the third are both worth hearing.

1:01 The gibberish comments weren't bots, they were kids
Dave Blanchard saw a sudden flood of incomprehensible comments on the Wild Card comment section on Spotify, assumed bots, and reported them to Spotify and deleted the posts. But Hannah Chin, a colleague at NPR ten years younger, opened the screenshots and immediately reached the opposite conclusion: these are kids. Her evidence was the display names with emoji you need a special character generator to type, the cartoon avatars she'd never seen, the back-and-forth short sentences with piles of exclamation points. Dave wasn't buying it at first, and replied, "That's an interesting theory."

6:05 Using playlists as the group chat entrance
Hannah kept digging and found how the kids operated: one kid creates a public playlist called Let's Chat Here or New Chat with a single podcast episode in it; other kids see the playlist, click into that episode, and chat in the comments. They also posted Google Forms quizzes, writing "only cool people can fill this out." Hannah said bots don't go post Google Forms, but Gen Alpha does, the way her own generation made UQuiz or BuzzFeed personality quizzes. That was the point at which Dave was convinced.

8:06 They picked NPR because the comment section was empty
The show contacted several commenters; only one, a 14-year-old girl named Ella, agreed to be interviewed, and she did it from the car while her father drove. Ella said the core of the group is about 20 kids, many in drama club, mostly girls, with strict parents who don't let them use regular social media. They first chatted in the comment section of a podcast that played TikTok videos; after that podcast got shut down, the kids started moving from playlist to playlist. Asked why they chose NPR shows, Ella said: we look for podcasts that don't have many comments, so we don't get mixed up in other people's comments.

11:08 Dave needed a generational translator
After learning the truth, Dave said he felt guilty for reporting them, and also felt old. He said, "I literally needed Hannah to be my generational translator," and that the episode made him acutely aware of his age and how out of date he is. Ella said she's sure that one day she'll be just as lost as Dave. The show puts this segment at the top, as the entry point to the whole episode's "intergenerational space travel" theme.

25:35 The wedding toast was a poem nobody understood
At 18, Courtney read a poem she wrote at her mother's second wedding, and her mother held it against her for thirty years. The poem opens with the mother walking in habitual darkness, every breath like her last, moves to the mother standing by the counter smoking, and then turns at the end to "you found roots, you found a soul worth worshipping." The mother said that on the wedding day she only heard the negative first half and never heard the kindness at the end; rereading it, Courtney admitted that presenting a bride with that dark a picture on her wedding day would indeed make it hard to hear the good part.

31:52 The body knew the marriage was wrong first
Two days after the wedding, the 49-year-old mother had a massive stroke. Courtney offers a theory: the mother's body, not her mind, had known all along that the marriage was a mistake. The mother agreed, saying she knew when she bought the wedding dress, that she wasn't that happy then, that she "anticipated this awfulness ahead of time," sensing it in every fiber. The exchange turns all the earlier argument about the wedding toast into a question of why her mother didn't listen to her intuition back then.

39:05 Only throwing out the stepfather repaired the mother-daughter bond
Last October, the mother fell in the kitchen Mr. X designed and broke her back; Mr. X was too drunk to help and only handed her the phone hours later so she could call an ambulance herself. The mother was hospitalized for months and gave Courtney power of attorney to go to court and get Mr. X out. Courtney said it was the hardest thing she's ever done, but they won. The mother said it was precisely because Courtney spent so much time here for that, that she realized how much her daughter cared about her. Mr. X drove them apart; throwing him out pulled them back together.

55:41 The mother says braiding shouldn't be the entry to toughness
Myra Flynn locks horns with her six-year-old daughter Avalon every morning over braiding, and she blurted out "sometimes what we need isn't comfortable," then immediately realized those were her own mother's words. She called her mother, Martha Mathis, expecting support, and her mother said: braiding shouldn't be the entry point for making a kid tough, because it carries too much racial and gender meaning; and six-year-old Avalon is already the toughest little girl there is. Her mother's advice was to let Avalon handle a small section of hair herself, because "she'll be gentle with herself."

item.title: Robots Are Still at the GPT-1 Stage — the Real Signal Is Success Rate, Not Loss
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-crossing-机器人还在-gpt-1-阶段-真正的信号是成功率不是-loss/
item.description: The signal for a Scaling Law in embodied AI has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean low success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.
item.content:encoded:
The signal for a Scaling Law in embodied AI has already appeared, but we're measuring the wrong metric: low loss does not mean low success rate, and fitting the 17 steps that never touch the object is meaningless.

Xu Mengdi, assistant professor at Tsinghua's Institute for Interdisciplinary Information Sciences, on data, world models and In-Context Learning in embodied AI — the mid-to-late section on the data flywheel and the loss trap is the most valuable part.

12:15 Pretraining is not everything; adaptation is
Xu Mengdi's CMU best doctoral thesis is called Building Adaptable Generalist Robots, and its core claim is: pretraining is extremely useful, but you cannot hope a robot will succeed 100% of the time on pretraining alone. The defining feature of the open world is that tasks keep changing — at home there are 20 objects today, a week later there are 30 of different kinds, and people's preferences change too. So a robot must be able to adapt to change in its deployment environment and improve itself. She explored two paths: In-Context Learning and test-time training; the latter changes only 0.5% of the adapter parameters, but change too much and it forgets its pretrained knowledge.

19:22 Why adaptation only started to matter now
Humans generalize well for two reasons: extremely strong priors, and learning things very fast. The mainstream approach until now has been to scale data and models so that multi-task and instruction-following abilities get stronger — effectively giving the model a strong enough prior first. But Xu Mengdi points out this does not mean adaptation is unimportant — it is just that people only recently realized it. And adaptation places demands on the base model: you don't want the robot's self-learning process in a real setting to be terrifying, like smashing a cup. So starting from pretraining is reasonable.

49:46 Low loss does not mean high success rate
This is the most counterintuitive technical judgment in the whole piece. There is a very tricky point in robotics: loss is not directly tied to success rate. Loss can be very low while the final success rate is not necessarily low — there will be a lot of oscillation. Her example: a task might take 20 steps in total, and the first 17 steps involve no contact with the object at all. Even if those 17 steps fit extremely well, if the error is relatively large at step 18 when contact with the object actually happens, the task fails easily. This is an imbalance in the time sequence. So a Scaling Law that actually means something should be: as data gradually increases and the model gradually grows, success rate on unseen tasks gradually rises.

50:47 Robots are still at the GPT-1 moment
Today's mainstream embodied models are still ‘pretraining + fine-tuning on the target domain’, which can be compared to the GPT-1 stage of language models — GPT-1 itself also needed targeted post-training to solve the corresponding tasks. What Xu Mengdi really wants to achieve is the GPT-3 moment: giving the model task information through ICL, through prompting, with no fine-tuning needed, telling the model what to do purely through context. That way fine-tuning's share drops even lower, it scales more easily to more scenarios and more tasks, and ordinary people can use it too.

58:49 The data flywheel is a chicken-and-egg problem
The hardest point is whether you can give the model a stable data flywheel. That requires putting the robot into end-user homes or service scenarios, having a suitable mentor to teach it, and the robot must show obvious progress after half an hour of being taught — only then will end users be willing to use it, and only then does the data flywheel start turning. But there is a chicken-and-egg problem here: the base model needs to be good enough and learn fast enough, yet the model also needs to get into the scenario first so users start using it, in order to draw out that base capability. So whether the data flywheel can be made to work is the riskiest point of all.

1:03:52 Data is defined by working backward from model capability
Data itself gets fed to the model, but the definition of data is not conjured out of thin air — it is defined by the model's capabilities. When people define data, what they are actually doing is: figuring out what capabilities the model really needs, and working backward to how the data should be collected. If you need smoother motion, the data should be of the smooth type; if you need fail-recovery ability, the data should be collected with failures and corrections in it. And right now everyone's definition of model capability is still fairly vague, so the data requirements are vague too.

1:05:54 Each of the four data types has its own place
Xu Mengdi's position is that of a fusionist, because different data teaches the model different things. Teleoperation data is closest to the robot body itself, suited to the post-training stage, making the model more directly relevant to the target domain. Simulation data easily produces position generalization and texture generalization, making the model more robust to visual change, and suits the front end of pretraining or mid-training. UMI data sits in the middle, more like robot data but cheaper to collect. Human data is the cheapest, can be spread widely across different scenarios, and what it teaches is scenario variation and task-relevant information, less tied to the specific shape of the morphology.

1:19:02 AI-written papers are obvious at a glance
Robotics papers have been doubling recently, and Xu Mengdi's way of coping is to scroll through articles promoted by the researchers she follows, because the author list itself has already done a layer of filtering. She can clearly see that some articles have a very large AI-written component. Her judgment: AI-written articles may pass review and actually get into some conferences, but overall the quality still won't be higher than human-written ones, because they look familiar while in fact many arguments are full of holes and there isn't much content. Once she discovers a paper is AI-written, her interest in it is discounted.

item.title: The Woman Who Killed Marat, and Why the Court Wouldn't Believe She Acted Alone
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-restishistory-刺杀马拉的女人-为什么法庭不信她独自行动/
item.description: Corday had written her declaration before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her about the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that someone from the provinces would think Marat a monster.
item.content:encoded:
Corday had written her declaration before the assassination, and after her arrest she insisted she acted alone. The revolutionary tribunal kept pressing her about the "chain of conspiracy" — they could not imagine that someone from the provinces would think Marat a monster.

High information density, weaving the institutional origins of the Terror, paper-money inflation and the Vendée war into a single causal chain; the second half's assassination details are especially valuable.

0:00 The assassination declaration was written before the act
When Corday was arrested she was carrying a declaration titled "To the Friends of Law and Peace in France." In it she named Marat "the most vile scoundrel," said he "has been condemned by the universe, and therefore is outside the law," and called on the French to "rise up. Strike. Strike." This text was not a post-hoc justification; it was written before the act — what she wanted was not escape, but to turn her death into a rallying point.

9:30 Marat was the first modern populist
Keith Michael Baker's new biography positions Marat as the first modern populist. His formula included: constantly invoking the capitalized "People," claiming the people are at every moment in danger of being betrayed by appeasers and traitors; an obsession with conspiracy theories, openly stating his goal was to keep readers "perpetually alert," lest they be dragged into the abyss by royalists, priests and the like. The episode points out that this "wake up, sheep" language is used by both left and right today.

21:57 Paper-money inflation pushed the poor into the streets
In early 1793 France suffered successive poor harvests, the national grain market collapsed, and the government, lacking money for war, could only print paper money, the assignat, with about four billion in circulation. This caused severe inflation, bread and sugar prices soared, protests occurred almost daily in the markets, and women's marches appeared in the streets of Paris. The episode stresses: these were the same conditions that had originally sparked the Revolution and the storming of the Bastille, and the poor would think, "The Revolution happened, yet life hasn't improved — so someone must be scheming."

32:13 The commander's defection confirmed the conspiracy theories
On 8 March 1793 the Austrians counter-attacked, defeating Dumouriez at Neerwinden, forcing him to withdraw from Belgium and Holland. He wanted to emulate Sulla and march on Paris as a military dictator, asking his subordinates, "Shall we march on Paris?" They answered no. On 5 April he rode over to the Austrian lines, taking with him a number of senior officers, including the future King of France, Louis Philippe. A volunteer wrote to his mother: "Whom can we trust now?"

38:27 The Terror machine was improvised
The episode stresses that the key institutions of the Terror had no blueprint, no plan; they were built as they went along, only later appearing as a machine, and many who helped build it were eventually swallowed by it. On 10 March the Revolutionary Tribunal was established to try political crimes, with death sentences to be carried out within 24 hours and no right of appeal, located in the Palais de Justice in Paris, with the existing Conciergerie prison in its basement. Danton said: "Let us be terrible, so that the people need not be."

42:37 The Girondins used new rules to strike back at Marat, and it backfired
Having just abolished parliamentary immunity, the Girondins, taking advantage of the many deputies away in the provinces, indicted Marat on 14 April, accusing him of inciting insurrection. Marat hid for three days, then, finding that Parisian street opinion was on his side, turned himself in for trial. On 24 April the trial opened at the Palais de Justice; the prosecutor, Fuquietanville, was a Montagnard supporter and allowed Marat a long self-defence. The ten-man jury acquitted him within hours, and Marat was carried back to the National Convention by about 800 people, wearing a crown of roses, chanting "vive la république, vive Marat." For the Girondins it was a total humiliation.

1:04:31 Corday buys a knife: a 15 cm black-handled kitchen knife
Around eight in the morning on 13 July, Charlotte Corday left her hotel, walked to the Palais-Royal arcades, bought a newspaper (which said the Convention would likely sentence the imprisoned Girondin deputies to death), and bought a black Paris hat with a green ribbon, replacing her white Norman-style hat. She entered a cutlery shop called Le Coutelier Badin and bought a kitchen knife with a black handle and a blade about 15 cm long. Between 11:30 a.m. and noon she took a carriage to Marat's home on the rue des Cordeliers, but without an appointment she was turned away by Marat's sister-in-law.

1:10:51 The court wouldn't believe a woman could act alone
Corday was arrested on the spot; one of her interrogators was Jean-Baptiste Drouet, the postmaster who had recognised Louis XVI's flight at Varennes. From the start she said she had acted alone. But the revolutionary tribunal repeatedly interrogated her about the "chain of conspiracy," convinced she must be part of a Girondin plot. The interrogator Montané said: impossible, because you say Marat is the source of all France's ills, yet Marat is precisely the one who never stopped exposing traitors and conspirators, so someone must have lied to you. Corday replied: you are mad; only in Paris do people see Marat, in other provinces he is taken for a monster. The court could not imagine that people from the provinces would think Marat a bad man.

item.title: Intel's Optane Died Because 3D NAND Was Too Cheap, Not Because the Tech Was Bad
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-asianometry-intel-的-optane-死于-3d-nand-太便宜-不是技术不行/
item.description: Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.
item.content:encoded:
Phase-change memory was worked on from 1970 to 2022, and every time it was squeezed out by cheaper flash. 3D XPoint was stuck between NAND and DRAM, worse than both, and in the end even Intel gave up on it.

A complete failure history of a memory technology, from RMM in 1970 to the Optane shutdown in 2022. Medium information density; the back half on data-center deployment and Micron's exit is the most valuable part.

3:07 The physics of phase-change memory is what makes it slow
Phase-change memory stores data by switching a material between a crystalline and an amorphous state: the crystalline state has low resistance, the amorphous state high resistance, and the two differ by three to four orders of magnitude. Melting the material and quenching it into the amorphous state is called RESET; the reverse is called SET. SET either melts the material into a liquid and lets it cool slowly into a crystal, or heats it to a temperature high enough to convert it directly to crystalline without melting. The author points out that SET is often the speed bottleneck for PCM. This physical mechanism has not changed since Stanford Ovshinsky discovered the phase-change behavior of chalcogenide compounds in the 1960s.

4:13 Intel built phase-change memory in 1970, then forgot
In 1970, RG Neale and DL Nelson of Energy Conversion Devices and Intel's Gordon Moore published an article in Electronics magazine announcing "Read-Mostly Memory," positioned between RAM and ROM, for storing program data that is read often but changed rarely. Each cell was a silicon diode plus a layer of phase-change material; Intel supplied the silicon substrate, ECD supplied the material. But in 1970 the minimum feature size was only 10 microns, power consumption was high, SET took milliseconds, and endurance was low. DRAM capacity was growing, EPROM arrived, and RMM disappeared. Years later someone asked the 79-year-old Moore about the article, and he said he had no memory of it at all.

9:25 Numonyx treated PCM as its only shot at a comeback
The rise of NAND sent NOR flash into a long decline, and in 2007 global NOR sales fell 9% year over year. Intel merged its NOR business with STMicroelectronics' flash business, forming the Swiss company Numonyx in 2008, with an investment from Francisco Partners and a bank loan. NOR had none of NAND's growth prospects, so Numonyx could only bet on PCM — PCM combined NOR's fast random reads with NAND's high-capacity storage, and in theory could replace both. In February 2008 Intel announced delivery of its first PCM prototype, Alverstone, at 128 megabit and 90 nanometers.

13:33 Mobile PCM was swept away in one wave by 3D NAND
PCM's entry strategy was to attack the mobile market, replacing the NOR flash that stores boot code while also storing data. In 2009 Samsung announced a 512 megabit PRAM at 60 nanometers, saying that paired with DRAM it could save more than 20% of power. Micron acquired Numonyx in 2010 for about $1.2 billion in stock, and in July 2012 finally shipped 1 gigabit PCM at 45 nanometers, which Nokia put into its Asha feature phones. But in August 2013 Samsung announced mass production of 24-layer 3D NAND, and 3D NAND then set off the steepest cost-decline curve in semiconductor history, and mobile PCM's most compelling rationale was gone. In January 2014 Micron announced it was pulling out of mobile PCM.

17:38 Intel and Micron were split on Optane's positioning from the start
In July 2018 Intel and Micron agreed to a friendly split, going their separate ways after completing joint development of the second generation of 3D XPoint. The disagreement was over product direction: Intel initially aimed Optane SSDs at consumer PCs and laptops, hoping to spread wafer costs across volume; Micron wanted to go straight into the data center. Jon Carter hinted back in 2016 that consumer systems did not really need 3D XPoint's low latency, non-volatility and endurance, or at least not enough to pay four to five times the price of NAND. In October 2018 Micron announced it would pay $1.5 billion to buy Intel's half of the IM Flash plant in Utah, and Intel switched to producing it itself.

22:47 Putting Optane in the data center meant redoing motherboards and software
In April 2019 the first DIMM-form-factor Optane DC Persistent Memory went on sale, four years after 3D XPoint was announced, and it required matching Xeon processors, chipsets and motherboards. It had two modes: Memory Mode pooled Optane and DRAM into one volatile memory pool, working out of the box, but its value depended on DRAM price swings; App Direct Mode was the genuinely valuable mode, letting software write persistent data into Optane so it was still there after a reboot. Restarting an Oracle or SAP database usually takes more than an hour to reload data from SSDs or hard drives, and Optane could eliminate that. One imprecise but directionally useful test showed a 12.5x improvement. But App Direct Mode required programmers to rethink data consistency.

24:51 Only 40% of 582 proofs of concept used the mode that actually mattered
In 2020 Intel updated Optane adoption, saying there were 582 proofs of concept in the pipeline, with SAP HANA and Oracle Exadata as the main users and the rest mostly in high-performance computing, infrastructure and some AI analytics. But only 40% used the more valuable App Direct Mode. Intel said it believed the industry would eventually adopt that mode, but it might take years. In the same period Intel announced the sale of its 3D NAND business to SK hynix for $9 billion, with Optane not part of the deal — seemingly an endorsement, but it also let people infer that Optane's implied loss in 2020 was more than $500 million.

25:52 After Micron left, Optane had only a single supplier
In March 2021 Micron announced it was immediately stopping 3D XPoint development, saying the Utah plant had long suffered from underutilization and dragged $400 million a year off the company, and the plant was later sold to Texas Instruments. Micron attributed the decision to the continuing fall in 3D NAND prices and to the hard changes data centers and applications would have to make to take full advantage of the product. Micron pivoted to betting on the open-standard interface CXL, because machine-learning systems made Micron realize that not just CPUs needed more memory — GPUs and AI accelerator ASICs did too. Micron's public exit severely weakened Optane: customers could rely only on Intel as a single source, and Optane was proprietary technology. In July 2022 Intel quietly announced the shutdown of the Optane business on an earnings call.

item.title: Huawei's Ascend chose the hardest road: no compatibility with Nvidia
item.link: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.guid: https://ourword.ai/podcast/en/p/2026-09-20-touzishizhan-华为昇腾选了一条最难的路-不兼容英伟达/
item.description: For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it.
item.content:encoded:
For three or four decades Chinese IT has been a follower. Ascend is Huawei's first product that doesn't solve a chokehold problem but instead walks into uncharted territory, starting at the same time as Nvidia. Xu Zhijun said: anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it.

The first half is about how the book was written, with low information density; from the two key decisions at Ascend's founding onward, Fang Xingdong gives a lot of first-hand detail and judgment that only appears in the book.

16:10 Ascend's harshest decision was not to be compatible with Nvidia
At Ascend's founding there were two choices. The first was whether AI chips should be specialized or general-purpose; Liao Heng, as chief scientist, judged that AI should be a general-purpose product, and the architectural choice has been proven right today. The second was harder: whether to be compatible with Nvidia. Many domestic chips chose compatibility, with the benefit that Nvidia's existing ecosystem and tools could all be shared. But Xu Zhijun was firm from the start that they had to take a different path. Fang Xingdong believes this choice took enormous nerve at the time, and that many times along the way it faced huge challenges — because the entire Chinese IT industry has been a follower industry for three or four decades, and had never developed on the basis of its own root technologies.

19:11 Anything you do as a follower gets more exhausting the longer you do it
Fang Xingdong recalls having dinner with Xu Zhijun three years ago, when Xu half muttered to himself: Huawei has done this for so many years, and the discovery is that anything you do as a follower always gets more exhausting the longer you do it. There are two kinds of following. In standardized products, Chinese companies can always close the gap and even overtake — but by the time they overtake, there is no profit left in the industry, as with 2G to 5G, PCs and phones. In non-standardized products, such as routers competing with Cisco for so many years, the gap has not closed. In Xu Zhijun's eyes, what Huawei did in the past was also following. So Ascend is special among the six products: the other five solve chokehold problems, addressing survival first, while Ascend was not choked in 2019 — it is a fully proactive compute product.

29:16 With process technology choked off, only system innovation can make it back
Each generation of industry chips gains roughly 20% or more in performance, mainly from the increase in transistor count driven by advanced process improvements. Huawei lost that premise and can only gain performance through system innovation and breakthroughs — stacked compute, interconnect, higher integration. Fang Xingdong explains with a car metaphor: previously you just had to make the engine stronger and stronger, but now the engine is constrained and can no longer be enlarged, so you can only make the car run well through architecture, weight reduction and cooling. Nvidia's answer is to keep working on the engine, because TSMC can still manufacture it. In the interview Liao Heng uses the metaphor of an 18-story pagoda: many companies, because of the great division of labor, are good at only one layer, while Huawei is forced to do manufacturing, ecosystem and chip design all at once.

34:21 Huawei has to pull the domestic supply chain up with it
Previously Huawei did design, relied on the global supply chain, had TSMC manufacture, could choose the best international partners for other components, buy American products directly and assemble them, sell at a good price with a brand premium, and earn decent profit. Now it cannot cooperate with foreign partners, TSMC cannot process for it, and domestic processes are still lacking in every respect, so Huawei has no choice but to support and pull up the domestic supply chain — only then does it have a way to survive and get products manufactured. So the challenge of the past seven years is not just improving its own capabilities but also pulling the entire supply chain along — without that, independent self-reliance is impossible. Manufacturing is not Huawei's main business, but it has to help companies like SMIC and Yangtze Memory keep advancing process, yield and quality.

37:40 Ascend's significance is not that Huawei survived, but that the industry has an engine
In the past, Huawei's product launches and iterations were still based on American root technologies and the industrial ecosystem, and the high-value components of a phone were basically foreign. Now Huawei's phones, including Ascend, almost 100% pull along the domestic supply chain. Fang Xingdong believes the greatest significance of the Tao Law is not that Huawei itself can survive and be self-reliant, but that China's entire semiconductor industry and entire IT industry have their own engine, which never existed before. Huawei's rapid development represents the rapid development of the entire industrial ecosystem. He also points out that the market, reading reports, news or public opinion, has not yet realized that we are at this inflection point in the cycle — people mention Nvidia and think it is formidable, and mention Huawei and say it is policy that makes everyone use it.

45:47 It is not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve
Fang Xingdong believes that doing communications versus doing IT is essentially not a question of difficulty but of cognition and resolve — whether you dare to do it. The most typical example is the GaussDB database: among these six products Ascend stood out, and the least conspicuous is probably Gauss, but the database is a half-century-old industry with a relatively stable market, and if it really gets choked off it is deadly. At the time Huawei wanted to acquire or support a domestic vendor, but after research found that none of them were up to it; domestic companies could only grow in the cracks left by American giants, with small scale, weak R&D capability and weak product innovation. So Huawei decided to do it itself, benchmarking Oracle, and from 2011 and 2012 invested 1 billion, 2 billion, 3 billion yuan a year, without knowing whether there would be any output in the future.

1:06:04 The future is two centers, not one replacing the other
Fang Xingdong judges that the shift of global high tech from a single system centered on the US to two centers is the general trend; politics will not allow a continued single center — the US will not allow it, and China will not allow it either. He believes a single center is itself abnormal, and only two centers can create competition — only with two systems does every consumer, every company and every country, large or small, have a choice, and not be choked into a forced either-or. So the mission of Huawei's six products is to go from being the second choice to being the better choice; the relationship with Nvidia is not simple substitution but each having its strengths, complementing each other, and co-opetition. He acknowledges that the American system is currently stronger, with its advantage mainly in advanced manufacturing, and that Huawei, under process constraints, relies on the Tao Law to avoid being left behind; once advanced process technology is also broken through, it can pursue both at once.

1:19:11 The tech war won in the short term, at a greater long-term cost
Fang Xingdong believes the US did indeed suppress Huawei through the tech war, but cannot solve the problem in the long term. He reasons: without the national confrontation of 2017 and 2018, Huawei might have been at least one-third of Nvidia and one-third of Apple, and might have been China's largest company by market cap; in 2019 Huawei had already surpassed Apple, and its global shipments briefly surpassed Samsung for one quarter. Nvidia is dominant today, and if Huawei had been advancing side by side with it in AI chips from the start, Nvidia could not be in this position today. He judges that once the party being attacked builds a self-cycle that does not rely on the outside, and the other side cannot eliminate it even under the harshest conditions, it will be even harder to eliminate later; it will only grow stronger, turning a monopoly into competition between two.
